- **Access:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), surviving padrones are held at the **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock), the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain), and on microfilm at the **Library of Congress**.
- **Digitization:** No indexed online database for padrones was returned by the tools. These are predominantly physical or microfilm records.
- **The FamilySearch collection "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870"** (collection ID 2085124) covers from 1819 onward and does not reach into the pre-1800 colonial period.
- **Federal census note:** The first US federal census for the Arkansas region would be 1820 (first census after Arkansas Territory was formed in 1819). There is no federal census for this area before 1803.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concessions / mercedes de tierras) issued by the colonial government. The grants were made in arpents (a French/Spanish land measure), not the later US township-and-range survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Grants for the Arkansas Post area were made by the Spanish provincial government in New Orleans. The Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office (BLM GLO) later confirmed (or rejected) many Spanish and French land grant claims after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Types:** Land concessions (original grants), confirmations of prior grants by US authorities after 1803, and related claims files.
- **Where held:** Original Spanish land grant documents are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville and at the **Arkansas History Commission**. US-era confirmations of colonial grants are held at the **BLM General Land Office** (accessible online at glorecords.blm.gov) and at the **National Archives** (NARA).
- **Digitization:** The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) includes some confirmed Spanish and French grant patents — search there for Arkansas land patents. Physical and microfilm records predominate for original Spanish-era documents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Spanish garrison at Arkansas Post participated in Spain's involvement in the American Revolutionary War (1779-1783), including the 1783 attack on the British at Arkansas Post. Other garrison activities span 1763-1800.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, service records, officer correspondence, and supply records for the Arkansas Post garrison. These are military-administrative records of the Spanish colonial army.
- **Where held:** Spanish military records from Louisiana are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) and the **Archivo General Militar de Segovia** (Spain). Some transcriptions and translations exist at the **Louisiana State Archives** and the **Historic New Orleans Collection**, as Louisiana administered the Arkansas district. The **Arkansas History Commission** holds some local copies and transcriptions.
- **Digitization:** No indexed online database for Spanish colonial military records in Arkansas was returned by the survey tools. Physical and microfilm access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Civil cases, estate proceedings, and disputes adjudicated at the local commandant's level at Arkansas Post, with appeal to New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Local post records, to the extent they survive, are at the **Arkansas History Commission**. Higher-level Spanish judicial records are in the **Archivo General de Indias**. The **Louisiana Historical Center** in New Orleans also holds records from the Louisiana colonial period that may touch Arkansas residents.
- **Digitization:** No digitized, indexed collections for pre-1800 probate or civil court records in the Arkansas region were returned by the tools.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** The "immigration" equivalent in this period is colonial settlement — French and Spanish settlers arriving at Arkansas Post. No passenger list series of the type associated with US ports applies.
- **Relevant records:** Spanish colonial license and passport records (*pasaportes*) for individuals moving within or into Louisiana, held at the **Archivo General de Indias** and the **Louisiana Historical Center**.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable in the modern sense. Spanish colonial subjects required licenses, not naturalization papers.

### Cemetery records
- **Context:** A Catholic cemetery served Arkansas Post. Physical burial registers may survive as part of the parish records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves coverage for a colonial-era post cemetery is essentially nil for the pre-1800 period — these sites focus on modern legible headstones and later 19th-century stones. Do not rely on them for this period.
- **Physical records:** Any sexton/burial records that survive would be part of the parish register series held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** or the **Arkansas History Commission**.

### Newspaper records
- **Availability:** None. There were no newspapers in the Arkansas region before 1800. The nearest printing was in New Orleans.
- **Action:** Not applicable for this period and place.

### Tax records
- **Context:** The Spanish colonial administration collected tribute and taxes. These records, to the extent they survive for the Arkansas Post area, would be administrative records held at the **Archivo General de Indias** or the **Louisiana Historical Center**.
- **Digitization:** No indexed online collection for pre-1800 Arkansas tax records was returned by the tools.

### Other record types
- **Correspondence and administrative records:** The commandant at Arkansas Post filed regular reports to the governor in New Orleans. These can name settlers, describe disputes, and record events. Held at the **Archivo General de Indias** and the **Louisiana Historical Center**.
- **Trade and fur trade records:** Licenses for trade with Native Americans and records of merchants operating at the post may survive in colonial administrative files.
- **Slavery records:** Enslaved persons were present at Arkansas Post. Records of slave transactions, manumissions, and enslaved individuals in estate inventories may appear in colonial court and notarial records at the **Louisiana Historical Center** and the **Archivo General de Indias**.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume (image group 008814402): Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763-1800, 64 images, browse-only, in Spanish | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Confirmed land patents including some Spanish/French colonial-era grants confirmed after 1803 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | No pre-1800 Arkansas-specific indexed collection was returned by the survey tools | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** The FamilySearch `collections_search` returned 3 collections for Arkansas, none of which covers the pre-1800 period. The `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1) matching the 1700-1800 window — this appears to be the complete result set for that query. The `external_links_search` returned 6 generic links (NARA, Ancestry census collection, FindAGrave, etc.) with no Arkansas-specific pre-1800 curated collections, indicating FamilySearch has no curated third-party links specific to this locality and period beyond general-purpose repositories.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock, AR) | Surviving Spanish colonial records including padrones, transcribed church registers, land records, and other colonial documents | In-person and some online finding aids; contact ahc.arkansas.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial administrative, military, church, land, and judicial records for Louisiana including the Arkansas Post district | In-person in Seville; partial microfilm at some US repositories; Portal de Archivos Espanoles (PARES) has some digitized finding aids |
| Library of Congress (Washington, DC) | Microfilm of selected Spanish colonial records including some padrones | In-person and some digital surrogates |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original or custody copies of Arkansas Post sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Contact the diocesan archives |
| Louisiana Historical Center / Louisiana State Museum (New Orleans, LA) | Spanish Louisiana administrative records, notarial records, and colonial court records that cover the Arkansas district | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Historic New Orleans Collection (New Orleans, LA) | Colonial Louisiana documents, transcriptions, and research materials relevant to Spanish Louisiana | In-person; some digital resources at hnoc.org |
| National Archives (NARA) | Post-1803 US-era confirmations of Spanish land grants; later territorial records from 1804 onward | In-person and online (Ancestry, Fold3 for some series) |

## Records NOT online
The following record types for the pre-1800 Arkansas colonial period are not available in any indexed online database, based on this survey:
- Spanish colonial padrones (census records) for Arkansas Post
- Spanish colonial land concession originals
- Spanish colonial military muster rolls and garrison records
- Spanish colonial civil/court records for Arkansas Post
- Colonial-era trade licenses and administrative correspondence
- Slavery-related colonial notarial and court records

Only 1 digitized volume of sacramental registers was found online (FamilySearch image group 008814402), and it is browse-only with no name index.

## Known record losses
- The survival rate of colonial-era records for Arkansas Post is poor. The post changed hands multiple times (French, British briefly during the Seven Years War, Spanish, French again, then US), and records were not systematically preserved through each transition.
- Records that remained at Arkansas Post itself were vulnerable to fire, flood (the Post sat on the Arkansas River), and neglect. What survives is largely what was sent upstream to New Orleans or back to Spain.
- The FamilySearch Wiki search results note that "surviving" records are held at the Commission and the Archivo — the word "surviving" signals that losses are known and significant.
- No specific fire or flood date destroying a known set of records was returned by the tools, but incomplete survival should be assumed as the default, not the exception.

## Research tips
- **Start with Arkansas Post.** Virtually all pre-1800 European genealogical documentation for the Arkansas region originates at Arkansas Post. If your ancestor was in the Arkansas region before 1800, they were almost certainly at or near this settlement. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), this is where the surviving records are anchored.
- **Work through New Orleans.** The colonial administration ran through New Orleans. Many records that mention Arkansas Post residents — notarial acts, court appeals, land grant petitions, commercial licenses — are held at New Orleans repositories (Louisiana Historical Center, Historic New Orleans Collection) rather than in Arkansas itself.
- **Search the Archivo General de Indias via PARES.** The Spanish national digital archive portal (pares.mcu.es) provides finding aids and some digitized images from the Archivo General de Indias. Search under "Luisiana" or "Puesto de Arkansas." Original documents are in 18th-century Spanish.
- **Records are in Spanish, French, and Latin.** All pre-1800 records are in one or more of these languages. Do not attempt to read colonial sacramental registers without knowledge of 18th-century Latin abbreviations and formulaic Spanish. Hire a professional paleographer/translator if needed.
- **The padron is the key census substitute.** Spanish padrones (household censuses) are the closest equivalent to a modern census. They were taken irregularly, not on a fixed schedule. Copies may exist in multiple repositories — check the Arkansas History Commission, the Library of Congress microfilm holdings, and the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Land grant confirmations as a finding aid.** After 1803, the US Board of Land Commissioners adjudicated Spanish and French land grant claims in Louisiana (including the Arkansas district). These confirmation files, held at NARA and searchable via the BLM GLO website, often name the original colonial grantee and neighbors, giving a pre-1800 date of occupancy even though the file itself dates to after 1803.
- **Look across the Louisiana border.** The Arkansas Post district was administered from New Orleans. Families in the Arkansas region had ties across what is now the Louisiana state line. Repositories in Louisiana (Louisiana Historical Center, Tulane University Louisiana Research Collection) hold significant colonial records relevant to Arkansas settlers.
- **No adjoining county table was available.** The FamilySearch Wiki place pages for Arkansas returned only generic content rather than a county-level page with a neighboring jurisdictions table, so specific neighboring counties cannot be named from the tool results. For research near the Arkansas-Louisiana border, extend searches into the Spanish colonial records for the Natchitoches and Ouachita districts of Spanish Louisiana.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality-guide's response:

---

**Locality Guide: Ohio circa 1790 (Northwest Territory)**  
*Guide written as **loc_001***.

---

### Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 is genuinely challenging because **Ohio did not yet exist as a state in 1790**. The entire region was called the **Northwest Territory**, organized by Congress in 1787. By 1790, only two counties had been carved out of it:

- **Washington County** (est. 1788) — covered most of eastern Ohio, headquartered at Marietta
- **Hamilton County** (est. 1790) — covered the southwest, headquartered at Cincinnati

Any record from that era belongs to one of those two territorial counties — **not** to any modern Ohio county name. County boundaries changed rapidly almost every year from 1790 to 1803, so the **first step before searching any record** is always identifying which county had jurisdiction over the exact location at the exact date.

---

### Key Record Gaps

1. **No federal census for Ohio in 1790** — Ohio did not appear until the **1800 census**.
2. **No civil vital registration** — Ohio did not require the registration of births and deaths until **1867** at the county level. There are simply no government birth or death records for 1790.
3. **Virginia Military District land records** are held in **Richmond, Virginia**, not in Ohio — an easy miss for researchers expecting Ohio repositories.

---

### Records That Do Exist

Despite these gaps, several record types survive from this early period:

| Record Type | Details |
|---|---|
| **Land patents** | Early land entries under the Virginia Military District and Ohio Company grants |
| **Tax records** | Washington County tax records, 1799–1803 (partially digitized on FamilySearch) |
| **Church records** | FamilySearch's *Ohio Church Records* collection begins as early as **1787** |
| **Territorial court records** | Held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus |

---

### Recommended Next Steps

Build a research plan around the specific ancestor and location, using:
- Land patents and early land grant records
- The 1799–1803 Washington County tax records
- Church records (FamilySearch's Ohio Church Records, from 1787)
- The **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus — the central physical repository for early territorial court and land records

args.query: Ohio Territory genealogy records pre-statehood 1787 1803
Northwest Territory Ohio history 1787 1803 statehood boundary changes

quirks: Before 1803, Ohio was part of the Northwest Territory — all civil authority was territorial, not state. Records created before statehood are filed under the territorial county that had jurisdiction (Washington County from 1788, Hamilton County from 1790), not under any modern Ohio county.

Washington County (1788) was the first county organized and covered most of what is now eastern Ohio; Hamilton County (1790) covered the southwest. All county-level records before 1803 fall under one of these two territorial counties — identify which one held jurisdiction at the event date before searching.

The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) used a metes-and-bounds survey system separate from the federal rectangular survey; Virginia Military District land-grant warrants are held at the Virginia State Library, not Ohio repositories.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Pre-Statehood Northwest Territory) (1787-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, encompassing present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Washington County was the first county organized within the territory in 1788. Hamilton County followed in 1790. Ohio achieved statehood on March 1, 1803, as the first state carved from the Northwest Territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County seat); Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787-1803); thereafter Ohio, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data for this territory in the 1780s-1803 period was not returned by the place_population tool. The 1800 federal census is the first enumeration capturing a meaningful Ohio population.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, land speculation. The Virginia Military District and Connecticut Western Reserve attracted waves of land-grant claimants and settlers from Virginia and Connecticut respectively.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, and New England. Native American peoples — including the Shawnee, Delaware (Lenape), Wyandot, and Miami — occupied much of the territory until military defeat and treaty cessions in the 1790s.
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker congregations were among the earliest established. Catholic missions had limited presence. Church infrastructure was sparse in 1790; circuit-riding ministers served wide areas.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); founding of Marietta (1788); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and Treaty of Greenville (1795), which opened most of Ohio to settlement; Jay Treaty (1795); Ohio statehood (March 1, 1803).

## Boundary changes
- **1787:** Northwest Territory established — the entire region falls under a single territorial government with no county subdivisions.
- **1788:** Washington County organized — covers most of the territory east of the Scioto River.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covers the southwestern portion of the territory.
- **1796-1802:** Rapid county subdivision as population grows; additional counties (Ross, Trumbull, Adams, Clermont, Fairfield, Columbiana, and others) are carved out. A researcher must determine which county had jurisdiction over the specific location at the date of the event — the answer changes year by year in this period.
- **1803:** Ohio statehood. All territorial county records continue in the successor county courthouses; no records transferred to a state archive at statehood.
- **Critical rule:** A record from 1790 Ohio is a record from the Northwest Territory. Search under the territorial county name (Washington or Hamilton), not the modern Ohio county name. The Ohio History Connection in Columbus holds the primary collection of early territorial and county court and land records. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory])

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki specific page for Ohio Vital Records did not return Ohio-specific content in this survey. Based on the generic wiki page returned, Ohio did not have statewide civil vital registration during the 1787-1803 period. County-level vital registration did not begin in Ohio until 1867; statewide registration began in 1908. No civil birth, marriage, or death records were required at the county or territorial level in 1790.
- **What exists for 1787-1803:** County marriage records begin as early as 1789 in some counties — FamilySearch holds "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (collection 1803785; 1,523,678 records, 761,839 images, indexed + images). This is the one civil vital-record series that exists for the period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785); county courthouses; Ohio History Connection.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration existed in Ohio in 1790. Church records are the only alternative for these events.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial records; Bible records; cemetery inscriptions.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker (Society of Friends), and Catholic congregations were active in Ohio from the late 1780s onward, though organized congregations were sparse before 1795.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (used as birth surrogates), marriages, burials, and membership rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (collection 2246917; 678,234 records, 339,117 images, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). Denominational archives (Presbyterian: Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia; Methodist: United Methodist Archives Center, Madison, NJ; Quaker: Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore) hold originals or transcriptions not on FamilySearch.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Given the near-total absence of civil vital records for the 1787-1803 period, church records are the primary — and often only — source for birth and death events. Circuit-riding ministers served multiple settlements and did not always keep consistent registers. Gaps are common.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census (1790) did not include the Northwest Territory; Ohio appears for the first time in the 1800 census. The 1800 census is therefore the earliest federal enumeration covering settlers in what is now Ohio.
- **Territorial/special enumerations:** No territorial census equivalent to a state census was conducted in the Northwest Territory before 1803. Militia musters and tax lists (see below) are the closest substitutes.
- **Access:** 1800 Ohio federal census — indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, court minutes. Territorial courts (Court of Common Pleas and the Territorial Supreme Court) exercised jurisdiction.
- **Date range:** Washington County court records begin 1788; Hamilton County begin 1790.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection, Columbus (https://www.ohiohistory.org/); individual county probate courts. Early volumes have been microfilmed and some are accessible at FamilySearch.
- **Digitization level:** Not returned as a named indexed collection in FamilySearch collections_search for the 1787-1803 window. Likely microfilm or physical only for the earliest volumes — contact Ohio History Connection directly.

### Land records
- **Survey systems:** Ohio was a federal land state, but three distinct survey systems operated in different zones:
  - **Seven Ranges / Congress Lands:** Federal rectangular survey, first surveys 1785-1787 in eastern Ohio.
  - **Virginia Military District:** Metes-and-bounds system between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers; reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Land-grant warrants are at the Virginia State Library, Richmond — not at Ohio repositories. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records])
  - **Connecticut Western Reserve:** Northeastern Ohio; surveyed on a township-range grid by the Connecticut Land Company. Records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records])
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (Bureau of Land Management General Land Office) for Congress Lands; Virginia for the Military District; Connecticut Land Company for the Western Reserve.
- **Types:** Land patents, warrants, deeds, tax records.
- **Date range:** Earliest patents from 1787. FamilySearch holds "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (collection 1542187; 234,567 records, 117,283 images, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187). BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) has federal patents.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (free, online); Virginia State Library (Virginia Military District warrants); Western Reserve Historical Society (Connecticut Western Reserve); Ohio History Connection and county recorder offices.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War / Ohio Indian Wars (1785-1795), culminating at Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794). Frontier militia service was widespread in 1790.
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls (territorial militia, 1788-1803); service records for the U.S. Army (Legion of the United States); pension files (for surviving veterans who later applied); bounty land warrants (Revolutionary War era, redeemed in Virginia Military District).
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files — available on Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ by subscription); Ohio History Connection (territorial militia records); Virginia State Library (Virginia Military District bounty warrants).
- **Digitization level:** NARA pension files are indexed + images on Fold3 and Ancestry. Militia muster rolls are largely physical or microfilm.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer/settler cemeteries throughout Washington and Hamilton counties from the late 1780s onward; many are small family plots that have not been formally indexed.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Ohio pioneer cemeteries, though early 1790s burials are sparsely represented.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely exist for 1790-era burials; headstone photographs and local transcriptions are the most common source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in the Northwest Territory was the Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, 1793). The Ohio Gazette (Marietta) began in 1801.
- **Where held:** Ohio Memory (https://www.ohiomemory.org/) holds digitized Ohio newspapers; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Ohio papers. Coverage for 1790-1803 is sparse — these papers are not fully digitized.
- **Content value:** Notices of land sales, court proceedings, and arrival of settlers; obituaries are uncommon in this early period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Ohio settlers in 1790 arrived overland from Pennsylvania, Virginia, or Kentucky — not through a port. No ocean-crossing immigration records apply to the majority of the 1790 Ohio population.
- **Record types for inland migration:** Pennsylvania and Virginia court records (where families originated); tavern licenses and road records; pension affidavits (which often describe migration routes). Naturalization declarations were filed in territorial and county courts for foreign-born settlers.
- **Where held:** NARA (naturalizations post-1906); county courts and Ohio History Connection (pre-1906 naturalizations in territorial court records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard an arriving vessel, including infants and children. When researching a family that immigrated before settling in Ohio, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Real property tax and personal property lists — the primary annual enumeration of heads of household in the pre-census territorial period.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch holds "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (collection 1987542; 345,890 records, 172,945 images, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542). Tax lists predate this — Washington County tax records 1799-1803 appear as a partially-indexed digitized volume in volume_search (DGS 005112240; 73 images, 12% name-indexed).
- **Where held:** County auditor offices; Ohio History Connection; FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for missing census coverage in the 1790-1800 gap. A man appearing on the 1800 tax list but absent from the 1800 census may still be locatable.

### Other record types
- **Territorial government records:** Acts of the Northwest Territory governor and territorial legislature, land cessions and treaties, and survey records — held at Ohio History Connection and NARA (Record Group 59, Territorial Papers).
- **Local histories and county histories:** Published in the 19th century, many Ohio county histories reprint early settler lists, court records, and biographical sketches drawn from records since lost. The Ohio History Connection library and WorldCat hold these.
- **Quaker meeting records:** The Society of Friends kept meticulous records of births, deaths, marriages, removals, and disownments. Significant Quaker settlement in eastern and southwestern Ohio from the early 1800s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); 2 digitized volumes (territorial land records; Washington County tax records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1800+); military pension files | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records (NARA originals) | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Ohio newspapers (sparse for 1790-1803) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Territorial Papers (RG 59); military records | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for the 1780-1810 window, and the tool confirmed this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2, no nextPageToken).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial and early county court records, land records, local histories, microfilm collection | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| County probate courts (Washington, Hamilton, and successors) | Deeds, wills, estate files, court minutes from county formation date | In-person or written request |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA | Virginia Military District land-grant warrants and patents | In-person or written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland, OH | Connecticut Western Reserve land and settlement records | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, DC / Chicago region) | Territorial Papers (RG 59); military pension and service records | In-person; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian congregation records | In-person or written request |
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore, PA | Quaker meeting records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes and plat books (pre-1800) are largely physical or microfilm only at Ohio History Connection.
- Militia muster rolls for the Northwest Indian War period (1788-1795) are mostly physical at Ohio History Connection and NARA.
- Virginia Military District original warrant files are at the Virginia State Library, not digitized or online.
- Connecticut Western Reserve settlement and proprietors' records at the Western Reserve Historical Society are not fully digitized.
- Most early church registers (1787-1800) are not fully indexed online — the FamilySearch Church Records collection (1787-1950) covers part of this gap but not all congregations.

## Known record losses
- Civil infrastructure was minimal in 1790; many events simply went unrecorded. No courthouse fire is the primary culprit here — the main gap is structural: most record-keeping systems (civil vital registration, probate courts, deed books) did not exist or had only just been established by 1790.
- Some early territorial court records are fragmentary because clerks were not always consistent in the early years of county organization.
- No statewide vital registration before 1867 (county level) means births and deaths from 1790 are entirely undocumented in civil records. Church records and Bible entries are the only substitutes.

## Research tips
- **Identify the county first.** Before searching any Ohio record, determine which county — Washington or Hamilton — had jurisdiction over the specific location in the specific year. County boundaries changed rapidly between 1788 and 1803. A map of Northwest Territory county formation by year is essential. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory])
- **Land records as a proxy for presence.** In the absence of a 1790 federal census for Ohio and without civil vital records, land patents, deed records, and tax lists are the most reliable means of placing an ancestor in a specific Ohio location in 1790.
- **Virginia Military District search strategy.** If the ancestor claimed land in the Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers), the warrant files are in Richmond, Virginia — not Ohio. Search the Virginia State Library in addition to Ohio repositories.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve strategy.** For northeastern Ohio ancestors, the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland holds land company records that name early settlers even before county organization.
- **Use the 1800 census and work backward.** The 1800 federal census (indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch) is the first enumeration of Ohio. If an ancestor appears there, the household composition can help reconstruct an approximate 1790 family structure.
- **Tax list as the 1790-1800 substitute.** Washington County tax records 1799-1803 are partially digitized on FamilySearch (DGS 005112240, 12% name-indexed, browse-only for the unindexed portion). For earlier years, contact Ohio History Connection for pre-1799 territorial tax lists.
- **Church records are the primary vital-event source.** No civil births or deaths were recorded in Ohio in 1790. Locate the denomination of the ancestor's family and contact the relevant denominational archive in addition to checking FamilySearch's Ohio Church Records collection (1787-1950, collection 2246917).
- **Territorial Papers at NARA.** NARA Record Group 59 (Territorial Papers, Northwest Territory) contains governor's correspondence, legislative proceedings, and land and judicial records for the pre-statehood period — not yet fully digitized but microfilmed.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** In 1790 the Ohio River formed the southern border. Families in southwestern Ohio had frequent dealings across the river in Kentucky (Jefferson and Mason counties). Kentucky deed and court records from this period may name Ohio settlers. Similarly, eastern Ohio settlers traveled through western Pennsylvania (Washington and Allegheny counties). The FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool did not return a neighboring-counties table for Ohio in this survey run, but these cross-border adjacencies are well-documented.
- **The FamilySearch wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned only generic content in this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for Ohio-specific guidance.**

- **Record types for inland migration:** Pennsylvania and Virginia court records (where families originated); tavern licenses and road records; pension affidavits (which often describe migration routes). Naturalization declarations were filed in territorial and county courts for foreign-born settlers.
- **Where held:** NARA (naturalizations post-1906); county courts and Ohio History Connection (pre-1906 naturalizations in territorial court records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard an arriving vessel, including infants and children. When researching a family that immigrated before settling in Ohio, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Real property tax and personal property lists — the primary annual enumeration of heads of household in the pre-census territorial period.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch holds "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (collection 1987542; 345,890 records, 172,945 images, indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542). Tax lists predate this — Washington County tax records 1799-1803 appear as a partially-indexed digitized volume in volume_search (DGS 005112240; 73 images, 12% name-indexed).
- **Where held:** County auditor offices; Ohio History Connection; FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for missing census coverage in the 1790-1800 gap. A man appearing on the 1800 tax list but absent from the 1800 census may still be locatable.

### Other record types
- **Territorial government records:** Acts of the Northwest Territory governor and territorial legislature, land cessions and treaties, and survey records — held at Ohio History Connection and NARA (Record Group 59, Territorial Papers).
- **Local histories and county histories:** Published in the 19th century, many Ohio county histories reprint early settler lists, court records, and biographical sketches drawn from records since lost. The Ohio History Connection library and WorldCat hold these.
- **Quaker meeting records:** The Society of Friends kept meticulous records of births, deaths, marriages, removals, and disownments. Significant Quaker settlement in eastern and southwestern Ohio from the early 1800s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); 2 digitized volumes (territorial land records; Washington County tax records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1800+); military pension files | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records (NARA originals) | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Ohio newspapers (sparse for 1790-1803) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Territorial Papers (RG 59); military records | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for the 1780-1810 window, and the tool confirmed this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2, no nextPageToken).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial and early county court records, land records, local histories, microfilm collection | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| County probate courts (Washington, Hamilton, and successors) | Deeds, wills, estate files, court minutes from county formation date | In-person or written request |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA | Virginia Military District land-grant warrants and patents | In-person or written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland, OH | Connecticut Western Reserve land and settlement records | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, DC / Chicago region) | Territorial Papers (RG 59); military pension and service records | In-person; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian congregation records | In-person or written request |
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore, PA | Quaker meeting records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes and plat books (pre-1800) are largely physical or microfilm only at Ohio History Connection.
- Militia muster rolls for the Northwest Indian War period (1788-1795) are mostly physical at Ohio History Connection and NARA.
- Virginia Military District original warrant files are at the Virginia State Library, not digitized or online.
- Connecticut Western Reserve settlement and proprietors' records at the Western Reserve Historical Society are not fully digitized.
- Most early church registers (1787-1800) are not fully indexed online — the FamilySearch Church Records collection (1787-1950) covers part of this gap but not all congregations.

## Known record losses
- Civil infrastructure was minimal in 1790; many events simply went unrecorded. No courthouse fire is the primary culprit here — the main gap is structural: most record-keeping systems (civil vital registration, probate courts, deed books) did not exist or had only just been established by 1790.
- Some early territorial court records are fragmentary because clerks were not always consistent in the early years of county organization.
- No statewide vital registration before 1867 (county level) means births and deaths from 1790 are entirely undocumented in civil records. Church records and Bible entries are the only substitutes.

## Research tips
- **Identify the county first.** Before searching any Ohio record, determine which county — Washington or Hamilton — had jurisdiction over the specific location in the specific year. County boundaries changed rapidly between 1788 and 1803. A map of Northwest Territory county formation by year is essential. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory])
- **Land records as a proxy for presence.** In the absence of a 1790 federal census for Ohio and without civil vital records, land patents, deed records, and tax lists are the most reliable means of placing an ancestor in a specific Ohio location in 1790.
- **Virginia Military District search strategy.** If the ancestor claimed land in the Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers), the warrant files are in Richmond, Virginia — not Ohio. Search the Virginia State Library in addition to Ohio repositories.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve strategy.** For northeastern Ohio ancestors, the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland holds land company records that name early settlers even before county organization.
- **Use the 1800 census and work backward.** The 1800 federal census (indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch) is the first enumeration of Ohio. If an ancestor appears there, the household composition can help reconstruct an approximate 1790 family structure.
- **Tax list as the 1790-1800 substitute.** Washington County tax records 1799-1803 are partially digitized on FamilySearch (DGS 005112240, 12% name-indexed, browse-only for the unindexed portion). For earlier years, contact Ohio History Connection for pre-1799 territorial tax lists.
- **Church records are the primary vital-event source.** No civil births or deaths were recorded in Ohio in 1790. Locate the denomination of the ancestor's family and contact the relevant denominational archive in addition to checking FamilySearch's Ohio Church Records collection (1787-1950, collection 2246917).
- **Territorial Papers at NARA.** NARA Record Group 59 (Territorial Papers, Northwest Territory) contains governor's correspondence, legislative proceedings, and land and judicial records for the pre-statehood period — not yet fully digitized but microfilmed.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** In 1790 the Ohio River formed the southern border. Families in southwestern Ohio had frequent dealings across the river in Kentucky (Jefferson and Mason counties). Kentucky deed and court records from this period may name Ohio settlers. Similarly, eastern Ohio settlers traveled through western Pennsylvania (Washington and Allegheny counties). The FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool did not return a neighboring-counties table for Ohio in this survey run, but these cross-border adjacencies are well-documented.
- **The FamilySearch wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned only generic content in this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for Ohio-specific guidance.**

output.text_response:
Here is the locality-guide agent's response:

---

This survey covers California during the Gold Rush and early post-Rush years (roughly 1848 to 1870). The state entered the union in 1850 with no prior territorial records, so all county and state record series begin at statehood.

**Key points for tracing California Gold Rush migrants:**

- **Civil registration** of births and marriages began at the county level in 1850, but was inconsistently practiced throughout the 1850s. Statewide mandatory registration came much later — meaning church records, the **1852 California state census**, and cemetery records are often the only surviving documentation of vital events for miners who arrived in those years.

- **Sea passengers** can sometimes be traced through **ship passenger manifests** held at the **National Archives Pacific Region** in San Bruno, California. Those who came overland left no equivalent manifest — the **1852 state census** is the best substitute for them.

- **Two critical warnings:**
  1. The **1850 federal census is partially destroyed** for California, so begin with the 1852 state census instead.
  2. The **1906 San Francisco earthquake** destroyed large portions of San Francisco County's early records, creating a significant gap for anyone connected to that city.

The locality guide has been saved to this project (as `loc_001`). The logical next step is to narrow to whichever specific California county your ancestor is connected to, so a more targeted research plan can be built around that county's own records and surviving repositories.

quirks: California became a state in 1850, bypassing territorial status; all county-level and state-level records begin at or after statehood.
The 1850 federal census (the first for California) is partially destroyed — some county returns are missing; supplement with the 1852 California state census.

No statewide civil registration of vital events existed during the 1850s; county-level birth and marriage registration began in 1850 but was inconsistently observed; statewide mandatory registration did not follow until much later. Rely on church records, cemetery records, and the 1852 state census to fill gaps.

The California Great Registers (voter registration) begin in 1866, not during the Gold Rush decade, but are a critical substitute for tracing men who arrived in the 1850s and remained into the 1860s–1870s.

Mining claim records are county-level, held at county recorders' offices; the FamilySearch volume (DGS 006601002) covering San Francisco 1849–1855 is browse-only with 0% name indexing — must be browsed image by image.
Port arrival registers for Sacramento (DGS 006601003, 1849–1858) are likewise browse-only and not full-text searchable.
Many '49ers arrived by sea through San Francisco; ship passenger manifests for that port are held at the National Archives, Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA).
Many arrivals came overland via the California Trail or the Santa Fe Trail; no single manifest captures them — diaries, trail records, and the 1852 state census are the best substitutes.
California was a federal-land state; land grants and patents are recorded with the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) and predate county deed books for the original grants.
Pre-American-period mission records (1769–1834) and Mexican-era land grants exist but cover a largely different, indigenous and Californio, population from the Gold Rush migrants.
The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections not available digitally.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California achieved statehood on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal public-land state).
- **Population during period:** Approximately 93,000 at the 1850 census, rising to 380,000 by 1860 and 560,000 by 1870. The Gold Rush (1848–1855) brought an estimated 300,000 migrants from the rest of the United States and abroad, per Wikipedia's California Gold Rush article.
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining dominated 1848–1855; by the late 1850s, agriculture, cattle ranching, commerce (San Francisco), and railroad construction became co-dominant.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American (especially from Missouri, Arkansas, and the Eastern Seaboard); Irish, Chinese, Chilean, Mexican (Californio), Peruvian, Australian, French, German, and other international immigrants. The population was predominantly male and transient in the rush years.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (carrying over from the Spanish mission period); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Episcopal churches founded rapidly after statehood. Catholic parishes are the best-documented early church record-keepers in California.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood, September 9, 1850; completion of the transcontinental railroad, 1869.

- **Search the Great Registers (1866–1910)** for men who came during the Rush and stayed. These voter registration records give name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description — often more detail than a census entry (FamilySearch collection 1923340, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340).
- **Mining claim registers are browse-only.** The San Francisco Mining Claim Registers volume (DGS 006601002) must be examined image by image with no name index and no full-text search. Plan time accordingly.
- **Port arrival registers are browse-only.** The Sacramento Port Arrival Registers volume (DGS 006601003) is likewise 0% indexed — browse page by page.
- **The Foreign Miners' Tax** (collected 1850 and 1852) is a high-value source uniquely naming immigrant miners by county. These records are physical only at county archives; they are not yet digitized.
- **Determine the county at the time of the event** before searching. Gold Rush counties were created rapidly and boundaries changed frequently in the 1850s. A miner in the southern Mother Lode in 1851 might be in a different county than the same location in 1855.
- **Search sea routes and overland trails separately.** Sea arrivals have manifests at NARA San Bruno; overland arrivals have no equivalent record — the 1852 state census and Bancroft Library trail diaries are the best substitutes.
- **The Bancroft Library and California State Library** hold manuscript collections unavailable anywhere else online — letters, diaries, mining company records, and biographical files from the Gold Rush era. Both institutions accept written inquiries.
- **Alta California newspaper** (San Francisco, 1849 onward) regularly published ship arrival lists and mining news naming individuals — check the California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu, free) before paying for a subscription service.
- **County and state histories** published in the 1880s–1890s contain biographical sketches of surviving '49ers. Many are freely digitized at the Internet Archive (archive.org). These often provide the only surviving narrative of a miner's origins, route, and activities.
- **Naturalization records before 1906** can appear in any court — county, district, or state — so search all courts in the county of residence, not just one.

**Locality Guide: New York City (Manhattan/New York County), 1700s Colonial Period**

Because there was **no civil government registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during this century, **church registers are the essential starting point**:

- **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest continuous series, beginning 1639
- **Trinity Church (Anglican)** — founded 1696
- **Presbyterian, Lutheran, Huguenot, Quaker, and Jewish congregations** — each kept their own registers

**Online / Digitized Resources:**
- One FamilySearch digitized volume exists specifically for this period: a **Dutch Reformed Church Register (1700–1776)** — browsed image by image (no name index), written entirely in Dutch
- FamilySearch state-level New York collections (church records, land, probate — beginning 1630s–1640s) overlap the entire century

**Physical Repositories to Consult:**
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | Colonial-era government and court records |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | City administrative records |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Manuscripts, church records, family papers |
| **New York Genealogical and Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Compiled records, published abstracts |

**Key Cautions:**
1. Many colonial-era records survive **only in physical repositories** or on microfilm not yet digitized.
2. **Dutch language skills** (or a translator) are needed for the oldest church registers.
3. Neighboring counties — **Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester** — were entirely separate jurisdictions; their records must be searched independently for families with cross-county ties.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established by the Dutch West India Company, 1626; seized by the English and renamed New York, 1664; remained an English/British colonial city until 1783.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City was itself the seat of New York County (Manhattan), and also the provincial capital of the Colony of New York.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New York (British Crown, 1664-1783); Province of New York.
- **Population during period:** No tool returned specific population figures for this period. Wikipedia notes New York City was a major commercial port and administrative center during the 1700s, with a population that grew substantially across the century.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, commerce, artisan crafts, merchant activity, and a substantial enslaved workforce. The city was the primary port of entry for goods and people along the northeastern seaboard.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch-descended families from the earlier colonial period, alongside English settlers following the 1664 takeover, and smaller communities of French Huguenots, Germans, Jews, and enslaved Africans.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (the oldest continuous congregation), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1696), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Quaker, and Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel, founded 1654).
- **Key historical events:** English seizure from the Dutch (1664); the city's role as a commercial hub throughout the 18th century; British occupation during the Seven Years' War period and again during the American Revolution (1776-1783); the city serving briefly as the first U.S. capital (1789-1790).

## Boundary changes
- The territory of New York City in the 1700s corresponded to Manhattan Island (New York County). The modern five-borough city did not exist — Kings County (Brooklyn), Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and the Bronx were entirely separate jurisdictions.
- There were no significant internal boundary changes to New York County/Manhattan during the 1700s.
- Records predating 1664 were created under Dutch colonial authority; after 1664, English and then British colonial administration took over, but Dutch Reformed Church records continued uninterrupted through both regimes.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic content in this session; the specific start date for any local or state system is not confirmed from the pages retrieved. Church registers are the sole primary vital record source for the entire colonial period.
- **What exists:** No government-issued birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1700s.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil registration; see Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The entire colonial century is a civil registration gap.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the functional equivalent of vital records for this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers begin 1639, continuous through the 1700s); Anglican/Church of England — Trinity Church (founded 1696); Presbyterian; Lutheran; French Reformed (Huguenot); Quaker; Jewish (Shearith Israel).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Some congregations also kept membership rolls and poor-relief lists.
- **FamilySearch collection:** New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (collection 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers 1640-1940 with 2,345,678 indexed records and images.
- **Digitized volume (browse-only):** One digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers covering 1700-1776 was found in volume_search (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images). It has 0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image.
- **Language:** The Dutch Reformed registers through at least the mid-18th century are in Dutch. The researcher must be able to read Dutch, or use a translator, to use these records.
- **Where held:** Original registers held variously by the individual congregations, the Reformed Church in America archives (New Brunswick Theological Seminary, New Jersey), the New-York Historical Society, and the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society. Trinity Church (Episcopal) maintains its own archive.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal decennial census is 1790, which falls at the very end of the colonial period. No federal enumeration covers 1700-1789.
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** The Colony of New York conducted irregular censuses and head-counts; these are held at the New York State Archives in Albany. The FamilySearch Wiki Census page returned only generic content in this session — specific years are not confirmed from the retrieved pages.
- **Substitutes:** Militia rolls and tax assessment lists are the closest functional equivalents to a census for locating individuals before 1790. The FamilySearch wiki search result notes that colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls listing men of military age, and that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. The relevant court was the Prerogative Court of New York (colonial-era), which had province-wide jurisdiction over wills.
- **Index:** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society — search this index before pulling original files.
- **FamilySearch collection:** New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (collection 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780), covering 1629-1971 with 987,654 records and images.
- **Court records:** The Mayor's Court handled civil and criminal cases; its records are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New-York Historical Society. Colonial-era court minutes are held at the New York State Archives.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany) for colonial Prerogative Court records; New York City Municipal Archives for city/county court records; New-York Historical Society for manuscript collections.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used English common-law conveyancing; the rectangular survey system was not used here).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants and patents in colonial New York were issued by the English/British Crown through the colonial governor. The New York State Archives holds the colonial land patent series. The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page returned only generic content in this session; specific series names are not confirmed from the retrieved pages beyond what the wiki_search result stated.
- **Types:** Deeds, conveyances, land grants, patents, and mortgages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (collection 2078654, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654), covering 1630-1975 with 1,567,890 records and images.
- **Where held:** New York County (Manhattan) deed books are held at the New York City Register's Office; colonial-era patents and grants at the New York State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King William's War (1689-1697), Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), the French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754-1763), and the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (list men of military age, useful for identifying residents), muster rolls, and pension records for Revolutionary War veterans.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives holds colonial militia records. Revolutionary War service and pension records are at NARA and available on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/). The New-York Historical Society also holds manuscript military collections.
- **Substitute use:** Militia rolls serve as a partial census substitute for the colonial period.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Churchyard (Anglican, one of the oldest surviving burial grounds in the city, records from the late 1600s); Dutch Reformed church burial grounds; Congregation Shearith Israel (the oldest Jewish congregation in North America, with a colonial-era burial ground).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage of many New York City historic cemeteries, but colonial-era stone survival and transcription is incomplete.
- **Physical records:** Trinity Church maintains its own burial register. The New York City Municipal Archives and the New-York Historical Society hold additional burial records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New-York Gazette (founded 1725, the first newspaper in New York) and the New-York Weekly Journal (founded 1733) are the primary colonial-era papers. Wikipedia confirms these existed. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized historical newspapers but colonial-era New York coverage is incomplete.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, estate and property notices, ship arrivals.
- **Where held:** The New-York Historical Society and the New York Public Library hold original runs on microfilm.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City was itself the primary port of entry for the northeastern colonies. Arrivals were recorded through various colonial-era mechanisms.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists, port arrival records, naturalization records (sworn in colonial courts), and British colonial alien registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds pre-federal passenger lists where they survive. The New York Genealogical and Biographical Society has compiled indexes. FamilySearch has digitized some colonial passenger list collections.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family group.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established by the Dutch West India Company, 1626; seized by the English and renamed New York, 1664; remained an English/British colonial city until 1783.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City was itself the seat of New York County (Manhattan), and also the provincial capital of the Colony of New York.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New York (British Crown, 1664-1783); Province of New York.
- **Population during period:** No tool returned specific population figures for this period. Wikipedia notes New York City was a major commercial port and administrative center during the 1700s, with a population that grew substantially across the century.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, commerce, artisan crafts, merchant activity, and a substantial enslaved workforce. The city was the primary port of entry for goods and people along the northeastern seaboard.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch-descended families from the earlier colonial period, alongside English settlers following the 1664 takeover, and smaller communities of French Huguenots, Germans, Jews, and enslaved Africans.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (the oldest continuous congregation), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1696), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Quaker, and Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel, founded 1654).
- **Key historical events:** English seizure from the Dutch (1664); the city's role as a commercial hub throughout the 18th century; British occupation during the Seven Years' War period and again during the American Revolution (1776-1783); the city serving briefly as the first U.S. capital (1789-1790).

## Boundary changes
- The territory of New York City in the 1700s corresponded to Manhattan Island (New York County). The modern five-borough city did not exist — Kings County (Brooklyn), Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and the Bronx were entirely separate jurisdictions.
- There were no significant internal boundary changes to New York County/Manhattan during the 1700s.
- Records predating 1664 were created under Dutch colonial authority; after 1664, English and then British colonial administration took over, but Dutch Reformed Church records continued uninterrupted through both regimes.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic content in this session; the specific start date for any local or state system is not confirmed from the pages retrieved. Church registers are the sole primary vital record source for the entire colonial period.
- **What exists:** No government-issued birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1700s.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil registration; see Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The entire colonial century is a civil registration gap.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the functional equivalent of vital records for this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers begin 1639, continuous through the 1700s); Anglican/Church of England — Trinity Church (founded 1696); Presbyterian; Lutheran; French Reformed (Huguenot); Quaker; Jewish (Shearith Israel).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Some congregations also kept membership rolls and poor-relief lists.
- **FamilySearch collection:** New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (collection 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers 1640-1940 with 2,345,678 indexed records and images.
- **Digitized volume (browse-only):** One digitized volume of Dutch Reformed Church Registers covering 1700-1776 was found in volume_search (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images). It has 0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image.
- **Language:** The Dutch Reformed registers through at least the mid-18th century are in Dutch. The researcher must be able to read Dutch, or use a translator, to use these records.
- **Where held:** Original registers held variously by the individual congregations, the Reformed Church in America archives (New Brunswick Theological Seminary, New Jersey), the New-York Historical Society, and the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society. Trinity Church (Episcopal) maintains its own archive.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal decennial census is 1790, which falls at the very end of the colonial period. No federal enumeration covers 1700-1789.
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** The Colony of New York conducted irregular censuses and head-counts; these are held at the New York State Archives in Albany. The FamilySearch Wiki Census page returned only generic content in this session — specific years are not confirmed from the retrieved pages.
- **Substitutes:** Militia rolls and tax assessment lists are the closest functional equivalents to a census for locating individuals before 1790. The FamilySearch wiki search result notes that colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls listing men of military age, and that tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. The relevant court was the Prerogative Court of New York (colonial-era), which had province-wide jurisdiction over wills.
- **Index:** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society — search this index before pulling original files.
- **FamilySearch collection:** New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (collection 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780), covering 1629-1971 with 987,654 records and images.
- **Court records:** The Mayor's Court handled civil and criminal cases; its records are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New-York Historical Society. Colonial-era court minutes are held at the New York State Archives.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany) for colonial Prerogative Court records; New York City Municipal Archives for city/county court records; New-York Historical Society for manuscript collections.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used English common-law conveyancing; the rectangular survey system was not used here).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New-York Gazette (founded 1725, the first newspaper in New York) and the New-York Weekly Journal (founded 1733) are the primary colonial-era papers. **Locality Guide: Virginia During the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)**

*Guide written as **loc_001** in your project.*

---

Here is a summary of the key records and repositories for tracing Virginia families connected to military service or wartime activities during 1775–1783:

---

### Important Context

Virginia did not have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during this era. Records were kept at the **county level**, and since Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814, researchers rely heavily on substitute sources.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

#### 1. **Military Pension Files — National Archives (NARA)**
The single most valuable source for Revolutionary War service. Pension applications often contain detailed family information, sworn depositions, and widow's claims. Held at NARA in Washington, D.C., and widely available on **Fold3** and **Ancestry**.

#### 2. **Revolutionary War Land Bounty Warrants**
Virginia granted land bounties to veterans. These files are held by the **Library of Virginia (LVA)** in Richmond and are available as browse-only digitized images on FamilySearch (must be examined image by image, as they are not name-indexed).

#### 3. **County Court Order Books & Deed Books**
Held at individual county courthouses and at the **Library of Virginia**. These record property transactions, estate settlements, and local civil matters during wartime. Augusta County court order books are partially indexed (61%) on FamilySearch.

#### 4. **County Personal Property Tax Lists & Land Tax Lists**
Beginning in **1782**, Virginia required annual personal property and land tax assessments. These lists are an essential substitute for the destroyed 1790 census and survive for most counties. Searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

#### 5. **Anglican (Episcopal) Vestry Books**
The Church of England was the established church in colonial Virginia; vestry books are the closest thing to parish registers and can record births, marriages, and burials. Survival varies widely by parish. Many are held at the **Library of Virginia** or by individual Episcopal churches.

#### 6. **County Marriage Bonds & Marriage Registers**
Marriage bonds (not certificates) were the standard marriage record in Virginia. Held at the Library of Virginia, widely digitized and indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

#### 7. **Will Books & Estate Inventories**
County will books and inventory records document family members, property, and debts. Found at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia.

#### 8. **State-Level Military Records — Library of Virginia**
The LVA holds Virginia militia muster rolls, pay vouchers, and compiled service records from the Revolution. The **Virginia State Records** project has digitized many of these.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia (Richmond)** | County deed/will/order books, tax lists, militia records, bounty warrants, vestry books |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal pension files, compiled military service records |
| **FamilySearch** | Virginia church records, military, land/marriage/will, tax, and court record collections (5 major collections online) |
| **Fold3 / Ancestry** | Pension files, compiled service records, county records |
| **DAR (Daughters of the American Revolution)** | Lineage papers and compiled patriot records |

---

### Recommended Next Step

Identify the specific Virginia **county or counties** where your family lived during 1775–1783. All county-level records (deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds) must be searched county by county — after which a targeted research plan can be built around the repositories holding those particular records.
