quirks: Virginia did not have statewide civil vital registration during 1775-1783 — church registers (Anglican/Episcopal vestry books, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Methodist records) and county court records are the primary substitutes for births, marriages, and deaths in this period.
The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — county tax lists from the 1780s are the closest substitute and name adult white males by county.

Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to Revolutionary War veterans — warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect veterans to their postwar land claims and can name family members.

Continental Line service records are at the National Archives (Record Group 93); Virginia militia records are at the Library of Virginia in Richmond — these are two separate repositories covering different troop types.

Pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15) often contain the most detailed family information of any Revolutionary War record, including wives' names, children, ages, and places of residence at time of application.
Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony — the volume of surviving military records is correspondingly large, but coverage is uneven across counties and units.

FamilySearch digitized 3 volumes covering this place and period; the Revolutionary War land bounty warrants volume (imageGroupNumber 005301447, 341 images, 1779-1800) and the state enumerations/tax lists volume (imageGroupNumber 005301449, 87 images, 1782-1799) are browse-only with no name index — they must be examined image by image. The Augusta County court order books volume (imageGroupNumber 005301448, 158 images, 1775-1795) is 61% name-indexed.

County court order books recorded a wide range of county business beyond lawsuits — militia musters, road assignments, poor relief payments, and estate settlements — and routinely name ordinary residents who appear in no other series.

Virginia is a state-land (not federal-land) state: land grants and patents flow from the colonial and then state government, not the federal Bureau of Land Management. Original land patents are at the Library of Virginia.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; it ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788 and became a state. County-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in North America.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain until 4 July 1776; thereafter an independent Commonwealth
- **Population during period:** Population data for the 1775–1783 window was not returned by the population tool for this query; Wikipedia notes Virginia was the most populous of the thirteen colonies and contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony.
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, mixed farming, timber, some iron manufacturing. The war disrupted commerce significantly, particularly in coastal and Tidewater areas.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers; significant enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley and western counties; some Welsh.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Church of England / later Episcopal) was the established church during the colonial period; Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Lutheran, and German Reformed congregations were present, particularly in the western counties.
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence (1776); Virginia Constitution adopted (1776); British raids on coastal Virginia; Benedict Arnold's invasion of Richmond (1781); Siege of Yorktown and British surrender (October 1781), effectively ending the war.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's county boundaries changed frequently during and after the Revolution as new counties were carved from existing ones. Always identify which county governed a specific locality at the date of the event, not the modern county.
- Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776 and divided into three counties (Jefferson, Lincoln, Fayette) in 1780 — families in what became Kentucky had their earlier records filed under Virginia counties.
- West Virginia did not separate from Virginia until 1863 — families in present-day West Virginia during the Revolution had their records filed under Virginia county jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did not have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey and did not specify the statewide registration start date — consult the Virginia Vital Records page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records directly for that detail.
- **What exists for this period:** No state-mandated civil registration. County courts recorded marriages (marriage bonds and minister's returns) at the county level. Births and deaths were not systematically registered by government during this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia, Richmond
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil vital registration exists for 1775–1783.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute — see Church Records below. Marriage bonds filed at the county courthouse survive for many Virginia counties.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church, with vestry books kept at parish level); Baptist; Presbyterian; Methodist; Quaker (Friends meetings); Lutheran; German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Anglican vestry books also recorded poor relief payments and levy assessments that name parishioners
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has indexed approximately 1,234,567 records in the collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection ID 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230). Original records are at the Library of Virginia, Virginia Historical Society, and individual denominational archives. The Episcopal Diocese of Virginia holds many surviving vestry books.
- **Language:** English
- **Note:** Anglican vestry books are among the most important pre-civil-registration sources for Virginia families. They recorded baptisms and burials as well as vestry levy lists naming taxable inhabitants.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790. The 1790 Virginia schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — no population schedule survives for Virginia in 1790.
- **Substitute — county tax lists (1782 onward):** Virginia began county personal property and land tax lists in 1782. These lists name adult white males (and sometimes free Black heads of household) by county each year and function as a near-census substitute. FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 005301449, 87 images, 1782–1799, full-text searchable) covering Virginia state enumerations and tax lists. This volume must be browsed image by image via https://www.familysearch.org — it is not name-indexed but is full-text searchable.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) provides indexed access to some of these lists.
- **Other enumerations:** No Virginia-specific colonial or state census for the 1775–1783 window was identified in the tools consulted.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship bonds, intestate administrations; county court order books recorded all county business
- **Date range:** County court records predate the Revolution in many counties, beginning at county formation
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals) and the Library of Virginia (microfilm and some originals). FamilySearch has approximately 1,789,012 indexed records in "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection ID 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). The Augusta County court order books volume (imageGroupNumber 005301448, 158 images, 1775–1795) is 61% name-indexed on FamilySearch and accessible online.
- **Note:** Probate inventories from the wartime period often list slaves, livestock, tools, and personal property that reveal occupation and economic status. Court order books record militia musters, tax assessments, and road assignments alongside estate matters.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land, not federal-land, state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial government issued patents; after independence, the Commonwealth of Virginia issued state grants. The Library of Virginia holds the original land patents and grants. Virginia is not a Bureau of Land Management state — do not search the BLM GLO for Virginia patents.
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds, grants, mortgages, tax records; post-war bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War veterans (see Military Records below)
- **Date range:** Patents date from the 1600s; deed books from county formation
- **Where held:** County deed books are at county courthouses and microfilmed at the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) contains approximately 2,567,890 indexed records including deeds, marriages, and wills.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflict:** American Revolutionary War, 1775–1783
- **Record types and repositories:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — National Archives, Record Group 93. Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
  - **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond. Militia service was separate from Continental Line service; many men served only locally in the militia.
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — National Archives, Record Group 15. These files frequently contain the richest family information of any Revolutionary War record: wives' names, children's names and ages, marriage dates, places of residence. Online on Fold3 (subscription) and partially on Ancestry.
  - **Virginia State Navy records** — Published; relevant for families connected to naval service on Virginia's rivers and Chesapeake Bay.
  - **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection ID 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) contains approximately 345,678 indexed records.
  - **Post-war bounty land warrants** — Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect veterans to their postwar land claims. FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 005301447, 341 images, 1779–1800) covering Revolutionary War land bounty warrants — this volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image by image. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR):** The DAR maintains an extensive lineage database; Virginia families are heavily represented. Patriot ancestors can be searched at dar.org.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial-era and Revolutionary-era burials are found in Anglican/Episcopal churchyards, family cemeteries on farm property, and community burial grounds. Many are not well documented.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) is a primary online source for Virginia cemetery inscriptions. Not all rural and family cemeteries from the 1775–1783 period have been recorded.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they exist, are held by individual congregations or are in poor condition for this early period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia had several newspapers during the Revolution, including the Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg, multiple competing editions). These published military notices, legal announcements, runaway slave advertisements, and some vital notices.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Newspapers.com and other digital archives hold some issues. The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation also holds relevant collections.
- **Content value:** Military appointments, death notices of officers, legal notices, estate advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Hampton Roads (Norfolk/Portsmouth), Alexandria
- **Record types:** Passenger lists are sparse for colonial/Revolutionary Virginia; most immigration from Britain and Ireland occurred before 1775. Loyalist emigration records (Loyalists departing Virginia during or after the war) may be found in British Loyalist Claims records held at The National Archives (UK) and published by the Public Archives of Canada.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable in the same sense for the 1775–1783 period — most residents were colonial-born or had arrived as British subjects. Post-war naturalization records begin in county courts.
- **Note:** Declarations of intention and naturalization petitions for immigrants who arrived after the war are held in county circuit courts and at the Library of Virginia.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax, land tax (both began 1782 at the county level in Virginia)
- **Date range:** 1782 onward (county level)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723). The browse-only FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 005301449) covers 1782–1799 and is full-text searchable but not name-indexed.
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed, county tax lists from 1782–1790 are the essential substitute for placing a person in a specific Virginia county during and immediately after the Revolution. A man present on a 1783 county tax list is placed in that county in that year.

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Families who remained loyal to the Crown faced confiscation of property. Virginia Loyalist Claims are documented in the British Loyalist Claims records at The National Archives (UK). Virginia also passed acts of attainder confiscating Loyalist property — these legislative acts are published in the Virginia Statutes at Large.
- **Legislative and executive records:** Virginia's Council of State journals and the House of Delegates journals for 1775–1783 record appointments of officers, bounty resolutions, and petitions from citizens — including petitions by widows of soldiers.
- **Organizational records:** County committees of safety (1775–1776) kept minutes and muster rolls at the county level; many are at the Library of Virginia.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories frequently reprint Revolutionary War muster rolls and biographical sketches of veteran families. The Library of Virginia and the Virginia Historical Society hold large collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (345,678 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (1,234,567 records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (2,567,890 records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (456,789 records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (1,789,012 records) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files (NARA RG 15); Continental service records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Overlapping collections; U.S. Federal Census; some Virginia-specific record sets | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | NARA Record Groups 93 and 15; some records free online | Free/Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Virginia Gazette and other colonial newspapers (partial) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search tool returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia for the 1775–1800 window (totalResults: 3); all 3 are detailed above. The collections_search returned 5 collections at the Virginia state scope. These represent the FamilySearch-held digitized material; additional microfilm-only holdings exist at the Library of Virginia and FamilySearch Library.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Continental Line and militia records; land patents; tax lists; court records microfilm; county deed books; pension files copies; published Virginia Military District of Ohio records | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some digitized |
| National Archives (Washington, DC / College Park) | NARA RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pension and bounty-land files), RG 360 (Papers of the Continental Congress) | In-person; Fold3 and Ancestry for many digitized series |
| Virginia Historical Society (Richmond) | Manuscript collections; family papers; published local histories; DAR lineage records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| County courthouses | Original deed books, will books, marriage bonds, order books | In-person or correspondence; check county clerk |
| Episcopal Diocese of Virginia Archives | Surviving Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and parish registers | Contact diocese; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| DAR Library (Washington, DC) | Lineage files, compiled genealogies, local history | In-person; dar.org searchable index |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia — many are available only on microfilm or in bound volumes; not fully digitized or indexed online.
- Original Anglican vestry books for many parishes — microfilmed but not all digitized.
- County committee of safety minutes (1775–1776) — largely in manuscript at the Library of Virginia.
- Original Loyalist Claims files — at The National Archives (UK), Kew; available on Ancestry in part.
- Original pension files — many are digitized on Fold3, but some files are damaged or incomplete.
- Colonial-era family cemetery records — typically not recorded in any repository.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists from 1782 onward are the established substitute.
- Some county courthouses suffered fires or losses in subsequent centuries (not during the Revolution itself) — individual county records vary in completeness. Always check whether a specific county courthouse experienced record loss before concluding a record does not exist.
- Some Anglican vestry books were lost or damaged during the disestablishment of the Church of England in Virginia after 1776.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** NARA RG 15 pension and bounty-land warrant application files are the single richest source for Revolutionary War family reconstruction. A widow's pension application in particular routinely names the marriage date, place, names of witnesses, and children. Search Fold3 first, then request the full file from NARA if not fully imaged. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Use county tax lists as a census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia federal census does not survive, the personal property and land tax lists beginning in 1782 are the essential tool for placing a person in a specific county year by year through the 1780s. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

---

This guide covers Virginia as a whole during the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783). Virginia kept records at the county level throughout this period, and there was no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths \u2014 the key sources for family reconstruction are military pension files at the National Archives, county court order books and deed books held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia in Richmond, Anglican vestry books (the closest thing to a parish register), and county personal property and land tax lists that begin in 1782 and serve as the essential substitute for the 1790 Virginia federal census, which was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Three digitized FamilySearch volumes match the period: a name-indexed set of Augusta County court order books (61% indexed), a browse-only set of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (must be examined image by image), and a full-text-searchable but not name-indexed set of state tax lists; five FamilySearch collections cover Virginia church, military, land/marriage/will, tax, and court records online.

The next step is to identify the specific Virginia county or counties where your family lived during 1775-1783, since all county-level records (deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds) must be searched at that county level \u2014 after which a targeted research plan can be built around the repositories that hold those particular county's records.

Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to Revolutionary War veterans — warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect veterans to their postwar land claims and can name family members.

Continental Line service records are at the National Archives (Record Group 93); Virginia militia records are at the Library of Virginia in Richmond — these are two separate repositories covering different troop types.

Pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15) often contain the most detailed family information of any Revolutionary War record, including wives' names, children, ages, and places of residence at time of application.
Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony — the volume of surviving military records is correspondingly large, but coverage is uneven across counties and units.

FamilySearch digitized 3 volumes covering this place and period; the Revolutionary War land bounty warrants volume (imageGroupNumber 005301447, 341 images, 1779-1800) and the state enumerations/tax lists volume (imageGroupNumber 005301449, 87 images, 1782-1799) are browse-only with no name index — they must be examined image by image. The Augusta County court order books volume (imageGroupNumber 005301448, 158 images, 1775-1795) is 61% name-indexed.

County court order books recorded a wide range of county business beyond lawsuits — militia musters, road assignments, poor relief payments, and estate settlements — and routinely name ordinary residents who appear in no other series.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; it ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788 and became a state. County-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in North America.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain until 4 July 1776; thereafter an independent Commonwealth
- **Population during period:** Population data for the 1775–1783 window was not returned by the population tool for this query; Wikipedia notes Virginia was the most populous of the thirteen colonies and contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony.
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, mixed farming, timber, some iron manufacturing. The war disrupted commerce significantly, particularly in coastal and Tidewater areas.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers; significant enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley and western counties; some Welsh.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Church of England / later Episcopal) was the established church during the colonial period; Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Lutheran, and German Reformed congregations were present, particularly in the western counties.
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence (1776); Virginia Constitution adopted (1776); British raids on coastal Virginia; Benedict Arnold's invasion of Richmond (1781); Siege of Yorktown and British surrender (October 1781), effectively ending the war.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's county boundaries changed frequently during and after the Revolution as new counties were carved from existing ones. Always identify which county governed a specific locality at the date of the event, not the modern county.
- Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776 and divided into three counties (Jefferson, Lincoln, Fayette) in 1780 — families in what became Kentucky had their earlier records filed under Virginia counties.
- West Virginia did not separate from Virginia until 1863 — families in present-day West Virginia during the Revolution had their records filed under Virginia county jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did not have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey and did not specify the statewide registration start date — consult the Virginia Vital Records page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records directly for that detail.
- **What exists for this period:** No state-mandated civil registration. County courts recorded marriages (marriage bonds and minister's returns) at the county level. Births and deaths were not systematically registered by government during this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia, Richmond
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil vital registration exists for 1775–1783.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute — see Church Records below. Marriage bonds filed at the county courthouse survive for many Virginia counties.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church, with vestry books kept at parish level); Baptist; Presbyterian; Methodist; Quaker (Friends meetings); Lutheran; German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Anglican vestry books also recorded poor relief payments and levy assessments that name parishioners
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has indexed approximately 1,234,567 records in the collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection ID 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230). Original records are at the Library of Virginia, Virginia Historical Society, and individual denominational archives. The Episcopal Diocese of Virginia holds many surviving vestry books.
- **Language:** English
- **Note:** Anglican vestry books are among the most important pre-civil-registration sources for Virginia families. They recorded baptisms and burials as well as vestry levy lists naming taxable inhabitants.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790. The 1790 Virginia schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — no population schedule survives for Virginia in 1790.
- **Substitute — county tax lists (1782 onward):** Virginia began county personal property and land tax lists in 1782. These lists name adult white males (and sometimes free Black heads of household) by county each year and function as a near-census substitute. FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 005301449, 87 images, 1782–1799, full-text searchable) covering Virginia state enumerations and tax lists. This volume must be browsed image by image via https://www.familysearch.org — it is not name-indexed but is full-text searchable.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) provides indexed access to some of these lists.
- **Other enumerations:** No Virginia-specific colonial or state census for the 1775–1783 window was identified in the tools consulted.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship bonds, intestate administrations; county court order books recorded all county business
- **Date range:** County court records predate the Revolution in many counties, beginning at county formation
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals) and the Library of Virginia (microfilm and some originals). FamilySearch has approximately 1,789,012 indexed records in "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection ID 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567). The Augusta County court order books volume (imageGroupNumber 005301448, 158 images, 1775–1795) is 61% name-indexed on FamilySearch and accessible online.
- **Note:** Probate inventories from the wartime period often list slaves, livestock, tools, and personal property that reveal occupation and economic status. Court order books record militia musters, tax assessments, and road assignments alongside estate matters.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land, not federal-land, state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial government issued patents; after independence, the Commonwealth of Virginia issued state grants. The Library of Virginia holds the original land patents and grants. Virginia is not a Bureau of Land Management state — do not search the BLM GLO for Virginia patents.
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds, grants, mortgages, tax records; post-war bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War veterans (see Military Records below)
- **Date range:** Patents date from the 1600s; deed books from county formation
- **Where held:** County deed books are at county courthouses and microfilmed at the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) contains approximately 2,567,890 indexed records including deeds, marriages, and wills.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflict:** American Revolutionary War, 1775–1783
- **Record types and repositories:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — National Archives, Record Group 93. Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
  - **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond. Militia service was separate from Continental Line service; many men served only locally in the militia.
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — National Archives, Record Group 15. These files frequently contain the richest family information of any Revolutionary War record: wives' names, children's names and ages, marriage dates, places of residence. Online on Fold3 (subscription) and partially on Ancestry.
  - **Virginia State Navy records** — Published; relevant for families connected to naval service on Virginia's rivers and Chesapeake Bay.
  - **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection ID 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) contains approximately 345,678 indexed records.
  - **Post-war bounty land warrants** — Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect veterans to their postwar land claims. FamilySearch has a browse-only digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 005301447, 341 images, 1779–1800) covering Revolutionary War land bounty warrants — this volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image by image. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR):** The DAR maintains an extensive lineage database; Virginia families are heavily represented. Patriot ancestors can be searched at dar.org.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial-era and Revolutionary-era burials are found in Anglican/Episcopal churchyards, family cemeteries on farm property, and community burial grounds. Many are not well documented.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) is a primary online source for Virginia cemetery inscriptions. Not all rural and family cemeteries from the 1775–1783 period have been recorded.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they exist, are held by individual congregations or are in poor condition for this early period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia had several newspapers during the Revolution, including the Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg, multiple competing editions). These published military notices, legal announcements, runaway slave advertisements, and some vital notices.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Newspapers.com and other digital archives hold some issues. The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation also holds relevant collections.
- **Content value:** Military appointments, death notices of officers, legal notices, estate advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Hampton Roads (Norfolk/Portsmouth), Alexandria
- **Record types:** Passenger lists are sparse for colonial/Revolutionary Virginia; most immigration from Britain and Ireland occurred before 1775. Loyalist emigration records (Loyalists departing Virginia during or after the war) may be found in British Loyalist Claims records held at The National Archives (UK) and published by the Public Archives of Canada.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable in the same sense for the 1775–1783 period — most residents were colonial-born or had arrived as British subjects. Post-war naturalization records begin in county courts.
- **Note:** Declarations of intention and naturalization petitions for immigrants who arrived after the war are held in county circuit courts and at the Library of Virginia.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax, land tax (both began 1782 at the county level in Virginia)
- **Date range:** 1782 onward (county level)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723). The browse-only FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 005301449) covers 1782–1799 and is full-text searchable but not name-indexed.
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed, county tax lists from 1782–1790 are the essential substitute for placing a person in a specific Virginia county during and immediately after the Revolution. A man present on a 1783 county tax list is placed in that county in that year.

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Families who remained loyal to the Crown faced confiscation of property. Virginia Loyalist Claims are documented in the British Loyalist Claims records at The National Archives (UK). Virginia also passed acts of attainder confiscating Loyalist property — these legislative acts are published in the Virginia Statutes at Large.
- **Legislative and executive records:** Virginia's Council of State journals and the House of Delegates journals for 1775–1783 record appointments of officers, bounty resolutions, and petitions from citizens — including petitions by widows of soldiers.
- **Organizational records:** County committees of safety (1775–1776) kept minutes and muster rolls at the county level; many are at the Library of Virginia.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories frequently reprint Revolutionary War muster rolls and biographical sketches of veteran families. The Library of Virginia and the Virginia Historical Society hold large collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (345,678 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (1,234,567 records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (2,567,890 records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (456,789 records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (1,789,012 records) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files (NARA RG 15); Continental service records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Overlapping collections; U.S. Federal Census; some Virginia-specific record sets | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | NARA Record Groups 93 and 15; some records free online | Free/Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Virginia Gazette and other colonial newspapers (partial) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search tool returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia for the 1775–1800 window (totalResults: 3); all 3 are detailed above. The collections_search returned 5 collections at the Virginia state scope. These represent the FamilySearch-held digitized material; additional microfilm-only holdings exist at the Library of Virginia and FamilySearch Library.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Continental Line and militia records; land patents; tax lists; court records microfilm; county deed books; pension files copies; published Virginia Military District of Ohio records | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some digitized |
| National Archives (Washington, DC / College Park) | NARA RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pension and bounty-land files), RG 360 (Papers of the Continental Congress) | In-person; Fold3 and Ancestry for many digitized series |
| Virginia Historical Society (Richmond) | Manuscript collections; family papers; published local histories; DAR lineage records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| County courthouses | Original deed books, will books, marriage bonds, order books | In-person or correspondence; check county clerk |
| Episcopal Diocese of Virginia Archives | Surviving Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and parish registers | Contact diocese; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| DAR Library (Washington, DC) | Lineage files, compiled genealogies, local history | In-person; dar.org searchable index |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia — many are available only on microfilm or in bound volumes; not fully digitized or indexed online.
- Original Anglican vestry books for many parishes — microfilmed but not all digitized.
- County committee of safety minutes (1775–1776) — largely in manuscript at the Library of Virginia.
- Original Loyalist Claims files — at The National Archives (UK), Kew; available on Ancestry in part.
- Original pension files — many are digitized on Fold3, but some files are damaged or incomplete.
- Colonial-era family cemetery records — typically not recorded in any repository.

## Known record losses
- The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists from 1782 onward are the established substitute.
- Some county courthouses suffered fires or losses in subsequent centuries (not during the Revolution itself) — individual county records vary in completeness. Always check whether a specific county courthouse experienced record loss before concluding a record does not exist.
- Some Anglican vestry books were lost or damaged during the disestablishment of the Church of England in Virginia after 1776.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** NARA RG 15 pension and bounty-land warrant application files are the single richest source for Revolutionary War family reconstruction. A widow's pension application in particular routinely names the marriage date, place, names of witnesses, and children. Search Fold3 first, then request the full file from NARA if not fully imaged. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Use county tax lists as a census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia federal census does not survive, the personal property and land tax lists beginning in 1782 are the essential tool for placing a person in a specific county year by year through the 1780s. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Search both Continental Line and militia records separately.** Many men served only in the militia, not the Continental Army; they appear in militia records at the Library of Virginia but not in NARA RG 93. Search both repositories.
- **Check Virginia Military District of Ohio records** if the family migrated westward after the war. Veterans who received bounty land warrants often located in Ohio; warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect them to their Virginia origins. ([Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Follow the county of residence, not just the state.** Virginia maintained records at the county level. Identifying which county a family lived in during 1775–1783 is essential before searching deed books, will books, and court order books.
- **Vestry books predate civil registration.** Anglican vestry books often contain the only record of a baptism, marriage, or burial for families of the established church before 1800.
- **Check the DAR lineage files.** Virginia is heavily represented in DAR records. A lineage already proven by another researcher can provide citations and clues even if it needs independent verification.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia-specific record types (Vital Records, Military Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) returned only generic content in this survey** — the dedicated Virginia topic pages should be consulted directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki for record-type-specific dates and details not available in this guide.

---

**New Orleans — Records, Disasters, and Where to Search**

New Orleans is one of the most disaster-affected genealogical research environments in the United States. Two catastrophic fires in **1788 and 1794** destroyed large portions of the colonial record base, and repeated **yellow fever epidemics** (the 1853 outbreak alone killed ~7,849 people), hurricanes, and floods caused ongoing archival losses throughout the early 1800s. A missing record for this place and time is most likely a disaster gap — not evidence that a person was absent or an event went unrecorded.

---

### What Survived and Where to Find It

**1. Sacramental Registers — St. Louis Cathedral**
- Begins 1731 (with gaps from the 1788 fire)
- Held by the **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives**
- Partially on FamilySearch: *Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925* (collection 1612905)
- These are the **primary substitute for civil vital records**, which did not exist at the state level until 1918.

**2. Notarial Acts — New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
- Over **30 million pages** of notarial acts from 1734
- Covers sales, wills, contracts, manumissions, successions, and more
- These replace the common-law deed books and courthouse probate files used in other states — **the single most important repository for this jurisdiction**
- FamilySearch holds one digitized notarial acts volume (1803–1820, image group 004990115, 167 images) — it is **0% name-indexed** and not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image by image

**3. Probate and Vital Records on FamilySearch**
- *Louisiana Probate Records 1756–1984* (collection 2078341)
- *Louisiana Death Index from 1819* (collection 1543892) — provides indexed access to some records

---

### Important Note on Territorial Labels
For the **1800–1812 territorial period**, records are labeled under **"Orleans Territory"** rather than the state of Louisiana. This affects how they surface in online databases — search under both labels to avoid missing records.

---

### Recommended Next Step
Build a research plan targeting your specific ancestor or family using these repositories in priority order: **church registers and notarial acts first**, then succession records and census enumerations.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by France in 1718. It passed to Spain in 1763, briefly reverted to France in 1800, was sold to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase (1803), and was included in Orleans Territory (1803-1812) before Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. Orleans Parish, coterminous with the city, was established as a Louisiana civil division at statehood.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (the parish and city are one unit; there is no separate county seat structure)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (1803-1812), then Louisiana (1812-)
- **Population during period:** Population data for this specific standard place was not returned by the population tool. Wikipedia records New Orleans as one of the largest U.S. cities by 1840, with a diverse population of Creoles, Anglo-Americans, free people of color, enslaved persons, and waves of immigrants from France, Spain, Germany, Ireland, and elsewhere.
- **Economy:** Entrepot trade (cotton, sugar, slaves), river commerce, and maritime industry dominated. New Orleans was the primary port of the Mississippi River valley throughout this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African and African-descended persons, German, Irish, and other European immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was dominant (the official church under French and Spanish colonial rule, and St. Louis Cathedral served as the primary parish). Protestant congregations — Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist — grew after the Louisiana Purchase as Anglo-American settlement increased.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (January 1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics (especially severe in 1832, 1837, 1847, 1853); hurricanes and periodic Mississippi River flooding. Two devastating fires — 1788 and 1794 — largely predate this period but created the record gaps researchers encounter.

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans has been continuously coterminous with Orleans Parish since Louisiana statehood in 1812. No boundary splits affect the city during the 1800-1860 target period.
- Records created before statehood (1800-1812) were generated under Orleans Territory, not the state of Louisiana. Search under territorial designations when using indexed collections, as some are filed separately from the post-1812 state series.
- Because Louisiana shifted from French to Spanish to French again before U.S. acquisition, colonial-era and early territorial records may be in French, Spanish, or both. The early 1800s fall at the transition: notarial acts and sacramental registers from 1800-1815 may be in either or both languages.

## Known record losses

This is the most critical section for New Orleans research.

**The fires of 1788 and 1794** (both under Spanish rule) destroyed the majority of the French Quarter's built environment and many governmental and church records created under the French colonial period (1718-1763) and the early Spanish period. While these predate the 1800-1860 target window, they mean:
- Any ancestor present in New Orleans before 1800 may have no surviving civil record from the colonial period.
- Gaps in church registers from St. Louis Cathedral reflect these losses — the 1731-1788 series has gaps, and reconstruction of some entries was attempted afterward.

**Yellow fever epidemics** (particularly 1832, 1837, 1847, 1853) and **hurricanes and floods** caused ongoing losses to both archival holdings and record-keeping continuity throughout the early 1800s. The 1853 epidemic was especially severe, killing an estimated 7,849 people in the city. Treat any gap in a record series as potentially disaster-related.

**Substitute sources when primary records are missing:**
- St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (surviving from 1731 with gaps): baptisms, marriages, burials — the most important substitute for missing civil vital records
- Notarial acts (New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, holdings from 1734): wills, sales, contracts, manumissions, successions — cover events that in common-law states would appear in courthouse records
- Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892): an index only (no images in this collection), but covers deaths from 1819 onward
- Published transcriptions and abstracts by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society and the New Orleans Genealogical Research Society

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did not begin statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths until 1918 (the FamilySearch wiki_read pages returned generic content and did not give a specific date for Louisiana; 1918 is the commonly cited statewide date, but the FamilySearch Louisiana Vital Records page was not returned by this tool run — researchers should verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly). For the 1800-1860 period, **no statewide civil registration existed**.
- **What exists:** The Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892, index only, no images) is a partial index of deaths. Parish Marriages 1837-1957 (FamilySearch collection 1798054) covers marriages from 1837.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collections above); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths for most of 1800-1860 are not in any civil registration system.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers and other Catholic parish registers are the primary vital record substitute. Notarial acts record marriages contracted before notaries.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant, with St. Louis Cathedral as the principal parish serving New Orleans from 1720); Episcopal, Presbyterian, and Methodist congregations established after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (sacramental registers); confirmation records. St. Louis Cathedral registers begin 1731 (with gaps from the 1788 fire).
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives holds diocesan records. FamilySearch has digitized a portion: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905), which covers sacramental registers across the state and overlaps significantly with New Orleans.
- **Language:** French and/or Spanish for most records through approximately 1815; increasingly English thereafter. Researchers must be able to read the original language or use a translator.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 is indexed + images. However, the indexed coverage within this collection for the 1800-1860 window for Orleans Parish specifically is not stated in tool results — search the collection and expect browse-only images for some volumes.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** New Orleans appears in U.S. federal censuses from 1810 (Orleans Territory was enumerated in 1810; Louisiana as a state from 1820). The 1890 federal census is largely destroyed nationwide — this does not affect the 1800-1860 window.
- **Territorial census:** A territorial census of Orleans Territory was taken ca. 1805-1806.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for Louisiana 1810-1860 are indexed and available on Ancestry.com (subscription) and partially on FamilySearch.
- **Note:** The Louisiana census records page was not returned by the tools in this run. Researchers should check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census for any state or special enumerations.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana terminology:** Probate is called "succession" in Louisiana civil law. Guardianship is called "tutorship."
- **Types:** Successions (testate and intestate), tutorships, interdictions, civil suits, criminal cases, and naturalizations. Because Louisiana follows the Napoleonic Code rather than common law, the content and structure of these records differs from other states.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341, Louisiana Probate Records 1756-1984, covers this period and is indexed + images.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (successor to earlier territorial courts); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; FamilySearch (collection 2078341).

### Land records (notarial acts)
- **Survey system:** French long-lot survey system (arpent system), not the U.S. rectangular survey. Land grants under French and Spanish colonial governments used this system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under the colonial and early territorial period, land grants were issued by the French and Spanish crowns, then confirmed (or disputed) by U.S. land commissioners after the Louisiana Purchase. The General Land Office (GLO) handled federal public-domain patents after 1803, but much of New Orleans's land had already been granted under colonial title.
- **Types:** Notarial acts (sales, mortgages, donations, exchanges) replace common-law deeds. These are held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, which holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 onward. This is one of the most important repositories for any New Orleans ancestor.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical and some digitized); Louisiana State Archives. FamilySearch volume search returned 1 digitized volume for 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, in French and English).
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images for the FamilySearch-held volume; the Notarial Archives have their own finding aids and partial digitization.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 and Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846-1848); early sectional tensions leading toward the Civil War.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives; bounty land warrants (War of 1812 service) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional facilities); Fold3 (subscription, digitized military records including pension files); Louisiana State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789, the oldest surviving cemetery in New Orleans), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), St. Patrick's Cemetery (est. 1841 for Irish Catholic immigrants), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (Garden District, est. 1833).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) has indexed many New Orleans cemeteries. The Save Our Cemeteries organization has done surveys of above-ground tombs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are held by individual cemeteries or the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. Many early burial records were lost.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (from 1804), the New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orleans (bilingual French/English, from 1827), the Daily Picayune (from 1837), and others. French-language papers served the Creole community throughout this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries (Louisiana Digital Library); Newspapers.com (subscription); the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division; the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (successions, sheriff sales, tutorships), runaway slave notices, and ship arrivals.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary southern U.S. port of entry. It was the second-largest port of immigrant arrival in the United States during the 1840s-1850s (after New York). Irish and German immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1830.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA microfilm and online databases); declarations of intention and naturalization records filed in Orleans Parish courts (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record).
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry.com (U.S. Federal Census Collection and passenger lists); FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (assessed at the parish level); personal property tax.
- **Date range:** Orleans Parish tax records exist from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; New Orleans City Archives; Louisiana Division of the New Orleans Public Library.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and can place an ancestor in New Orleans in the years between censuses.

### Other record types
- **Records of enslaved persons:** Because New Orleans was a major slave-trading center, records of enslaved people appear in notarial acts (bills of sale, manumissions, hiring contracts), Catholic baptismal registers (which recorded enslaved baptisms), and succession/probate inventories. The New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives are the key repositories.
- **Free people of color (gens de couleur libres):** New Orleans had a large, legally recognized community of free people of color. Their records appear in sacramental registers, notarial acts, successions, and court records, though often in a separate series or with notation of status.
- **City directories:** New Orleans city directories were published from the 1820s onward and can place an ancestor at a specific address between census years.
- **Published local and family histories:** The Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society has published abstracts of early records. The Historic New Orleans Collection holds manuscript and published materials.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (coll. 1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892); 1 digitized volume of notarial acts 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1810-1860 for Louisiana); passenger arrival lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions, New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including New Orleans papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization and military | Free/fee for copies |
| Louisiana Digital Library (LSU) | Digitized Louisiana newspapers and other materials | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish/New Orleans for the 1800-1860 period; this is the complete result for the first page of that query. The collections_search returned 4 Louisiana-level collections. This survey does not represent the full holdings of physical repositories.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734, including wills, sales, contracts, manumissions | In-person research room; partial digitization |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes from 1731 (with gaps) | Contact the archives; some records on FamilySearch microfilm |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, tax records, succession records, military records | In-person and some online finding aids |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City directories, local history, newspapers, birth/death records held by the city | In-person; some digitized |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscript collections, maps, photographs, published histories | In-person research center |
| NARA Southeast Regional Archives (Atlanta) | Federal court records, census records for Louisiana | In-person and online request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Original succession, civil, and court records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Most original notarial acts (beyond the 1 FamilySearch volume for 1803-1820)
- Original sacramental registers not yet digitized by FamilySearch
- Orleans Parish tax records
- City directories pre-1860 (some available through local libraries)
- Records of enslaved persons held in manuscript collections
- Most manuscript collections at the Historic New Orleans Collection
- Sexton records of individual cemeteries

## Known record losses
- **Fire of 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings and many governmental and church records from the French colonial period. The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral from 1731-1788 have gaps attributable to this fire.
- **Fire of 1794:** A second major fire destroyed additional records and rebuilt structures.
- **Yellow fever epidemics:** The 1832, 1837, 1847, and 1853 epidemics disrupted record-keeping and killed thousands; the 1853 epidemic alone killed an estimated 7,849 people. Gaps in any civil or church series during epidemic years should be assumed to be disaster-related, not evidence of absence.
- **Hurricanes and floods:** The location of New Orleans at or below sea level and on the Gulf Coast made it repeatedly vulnerable to storm and flood damage to archival holdings throughout the 19th century.

**Substitute sources for lost records:**
1. St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (surviving portions from 1731, at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and on FamilySearch microfilm)
2. Notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (from 1734)
3. Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892 — index only)
4. Newspaper death notices and obituaries (Louisiana Digital Library, Newspapers.com)
5. Succession records at Orleans Parish Civil District Court and on FamilySearch (collection 2078341)
6. Published abstracts and transcriptions by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society

## Research tips
- **Think notarial, not common-law.** In Louisiana, legal transactions are recorded in notarial acts, not deed books. If you cannot find a land record, probate file, or contract in a courthouse deed or will book (there are none in the common-law sense), look in the notarial acts. See the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System.
- **Records exist in three languages.** Early New Orleans records are in French, Spanish, and English, often within the same series. Know which language applies to which period and have translation resources available.
- **Treat every missing year as a disaster gap.** Because of the fires, epidemics, hurricanes, and floods documented above, a missing record in a series is more likely a disaster loss than evidence the person was absent or the event did not occur.
- **Search sacramental registers first, not last.** For events before 1900, the Catholic church register is frequently the only surviving record of a birth, marriage, or death. St. Louis Cathedral registers begin in 1731. The FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925) is the starting point online.
- **Free people of color and enslaved persons have distinct record trails.** The gens de couleur libres community appears in sacramental registers, notarial acts, and succession records, sometimes in a separately designated series. Enslaved individuals are documented primarily in notarial acts and Catholic baptismal registers.
- **Use the New Orleans Notarial Archives.** This repository (https://www.notarialarchives.org) holds over 30 million pages from 1734, more comprehensive than any online database for this place and period, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters.
- **Check both territorial and state series.** Records from 1803-1812 are filed under Orleans Territory, not the state of Louisiana. Some online databases index them separately.
- **Immigration research:** New Orleans was the second-largest U.S. port of immigrant entry by the 1840s-1850s. Passenger arrival lists for New Orleans are at NARA and are indexed on Ancestry.com — search these for any ancestor arriving in the U.S. through the Gulf South.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Orleans Parish is surrounded by Jefferson Parish (west/south), St. Bernard Parish (east/south), St. Tammany Parish (north, across Lake Pontchartrain), and St. John the Baptist Parish (west). Families near parish boundaries may have generated records in adjacent parishes. The neighboring parishes table from the New Orleans wiki home page was not returned by the wiki_place_page tool in this run — researchers should check the FamilySearch wiki for the neighboring parishes list directly.
