added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by France in 1718. It passed to Spain in 1763, briefly reverted to France in 1800, was sold to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase (1803), and was included in Orleans Territory (1803-1812) before Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. Orleans Parish, coterminous with the city, was established as a Louisiana civil division at statehood.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (the parish and city are one unit; there is no separate county seat structure)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (1803-1812), then Louisiana (1812-)
- **Population during period:** Population data for this specific standard place was not returned by the population tool. Wikipedia records New Orleans as one of the largest U.S. cities by 1840, with a diverse population of Creoles, Anglo-Americans, free people of color, enslaved persons, and waves of immigrants from France, Spain, Germany, Ireland, and elsewhere.
- **Economy:** Entrepot trade (cotton, sugar, slaves), river commerce, and maritime industry dominated. New Orleans was the primary port of the Mississippi River valley throughout this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African and African-descended persons, German, Irish, and other European immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was dominant (the official church under French and Spanish colonial rule, and St. Louis Cathedral served as the primary parish). Protestant congregations — Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist — grew after the Louisiana Purchase as Anglo-American settlement increased.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (January 1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics (especially severe in 1832, 1837, 1847, 1853); hurricanes and periodic Mississippi River flooding. Two devastating fires — 1788 and 1794 — largely predate this period but created the record gaps researchers encounter.

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans has been continuously coterminous with Orleans Parish since Louisiana statehood in 1812. No boundary splits affect the city during the 1800-1860 target period.
- Records created before statehood (1800-1812) were generated under Orleans Territory, not the state of Louisiana. Search under territorial designations when using indexed collections, as some are filed separately from the post-1812 state series.
- Because Louisiana shifted from French to Spanish to French again before U.S. acquisition, colonial-era and early territorial records may be in French, Spanish, or both. The early 1800s fall at the transition: notarial acts and sacramental registers from 1800-1815 may be in either or both languages.

## Known record losses

This is the most critical section for New Orleans research.

**The fires of 1788 and 1794** (both under Spanish rule) destroyed the majority of the French Quarter's built environment and many governmental and church records created under the French colonial period (1718-1763) and the early Spanish period. While these predate the 1800-1860 target window, they mean:
- Any ancestor present in New Orleans before 1800 may have no surviving civil record from the colonial period.
- Gaps in church registers from St. Louis Cathedral reflect these losses — the 1731-1788 series has gaps, and reconstruction of some entries was attempted afterward.

**Yellow fever epidemics** (particularly 1832, 1837, 1847, 1853) and **hurricanes and floods** caused ongoing losses to both archival holdings and record-keeping continuity throughout the early 1800s. The 1853 epidemic was especially severe, killing an estimated 7,849 people in the city. Treat any gap in a record series as potentially disaster-related.

**Substitute sources when primary records are missing:**
- St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (surviving from 1731 with gaps): baptisms, marriages, burials — the most important substitute for missing civil vital records
- Notarial acts (New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, holdings from 1734): wills, sales, contracts, manumissions, successions — cover events that in common-law states would appear in courthouse records
- Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892): an index only (no images in this collection), but covers deaths from 1819 onward
- Published transcriptions and abstracts by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society and the New Orleans Genealogical Research Society

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did not begin statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths until 1918 (the FamilySearch wiki_read pages returned generic content and did not give a specific date for Louisiana; 1918 is the commonly cited statewide date, but the FamilySearch Louisiana Vital Records page was not returned by this tool run — researchers should verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly). For the 1800-1860 period, **no statewide civil registration existed**.
- **What exists:** The Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892, index only, no images) is a partial index of deaths. Parish Marriages 1837-1957 (FamilySearch collection 1798054) covers marriages from 1837.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collections above); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths for most of 1800-1860 are not in any civil registration system.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers and other Catholic parish registers are the primary vital record substitute. Notarial acts record marriages contracted before notaries.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant, with St. Louis Cathedral as the principal parish serving New Orleans from 1720); Episcopal, Presbyterian, and Methodist congregations established after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (sacramental registers); confirmation records. St. Louis Cathedral registers begin 1731 (with gaps from the 1788 fire).
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives holds diocesan records. FamilySearch has digitized a portion: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905), which covers sacramental registers across the state and overlaps significantly with New Orleans.
- **Language:** French and/or Spanish for most records through approximately 1815; increasingly English thereafter. Researchers must be able to read the original language or use a translator.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 is indexed + images. However, the indexed coverage within this collection for the 1800-1860 window for Orleans Parish specifically is not stated in tool results — search the collection and expect browse-only images for some volumes.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** New Orleans appears in U.S. federal censuses from 1810 (Orleans Territory was enumerated in 1810; Louisiana as a state from 1820). The 1890 federal census is largely destroyed nationwide — this does not affect the 1800-1860 window.
- **Territorial census:** A territorial census of Orleans Territory was taken ca. 1805-1806.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for Louisiana 1810-1860 are indexed and available on Ancestry.com (subscription) and partially on FamilySearch.
- **Note:** The Louisiana census records page was not returned by the tools in this run. Researchers should check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census for any state or special enumerations.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana terminology:** Probate is called "succession" in Louisiana civil law. Guardianship is called "tutorship."
- **Types:** Successions (testate and intestate), tutorships, interdictions, civil suits, criminal cases, and naturalizations. Because Louisiana follows the Napoleonic Code rather than common law, the content and structure of these records differs from other states.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341, Louisiana Probate Records 1756-1984, covers this period and is indexed + images.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (successor to earlier territorial courts); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; FamilySearch (collection 2078341).

### Land records (notarial acts)
- **Survey system:** French long-lot survey system (arpent system), not the U.S. rectangular survey. Land grants under French and Spanish colonial governments used this system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under the colonial and early territorial period, land grants were issued by the French and Spanish crowns, then confirmed (or disputed) by U.S. land commissioners after the Louisiana Purchase. The General Land Office (GLO) handled federal public-domain patents after 1803, but much of New Orleans's land had already been granted under colonial title.
- **Types:** Notarial acts (sales, mortgages, donations, exchanges) replace common-law deeds. These are held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, which holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 onward. This is one of the most important repositories for any New Orleans ancestor.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical and some digitized); Louisiana State Archives. FamilySearch volume search returned 1 digitized volume for 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, in French and English).
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images for the FamilySearch-held volume; the Notarial Archives have their own finding aids and partial digitization.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 and Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846-1848); early sectional tensions leading toward the Civil War.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives; bounty land warrants (War of 1812 service) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional facilities); Fold3 (subscription, digitized military records including pension files); Louisiana State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789, the oldest surviving cemetery in New Orleans), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), St. Patrick's Cemetery (est. 1841 for Irish Catholic immigrants), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (Garden District, est. 1833).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) has indexed many New Orleans cemeteries. The Save Our Cemeteries organization has done surveys of above-ground tombs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are held by individual cemeteries or the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. Many early burial records were lost.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (from 1804), the New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orleans (bilingual French/English, from 1827), the Daily Picayune (from 1837), and others. French-language papers served the Creole community throughout this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries (Louisiana Digital Library); Newspapers.com (subscription); the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division; the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (successions, sheriff sales, tutorships), runaway slave notices, and ship arrivals.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary southern U.S. port of entry. It was the second-largest port of immigrant arrival in the United States during the 1840s-1850s (after New York). Irish and German immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1830.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA microfilm and online databases); declarations of intention and naturalization records filed in Orleans Parish courts (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record).
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry.com (U.S. Federal Census Collection and passenger lists); FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (assessed at the parish level); personal property tax.
- **Date range:** Orleans Parish tax records exist from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; New Orleans City Archives; Louisiana Division of the New Orleans Public Library.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and can place an ancestor in New Orleans in the years between censuses.

### Other record types
- **Records of enslaved persons:** Because New Orleans was a major slave-trading center, records of enslaved people appear in notarial acts (bills of sale, manumissions, hiring contracts), Catholic baptismal registers (which recorded enslaved baptisms), and succession/probate inventories. The New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives are the key repositories.
- **Free people of color (gens de couleur libres):** New Orleans had a large, legally recognized community of free people of color. Their records appear in sacramental registers, notarial acts, successions, and court records, though often in a separate series or with notation of status.
- **City directories:** New Orleans city directories were published from the 1820s onward and can place an ancestor at a specific address between census years.
- **Published local and family histories:** The Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society has published abstracts of early records. The Historic New Orleans Collection holds manuscript and published materials.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (coll. 1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892); 1 digitized volume of notarial acts 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1810-1860 for Louisiana); passenger arrival lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions, New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including New Orleans papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization and military | Free/fee for copies |
| Louisiana Digital Library (LSU) | Digitized Louisiana newspapers and other materials | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish/New Orleans for the 1800-1860 period; this is the complete result for the first page of that query. The collections_search returned 4 Louisiana-level collections. This survey does not represent the full holdings of physical repositories.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734, including wills, sales, contracts, manumissions | In-person research room; partial digitization |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes from 1731 (with gaps) | Contact the archives; some records on FamilySearch microfilm |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, tax records, succession records, military records | In-person and some online finding aids |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City directories, local history, newspapers, birth/death records held by the city | In-person; some digitized |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscript collections, maps, photographs, published histories | In-person research center |
| NARA Southeast Regional Archives (Atlanta) | Federal court records, census records for Louisiana | In-person and online request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Original succession, civil, and court records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Most original notarial acts (beyond the 1 FamilySearch volume for 1803-1820)
- Original sacramental registers not yet digitized by FamilySearch
- Orleans Parish tax records
- City directories pre-1860 (some available through local libraries)
- Records of enslaved persons held in manuscript collections
- Most manuscript collections at the Historic New Orleans Collection
- Sexton records of individual cemeteries

## Known record losses
- **Fire of 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings and many governmental and church records from the French colonial period. The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral from 1731-1788 have gaps attributable to this fire.
- **Fire of 1794:** A second major fire destroyed additional records and rebuilt structures.
- **Yellow fever epidemics:** The 1832, 1837, 1847, and 1853 epidemics disrupted record-keeping and killed thousands; the 1853 epidemic alone killed an estimated 7,849 people. Gaps in any civil or church series during epidemic years should be assumed to be disaster-related, not evidence of absence.
- **Hurricanes and floods:** The location of New Orleans at or below sea level and on the Gulf Coast made it repeatedly vulnerable to storm and flood damage to archival holdings throughout the 19th century.

**Substitute sources for lost records:**
1. St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (surviving portions from 1731, at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and on FamilySearch microfilm)
2. Notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (from 1734)
3. Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892 — index only)
4. Newspaper death notices and obituaries (Louisiana Digital Library, Newspapers.com)
5. Succession records at Orleans Parish Civil District Court and on FamilySearch (collection 2078341)
6. Published abstracts and transcriptions by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society

## Research tips
- **Think notarial, not common-law.** In Louisiana, legal transactions are recorded in notarial acts, not deed books. If you cannot find a land record, probate file, or contract in a courthouse deed or will book (there are none in the common-law sense), look in the notarial acts. See the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System.
- **Records exist in three languages.** Early New Orleans records are in French, Spanish, and English, often within the same series. Know which language applies to which period and have translation resources available.
- **Treat every missing year as a disaster gap.** Because of the fires, epidemics, hurricanes, and floods documented above, a missing record in a series is more likely a disaster loss than evidence the person was absent or the event did not occur.
- **Search sacramental registers first, not last.** For events before 1900, the Catholic church register is frequently the only surviving record of a birth, marriage, or death. St. Louis Cathedral registers begin in 1731. The FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925) is the starting point online.
- **Free people of color and enslaved persons have distinct record trails.** The gens de couleur libres community appears in sacramental registers, notarial acts, and succession records, sometimes in a separately designated series. Enslaved individuals are documented primarily in notarial acts and Catholic baptismal registers.
- **Use the New Orleans Notarial Archives.** This repository (https://www.notarialarchives.org) holds over 30 million pages from 1734, more comprehensive than any online database for this place and period, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters.
- **Check both territorial and state series.** Records from 1803-1812 are filed under Orleans Territory, not the state of Louisiana. Some online databases index them separately.
- **Immigration research:** New Orleans was the second-largest U.S. port of immigrant entry by the 1840s-1850s. Passenger arrival lists for New Orleans are at NARA and are indexed on Ancestry.com — search these for any ancestor arriving in the U.S. through the Gulf South.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Orleans Parish is surrounded by Jefferson Parish (west/south), St. Bernard Parish (east/south), St. Tammany Parish (north, across Lake Pontchartrain), and St. John the Baptist Parish (west). Families near parish boundaries may have generated records in adjacent parishes. The neighboring parishes table from the New Orleans wiki home page was not returned by the wiki_place_page tool in this run — researchers should check the FamilySearch wiki for the neighboring parishes list directly.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port Arrival Records (1840–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Port status:** One of five major U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s; the primary entry point for Irish Famine immigrants (1845–1852)
- **Population context:** By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting massive arrivals throughout the 1840s
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, manufacturing, domestic service; immigrant labor concentrated in construction, domestic work, and the docks
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Irish during the Famine years; also English, German, and Canadian arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish immigrants), Congregationalist, Episcopal, Baptist, Methodist
- **Key historical events:** Great Irish Famine (1845–1852) drove the largest wave; immigrants often arrived destitute and settled in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods before dispersing inland

## Boundary changes
- Boston was incorporated as a city in 1822 and boundaries were stable during the 1840s–1870s target period
- Suffolk County, formed in 1643, contained Boston throughout this period
- No boundary changes affect which records apply

## Available record types

### Passenger lists (customs records) — PRIMARY SOURCE
- **Date range:** 1820–1891 for the Port of Boston
- **Record set:** Customs passenger lists (not immigration inspector manifests — those begin in 1891)
- **What they contain:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin; they do NOT typically give town of birth or last residence for this era
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312
- **Digitization:** 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images) covers 1840–1850; only 3% name-indexed but **full-text searchable** — search via FamilySearch fulltext search rather than the name index
- **NARA originals:** National Archives Record Group 36; physical holdings at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)
- **Also indexed on:** Ancestry.com (subscription)
- **Critical limitation:** 1840s lists are much less detailed than post-1891 Ellis Island-era manifests. Do not expect home village or next-of-kin information.

### Naturalization records
- **Date range:** 1790–1906 (pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection 1459213) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213
- **Courts holding records:** Suffolk County Superior Court; U.S. Circuit Court, District of Massachusetts; U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts — all in Boston
- **Process:** Declaration of intention ("first papers") typically filed 2–5 years before the petition for naturalization ("second papers"); both documents are worth locating
- **What they contain:** Name, age, country of birth/allegiance, date of arrival; later records add town of birth and physical description
- **NARA originals:** Pre-1906 federal court naturalizations at National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Massachusetts began town-level vital registration in 1842; statewide collection and indexing grew through the 1840s–1850s
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, deaths recorded at the town (not county) level — search under Boston, not Suffolk County
- **Gaps:** Coverage is incomplete for the 1840s, especially for immigrant families; many Irish arrivals were not registered or died before any record was made
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church baptismal and burial records (see Church Records below)

### Church records
- **Denominations serving Irish immigrants:** Roman Catholic — Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's Parish (both Boston)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; confirmations are a separate dated entry and may fall years after baptism
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Archdiocese of Boston archives:** Holds original Catholic parish registers; the key early parishes for Irish immigrants are the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's
- **Language:** English (Catholic records in Massachusetts were kept in English, not Latin, for this period, though sacramental formulae may appear in Latin)
- **Note:** Catholic parish registers for the 1840s often predate complete civil registration and may be the only documentation of a family's vital events

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870 — all available; the 1890 census was largely destroyed
- **1850 and later:** Name every household member with age, birthplace, and occupation — essential for identifying immigrant families
- **1840:** Lists only the head of household by name; other members counted by age/sex category
- **Access:** Indexed on FamilySearch (free), Ancestry.com (subscription), and MyHeritage (subscription)
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870 — record deaths in the year preceding the census; useful for immigrants who died shortly after arrival

### The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" advertisements
- **Unique resource:** The Pilot, an Irish Catholic newspaper, published missing-persons advertisements from the 1830s through the 1920s, placed by Irish immigrants searching for relatives who had scattered after arriving in America
- **What they contain:** Name, county of origin in Ireland, approximate arrival date, last known U.S. location
- **Access:** Searchable database at the Boston College Burns Library (free online); https://infowanted.bc.edu
- **Value:** May be the only record that names the specific Irish county of origin for a 1840s arrival

### Probate records
- **Court:** Suffolk County Probate Court, Boston
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Value for immigrants:** Wills and administrations name heirs and can establish family relationships when no vital records exist; even intestate (no will) administrations list surviving family members

### Military records
- **Relevant conflict:** U.S. Civil War (1861–1865) — many 1840s immigrant men served
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA; pension files are particularly rich, often including affidavits that name wife, children, and place of birth
- **Access:** Fold3.com (subscription) for service records; Ancestry.com for pension indexes; originals at NARA, Washington D.C.

### Newspaper records
- **The Boston Pilot:** Irish Catholic; Missing Persons ads and community news (see above)
- **Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Herald, Boston Journal:** Local papers covering arrival notices, obituaries, and legal notices
- **Access:** Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank (subscription); some Boston Public Library microfilm holdings free on-site

### Tax records
- **Type:** Boston city tax assessments (property and poll tax)
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives; some years microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Substitute value:** Can place an immigrant in Boston between census years; poll tax lists include adult males even if they owned no property

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger Lists 1820-1891 (coll. 1784312); Naturalization Records 1790-1906 (coll. 1459213); Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (coll. 2061550); Church Records 1630-1920 (coll. 1921657); Probate Records 1635-1991 (coll. 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Passenger lists, census, naturalization, vital records | Subscription |
| Boston College Burns Library | Boston Pilot Missing Persons database | Free (infowanted.bc.edu) |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | RG 36 passenger lists, naturalization, military | Free finding aids; records on-site or via Ancestry/Fold3 |
| Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank | Boston newspaper archives | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210) for 1840–1850 covering Port of Boston passenger lists; this is the complete result set for that query. The FamilySearch collections_search returned 5 Massachusetts-level collections, all detailed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | NARA RG 36 passenger list originals; pre-1906 federal court naturalization records | In-person; some records on Ancestry |
| Suffolk County Probate Court, Boston | Probate files | In-person / mail |
| City of Boston Archives | Tax assessments, city records | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives directly |
| Boston Public Library | Microfilm, city directories, local newspapers | In-person; some digital |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | State vital records indexes, court records | In-person / online |

## Records NOT online
- City of Boston tax assessment records for most years
- Many original Catholic parish registers (FamilySearch has some microfilm; originals at the Archdiocese)
- State-level passenger arrival bonds and pauper records filed by the Commonwealth
- Boston almshouse and poor-relief records (immigrants arriving destitute were documented by Boston's Overseers of the Poor)

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic courthouse fire or record loss is documented for Boston in this period
- The U.S. federal census of 1890 was largely destroyed by fire and water damage in 1921 — there is no 1890 census for Boston
- Some early Catholic parish registers from the 1840s are incomplete or fragile; the Archdiocese should be consulted directly for access

## Research tips
- **Start with passenger lists, then naturalization, then census.** A name found on the 1840s customs list gives arrival context; the naturalization declaration (filed 2–5 years later) may give birthplace; the 1850 census shows the family settled somewhere
- **The Boston Pilot Missing Persons database is essential for Irish research** — it is the most specific source for county of origin in Ireland for this era (https://infowanted.bc.edu)
- **Search the fulltext of the Port of Boston passenger volume** (imageGroupNumber 003345210) rather than the name index — it is only 3% indexed but is full-text searchable on FamilySearch
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations are filed in any court, not just federal court** — check Suffolk County Superior Court records as well as the U.S. District Court in Boston, per the FamilySearch Wiki immigration article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **If the immigrant moved inland after arrival** (as is consistent with a person born ca. 1845 in Pennsylvania), search for naturalization records in Pennsylvania as well as Massachusetts — the declaration of intention was often filed in the state of residence, not the state of arrival
- **Vital records in the 1840s are at the town level in Massachusetts** — search under Boston, not Suffolk County, in both FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Catholic baptismal records may be the only evidence of children born in the 1840s** — civil registration was not comprehensive in those early years
- **City directories** (Boston directories survive from the 1820s onward) can place an immigrant at a specific address in the years between censuses; the Boston Public Library holds these
- **Check the mortality schedules** for 1850 and 1860 — immigrants who died within a year of the census date are listed with age, birthplace, and cause of death

- **The Boston Pilot Missing Persons database is essential for Irish research** — it is the most specific source for county of origin in Ireland for this era (https://infowanted.bc.edu)
- **Search the fulltext of the Port of Boston passenger volume** (imageGroupNumber 003345210) rather than the name index — it is only 3% indexed but is full-text searchable on FamilySearch
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations are filed in any court, not just federal court** — check Suffolk County Superior Court records as well as the U.S. District Court in Boston, per the FamilySearch Wiki immigration article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **If the immigrant moved inland after arrival** (as is consistent with a person born ca. 1845 in Pennsylvania), search for naturalization records in Pennsylvania as well as Massachusetts — the declaration of intention was often filed in the state of residence, not the state of arrival
- **Vital records in the 1840s are at the town level in Massachusetts** — search under Boston, not Suffolk County, in both FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Catholic baptismal records may be the only evidence of children born in the 1840s** — civil registration was not comprehensive in those early years
- **City directories** (Boston directories survive from the 1820s onward) can place an immigrant at a specific address in the years between censuses; the Boston Public Library holds these
- **Check the mortality schedules** for 1850 and 1860 — immigrants who died within a year of the census date are listed with age, birthplace, and cause of death

**Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma — Mid-1800s Native American Records**

*(Saved as **loc_001** in your project.)*

---

**Key Framing**

Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) operated entirely outside normal state and county record-keeping until statehood in 1907. Mid-1800s records for these families live in:

- **Tribal nations' own archives**
- **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) files** at the National Archives, Fort Worth (the essential physical repository)
- **Missionary church collections**

---

**The Dawes Rolls Caveat**

The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the most-used tribal enrollment database, but they **postdate** the mid-1800s. To reach mid-century ancestors you must:

1. Start with **pre-Dawes rolls** for the mid-1800s:
   - **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)**
   - **Drennen Roll (1852)**
   - Annuity payment rolls (vary by tribe and decade)
2. Use **Dawes enrollment cards** as a *bridge back* to parents and grandparents named in them.

---

**Major Record Sets & Repositories**

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| **National Archives, Fort Worth** | BIA agency correspondence, allotment files, pre-Dawes rolls — much undigitized |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections: tribal censuses/rolls, early land records, mission church records, territorial marriages — 1.3M+ records combined |
| **Tribal archives** (Five Civilized Tribes, etc.) | Tribal citizenship records, council minutes, court records |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Newspapers, territorial records, some BIA microfilm |

---

**Next Step**

Identify which tribal nation your ancestors belonged to — Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek (Muscogee), Seminole, or another nation — then build a targeted plan using the pre-Dawes rolls for the mid-1800s and the Dawes cards as the genealogical bridge to confirm family relationships.

quirks: Indian Territory did not become the state of Oklahoma until 1907 — records before statehood are held under Indian Territory or the individual tribal nations, not an Oklahoma state series.

The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914) are the definitive enrollment for the Five Civilized Tribes but post-date the mid-1800s; for earlier generations use pre-Dawes rolls: Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852), and similar annuity/payment rolls.

Each of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) maintained its own government and records; tribal affiliation determines which tribal archive and which BIA agency records apply.
Freedmen — formerly enslaved people of tribal members — were enrolled on separate Freedmen rolls within the Dawes series and require a parallel search path distinct from the 'by blood' rolls.
BIA agency records (annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records) are held at the National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region), not at state or county repositories.
Federal censuses did not cover Indian Territory populations the same way as states; tribal censuses and annuity rolls serve as the primary census substitutes for the 1830-1900 period.
Missionary records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) can name individuals before civil or tribal records appear; they are held partly at NARA and partly at denominational archives.

Land allotment records under the Dawes Act connect directly to the Dawes Rolls — an ancestor's allotment file at NARA Fort Worth cross-references their enrollment card and can document family members.
Oklahoma did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1908, one year after statehood; no civil vital registration existed for Indian Territory in the mid-1800s.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma — Native American Tribal Records (1830-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory was designated by the federal government beginning in 1830 under the Indian Removal Act. Oklahoma Territory was carved out in 1890. Both merged into the state of Oklahoma in 1907.
- **Administrative center:** The Five Civilized Tribes each maintained their own tribal capitals (e.g., Tahlequah for Cherokee, Tishomingo for Chickasaw).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government / United States; no standard state-level parent before 1907.
- **Population during period:** Indian Territory population grew substantially after forced removal in the 1830s. Population data from `place_population` was not returned for this jurisdiction — consult NARA and tribal census records for figures.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, cattle ranching, some commercial agriculture; later coal mining and railroads in the territory.
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole); Freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members); later white settlers and intermarried citizens.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward; each denomination maintained registers.
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears (1830s forced removal); Civil War (tribes were divided, some signed Confederate treaties); Dawes Act allotment (1887); Oklahoma statehood (1907).

## Boundary changes
- Indian Territory boundaries shifted repeatedly as the federal government reduced the territory through land runs (1889 onward) and creation of Oklahoma Territory (1890).
- Before 1890, nearly all of present-day Oklahoma was Indian Territory. From 1890 to 1907, the western portion was Oklahoma Territory and the eastern portion remained Indian Territory.
- Records before 1907 are NOT filed under Oklahoma state series — they are held under Indian Territory, individual tribal governments, or the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
- On statehood (1907), the two territories merged. State-level records begin at that point.

## Available record types

### Tribal rolls and enrollment records
- **Most important series:** The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914), compiled by the Dawes Commission, are the foundational enrollment for the Five Civilized Tribes. They record name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. Separate rolls exist for Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole — and a parallel Freedmen roll for each tribe.
- **Pre-Dawes rolls (critical for mid-1800s):** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852), and various annuity payment rolls. These are the primary genealogical tools for the target period.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection 1987432) covers this period with 567,890 records and 283,945 images — indexed.
- **Digitization level:** The volume search returned one digitized volume (image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable) covering tribal enrollment cards for Indian Territory 1840-1870.
- **Where held:** Originals and microfilm at the National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region). Indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma did NOT require statewide civil registration until 1908. No civil vital registration existed for Indian Territory in the mid-1800s.
- **What exists for the period:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records for the target period. Tribal records, church registers, and family bibles are the substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Missionary church registers (baptism, marriage, burial); tribal court marriage records; family bibles; cemetery inscriptions.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (collection 2134789) begins only at the territorial/statehood era.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma_Vital_Records did not return jurisdiction-specific content** — consult NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma Historical Society directly for further detail.

### Church and missionary records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward.
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, baptisms, marriages, burials, and school students.
- **Where held:** Partly at NARA; partly at denominational archives (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society, United Methodist Archives). The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321) covers this period with 123,456 records and 61,728 images.
- **Language:** English; some records in tribal languages (Cherokee syllabary was in use by the 1820s).
- **Note:** Missionary records can name individuals a generation or more before tribal rolls or civil records appear and are a primary source for the mid-1800s.

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records
- **Record types:** Annuity payment rolls (name every enrolled tribal member receiving payment), correspondence files, school enrollment records, census substitutes.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region), Record Group 75. These are largely physical or microfilm — not comprehensively digitized or indexed online.
- **Access:** In-person or microfilm loan through NARA. Catalog search at Archives.gov under Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs).
- **Digitization level:** Largely browse-only microfilm or physical only — a significant gap in online access for the mid-1800s.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory populations were enumerated inconsistently in the national federal census before statehood. The 1900 federal census was the first to include Indian Territory comprehensively.
- **Tribal/agency censuses:** Annuity rolls and periodic tribal censuses serve as the primary substitute. These are within the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" FamilySearch collection.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Collection 1987432, 1851-1959, indexed.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma_Census did not return jurisdiction-specific content** — gaps in online guidance should be supplemented by the NARA catalog at Archives.gov.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory had its own land system administered by tribal governments and the federal government; allotments under the Dawes Act (post-1887) were assigned to individual tribal members.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (Bureau of Indian Affairs / Dawes Commission) for allotments; individual tribal governments for earlier land assignments.
- **Types:** Allotment files, land patents, tribal land grants, deeds.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection 1541872) covers this period with 234,567 records and 117,283 images — indexed.
- **Where held:** Allotment records at NARA Fort Worth. BLM General Land Office (GLO) at glorecords.blm.gov for federal land patents.
- **Research tip:** An ancestor's allotment file directly cross-references their Dawes Roll enrollment card, making land records a bridge into tribal rolls.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma_Land_and_Property did not return jurisdiction-specific content** — consult NARA Fort Worth directly.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Each tribal nation had its own courts. Probate, guardianship, and civil matters were handled tribally until statehood.
- **Where held:** After statehood (1907), county district courts in Oklahoma. Before statehood, tribal court records — held at tribal archives and NARA Fort Worth.
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical or microfilm only for the pre-statehood era.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865) — all five tribes had members in both Union and Confederate forces; some tribes signed Confederate treaties. Indian Wars (various dates).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, unit rosters. The Fold3 database (fold3.com, subscription) holds significant Civil War and Indian Wars military records.
- **Where held:** NARA in Washington, D.C. (service records, pensions); NARA Fort Worth (some Indian-specific military records).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal cemeteries throughout Indian Territory, often associated with churches or communities.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has coverage for many Oklahoma cemeteries, though mid-1800s stones are less consistently photographed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for the mid-1800s; cemetery surveys by genealogical societies are the most practical access point.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Phoenix (begun 1828, published in both English and Cherokee) is a significant early source. Later territorial papers published legal notices, marriage announcements, and obituaries.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov); tribal newspaper archives.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** The Trail of Tears was a forced removal, not a voluntary immigration. Removal records (lists of individuals relocated) are held at NARA under Record Group 75.
- **Types:** Emigration rolls documenting individuals removed from the Southeast; overseer reports; annuity rolls tied to removal treaties.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and Fort Worth); indexed partially on FamilySearch.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Individual tribal nations assessed their members; federal tax records applied to non-tribal citizens in the territory.
- **Substitute value:** Annuity payment rolls serve the same function as tax/census substitutes — they name every enrolled member receiving payment in a given year.

### School and institutional records
- **Types:** Boarding school enrollment records (e.g., Carlisle Indian Industrial School, tribal academies); mission school registers.
- **Where held:** NARA (Record Group 75 for federal Indian schools); denominational archives for mission schools.
- **Note:** Boarding school records can document children removed from families and are a significant genealogical source for the late 1800s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907 (234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965 (123,456 records); 1 digitized volume of tribal enrollment cards (940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records; federal census records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War military records for Indian Territory units | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Historical newspapers including Cherokee Phoenix | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Catalog access to Record Group 75 (BIA) for ordering copies | Free catalog; copy fees apply |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching Indian Territory 1830-1910; additional volumes may exist at broader or narrower jurisdictional levels not captured in this page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma — Native American Tribal Records (1830-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory was designated by the federal government beginning in 1830 under the Indian Removal Act. Oklahoma Territory was carved out in 1890. Both merged into the state of Oklahoma in 1907.
- **Administrative center:** The Five Civilized Tribes each maintained their own tribal capitals (e.g., Tahlequah for Cherokee, Tishomingo for Chickasaw).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government / United States; no standard state-level parent before 1907.
- **Population during period:** Indian Territory population grew substantially after forced removal in the 1830s. Population data from `place_population` was not returned for this jurisdiction — consult NARA and tribal census records for figures.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, cattle ranching, some commercial agriculture; later coal mining and railroads in the territory.
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole); Freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members); later white settlers and intermarried citizens.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward; each denomination maintained registers.
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears (1830s forced removal); Civil War (tribes were divided, some signed Confederate treaties); Dawes Act allotment (1887); Oklahoma statehood (1907).

## Boundary changes
- Indian Territory boundaries shifted repeatedly as the federal government reduced the territory through land runs (1889 onward) and creation of Oklahoma Territory (1890).
- Before 1890, nearly all of present-day Oklahoma was Indian Territory. From 1890 to 1907, the western portion was Oklahoma Territory and the eastern portion remained Indian Territory.
- Records before 1907 are NOT filed under Oklahoma state series — they are held under Indian Territory, individual tribal governments, or the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
- On statehood (1907), the two territories merged. State-level records begin at that point.

## Available record types

### Tribal rolls and enrollment records
- **Most important series:** The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914), compiled by the Dawes Commission, are the foundational enrollment for the Five Civilized Tribes. They record name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. Separate rolls exist for Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole — and a parallel Freedmen roll for each tribe.
- **Pre-Dawes rolls (critical for mid-1800s):** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852), and various annuity payment rolls. These are the primary genealogical tools for the target period.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection 1987432) covers this period with 567,890 records and 283,945 images — indexed.
- **Digitization level:** The volume search returned one digitized volume (image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable) covering tribal enrollment cards for Indian Territory 1840-1870.
- **Where held:** Originals and microfilm at the National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region). Indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma did NOT require statewide civil registration until 1908. No civil vital registration existed for Indian Territory in the mid-1800s.
- **What exists for the period:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records for the target period. Tribal records, church registers, and family bibles are the substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Missionary church registers (baptism, marriage, burial); tribal court marriage records; family bibles; cemetery inscriptions.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (collection 2134789) begins only at the territorial/statehood era.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma_Vital_Records did not return jurisdiction-specific content** — consult NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma Historical Society directly for further detail.

### Church and missionary records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward.
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, baptisms, marriages, burials, and school students.
- **Where held:** Partly at NARA; partly at denominational archives (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society, United Methodist Archives). The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321) covers this period with 123,456 records and 61,728 images.
- **Language:** English; some records in tribal languages (Cherokee syllabary was in use by the 1820s).
- **Note:** Missionary records can name individuals a generation or more before tribal rolls or civil records appear and are a primary source for the mid-1800s.

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records
- **Record types:** Annuity payment rolls (name every enrolled tribal member receiving payment), correspondence files, school enrollment records, census substitutes.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region), Record Group 75. These are largely physical or microfilm — not comprehensively digitized or indexed online.
- **Access:** In-person or microfilm loan through NARA. Catalog search at Archives.gov under Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs).
- **Digitization level:** Largely browse-only microfilm or physical only — a significant gap in online access for the mid-1800s.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory populations were enumerated inconsistently in the national federal census before statehood. The 1900 federal census was the first to include Indian Territory comprehensively.
- **Tribal/agency censuses:** Annuity rolls and periodic tribal censuses serve as the primary substitute. These are within the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" FamilySearch collection.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Collection 1987432, 1851-1959, indexed.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma_Census did not return jurisdiction-specific content** — gaps in online guidance should be supplemented by the NARA catalog at Archives.gov.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory had its own land system administered by tribal governments and the federal government; allotments under the Dawes Act (post-1887) were assigned to individual tribal members.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (Bureau of Indian Affairs / Dawes Commission) for allotments; individual tribal governments for earlier land assignments.
- **Types:** Allotment files, land patents, tribal land grants, deeds.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection 1541872) covers this period with 234,567 records and 117,283 images — indexed.
- **Where held:** Allotment records at NARA Fort Worth. BLM General Land Office (GLO) at glorecords.blm.gov for federal land patents.
- **Research tip:** An ancestor's allotment file directly cross-references their Dawes Roll enrollment card, making land records a bridge into tribal rolls.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Oklahoma_Land_and_Property did not return jurisdiction-specific content** — consult NARA Fort Worth directly.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Each tribal nation had its own courts. Probate, guardianship, and civil matters were handled tribally until statehood.
- **Where held:** After statehood (1907), county district courts in Oklahoma. Before statehood, tribal court records — held at tribal archives and NARA Fort Worth.
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical or microfilm only for the pre-statehood era.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865) — all five tribes had members in both Union and Confederate forces; some tribes signed Confederate treaties. Indian Wars (various dates).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, unit rosters. The Fold3 database (fold3.com, subscription) holds significant Civil War and Indian Wars military records.
- **Where held:** NARA in Washington, D.C. (service records, pensions); NARA Fort Worth (some Indian-specific military records).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal cemeteries throughout Indian Territory, often associated with churches or communities.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has coverage for many Oklahoma cemeteries, though mid-1800s stones are less consistently photographed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for the mid-1800s; cemetery surveys by genealogical societies are the most practical access point.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Phoenix (begun 1828, published in both English and Cherokee) is a significant early source. Later territorial papers published legal notices, marriage announcements, and obituaries.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov); tribal newspaper archives.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** The Trail of Tears was a forced removal, not a voluntary immigration. Removal records (lists of individuals relocated) are held at NARA under Record Group 75.
- **Types:** Emigration rolls documenting individuals removed from the Southeast; overseer reports; annuity rolls tied to removal treaties.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and Fort Worth); indexed partially on FamilySearch.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Individual tribal nations assessed their members; federal tax records applied to non-tribal citizens in the territory.
- **Substitute value:** Annuity payment rolls serve the same function as tax/census substitutes — they name every enrolled member receiving payment in a given year.

### School and institutional records
- **Types:** Boarding school enrollment records (e.g., Carlisle Indian Industrial School, tribal academies); mission school registers.
- **Where held:** NARA (Record Group 75 for federal Indian schools); denominational archives for mission schools.
- **Note:** Boarding school records can document children removed from families and are a significant genealogical source for the late 1800s.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker Community Records (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was granted to William Penn in 1681; first settlement 1682. It became a Commonwealth upon independence (1776).
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital and center of Quaker life)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial), then independent Commonwealth
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this range. The first federal census (1790) enumerated 434,373 persons in Pennsylvania.
- **Economy:** Mixed agriculture, grain milling, iron manufacture, Atlantic trade; Philadelphia was the largest city in British North America.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (dominant in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware counties), German Reformed/Lutheran settlers (Lancaster, York, Berks counties), Scots-Irish Presbyterians (interior and frontier counties), Welsh Quakers (Montgomery County townships).
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Reformed, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Brethren (Dunkers), Baptist, Methodist (arriving late 1700s).
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783) — Quakers faced intense pressure over pacifism and were disowned in large numbers for military service; Constitutional Convention (Philadelphia, 1787).

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's exterior boundaries were largely stable across the period. Interior county boundaries changed frequently as new counties were carved from existing ones.
- At 1750, the original counties of Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, and Lancaster dominated. York (1749), Cumberland (1750), Berks (1752), Northampton (1752), Bedford (1771), Westmoreland (1773), and others formed during the period — records before a county's formation date are held by its parent county.
- Always identify which county existed on the date of the event, not the modern county, and search the parent if the county had not yet formed.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration until 1906 (per the FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)). No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for the late 1700s.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker meeting records are the primary substitute. See Church Records section below.
- **Where held:** For the 1750–1800 period, there are no civil vital records to consult.

### Church records — Quaker (Society of Friends)
This is the central record type for this research objective.

**Meeting structure and records created:**
- **Monthly meetings** — The basic unit. Recorded births (registrations, not baptisms), marriages (by consent of the meeting, not a clergyman), deaths, disownments, and certificates of removal. These are the richest genealogical sources.
- **Quarterly meetings** — Grouped several monthly meetings; kept oversight minutes. Less individual detail but useful for locating which monthly meeting a family belonged to.
- **Yearly meeting** — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed Pennsylvania and New Jersey meetings. Kept broader policy minutes. FamilySearch has digitized 1 volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322, 145 images, 1750–1800; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image**).

**Specific record types within Quaker meetings:**
| Record type | What it contains | Genealogical value |
|---|---|---|
| Birth/Naming registers | Name, parents' names, date | Direct vital record substitute |
| Marriage certificates | Names of both parties, parents, all witnesses | Can yield dozens of family names per document |
| Death/Burial registers | Name, date, sometimes age or relationship | Direct vital record substitute |
| Certificates of removal | Family names, origin meeting, destination meeting | Essential for tracing migration |
| Disownment minutes | Name, reason, family context | Names people even if excommunicated |
| Reinstatement records | Follows disownment; names and circumstances | Can resolve gaps after military service period |

**Where Quaker records are held:**
1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) — the largest repository of American Quaker records. Holds original meeting minutes, registers, and certificates for the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting area. Access: in-person and finding aids online at swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library.
2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA) — the second major repository. Significant holdings for Philadelphia-area monthly meetings.
3. **FamilySearch microfilm** — FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting registers and minutes; search the FamilySearch Catalog (catalog.familysearch.org) by county and "Friends" or "Quakers" to identify available film numbers.
4. **Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy** — 6 volumes abstracting Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and other state meeting records. The standard first search tool. Available in major genealogical libraries and on microfilm. FamilySearch has microfilmed the underlying records that Hinshaw abstracted.

**Access level:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (FamilySearch image group 001188322) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Most monthly meeting registers on FamilySearch are similarly browse-only for this period. Hinshaw's abstracts are the indexed entry point.

**Key counties with dense Quaker populations (late 1700s):**
- Philadelphia County (Philadelphia Monthly Meeting, Abington Monthly Meeting, others)
- Chester County (many rural monthly meetings; dense Quaker settlement)
- Bucks County (Bucks Quarter; many meetings)
- Delaware County (separated from Chester County in 1789)
- Montgomery County (separated from Philadelphia County in 1784; Welsh Quaker settlements at Gwynedd, Merion, Radnor)

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790. It is available and indexed. The 1800 federal census is also available. These are the only enumerations within the 1750–1800 window that name heads of household. Neither pre-revolutionary colonial census nor a Pennsylvania state census covers this period in a comparable way.
- **Tax records as census substitutes:** Pennsylvania county tax lists from the 1750s–1780s name taxable residents and can place a family in a specific township before 1790. These are held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and online (FamilySearch, Ancestry).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, intestate administrations, guardianships, inventories, distribution records.
- **Date range:** Available from county formation; Philadelphia County probate begins in the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Each county's Register of Wills held probate. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds many historic series. FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) contains 3,200,560 images — **browse-only** (0 indexed records listed; images must be browsed).
- **Quaker note:** Quaker wills sometimes reference meeting membership or bequeath funds to the meeting. A will may confirm family structure that meeting records document.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; the Penn proprietorship granted land, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Penn family Land Office granted patents through the colonial period; the Commonwealth Land Office continued after independence. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original warrant, survey, and patent records.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds (county recorder of deeds), and tax records.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for original grants; county courthouses for deeds.
- **Quaker note:** Quaker communities often settled in clusters. A neighbor search in land records can identify other meeting members adjacent to the family of interest.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Quaker note:** Quaker discipline forbade military service. Those who served were typically disowned. Revolutionary War pension files (at NARA) and state militia records may name Quakers who did serve, and those names often appear in the meeting's disownment minutes as a cross-check.
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files, Continental Army service records); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records); Fold3.com (digitized pension files).

### Cemetery records
- Quaker meetings maintained burial grounds adjacent to meetinghouses. Quaker graves in the 1700s were typically plain and unmarked or minimally marked.
- **Sexton records:** Some monthly meetings kept burial registers (captured in Hinshaw's abstracts and FamilySearch microfilm).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com has entries for some Quaker burial grounds, but coverage for 18th-century graves is sparse.

### Newspaper records
- The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) published marriage and death notices; Quakers sometimes appeared, though the Society officially discouraged ostentation.
- **Where held:** Accessible via Accessible Archives and Newspapers.com; also microfilmed and at the Library of Congress.

### Immigration and emigration records
- Many Pennsylvania Quakers arrived from England and Wales in the 1680s–1720s; by the 1750s most were second or third generation. Certificates of removal within the meeting network document internal migration.
- For those still immigrating: Philadelphia was the primary port of entry. Pennsylvania ship passenger lists are available at NARA and online (Ancestry, FamilySearch).
- Quaker meetings in England (particularly London Yearly Meeting) and Wales may hold corresponding certificates of removal for ancestors who emigrated earlier.

### Tax records
- Pennsylvania county tax lists (assessments) survive from the 1750s onward for many counties and name taxable residents, including non-landowners.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, county historical societies. Published abstracts exist for some counties.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can place a family in a specific township in the years between censuses and before the 1790 federal census.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections relevant to this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322; browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 and 1800 federal censuses (indexed); Pennsylvania passenger lists; some county deed abstracts | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Revolutionary War pension files, Continental Army records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Pennsylvania Gazette and other colonial-era papers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave.com | Quaker burial ground listings (variable coverage) | Free |

**Coverage note:** FamilySearch volume search returned 1 digitized volume matching Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 (the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes). This is not the complete picture — additional monthly meeting registers have been microfilmed and are in the FamilySearch Catalog but may not surface in volume search. Always also search the FamilySearch Catalog directly for county-level Quaker records.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Original Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records, monthly meeting minutes, registers, certificates | In-person; finding aids online |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Philadelphia-area meeting records, Quaker publications | In-person; finding aids online |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Colonial and Commonwealth land records, militia records, early county records | In-person; some online |
| County courthouses / Register of Wills | County probate, deeds, tax assessment records | In-person or mail |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) | Broad manuscript holdings including Quaker-adjacent records | In-person; some digitized |

## Records NOT online
- Most individual monthly meeting registers and minutes for the 1750–1800 period are on FamilySearch microfilm but are NOT name-indexed — they must be browsed or located via Hinshaw's abstracts first.
- Original certificates of removal are largely held at Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or Haverford, not digitized.
- Pennsylvania colonial tax lists are often only partially digitized; many remain physical-only at the State Archives or county historical societies.
- Welsh and English meeting records (for immigrant ancestors) require contact with the relevant meeting archive in Britain.

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic statewide loss of Quaker records is known for Pennsylvania. Individual meetings may have gaps due to poor storage, but the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting network was unusually well organized and its records largely survive.
- Some county courthouse records from the revolutionary period are incomplete due to wartime disruption.

## Research tips
- **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia before the original minutes.** The 6-volume abstract set is the indexed entry point to Pennsylvania Quaker records. Once you find a family in Hinshaw, note the meeting name and then pull the original minutes via FamilySearch microfilm or the Swarthmore/Haverford collections for full detail. ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))
- **Identify the specific monthly meeting.** Each family belonged to a monthly meeting, not just a yearly meeting. Knowing the meeting (e.g., Gwynedd Monthly Meeting, Abington Monthly Meeting, Falls Monthly Meeting) is essential before searching; the FamilySearch Catalog is organized at this level.
- **Certificates of removal follow the family across moves.** If a family disappears from a meeting's minutes, search for a certificate of removal. The destination meeting's records should contain a corresponding certificate of arrival.
- **Quaker calendar conventions.** Before searching original minutes, understand that months were numbered. "1st Month" = January after 1752 (when England adopted the Gregorian calendar). Before 1752, "1st Month" was March under the Old Style calendar. Dates near the turn of the year may need double-dating.
- **Disownment is not the end of the record trail.** A disowned member may later be reinstated; the reinstatement record names them again and often explains the original offense. Disowned relatives sometimes appear as witnesses on later certificates for family members still in good standing.
- **Cross-reference with neighboring counties' meetings.** Monthly meeting territories did not always follow county lines. A family in one county might belong to a meeting headquartered in an adjacent county. The Swarthmore finding aids organize records by meeting, not by county.
- **1790 federal census as a locator.** The 1790 census is the first systematic name-indexed tool for placing a Pennsylvania family in a specific county and township — use it to anchor which county (and therefore which meeting records) to search for the decade before.
- **The wiki pages for Pennsylvania Church Records** ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)) provide the foundational research guidance for this jurisdiction.
