These are the only enumerations within the 1750–1800 window that name heads of household. Neither pre-revolutionary colonial census nor a Pennsylvania state census covers this period in a comparable way.
- **Tax records as census substitutes:** Pennsylvania county tax lists from the 1750s–1780s name taxable residents and can place a family in a specific township before 1790. These are held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and online (FamilySearch, Ancestry).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, intestate administrations, guardianships, inventories, distribution records.
- **Date range:** Available from county formation; Philadelphia County probate begins in the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Each county's Register of Wills held probate. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds many historic series. FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) contains 3,200,560 images — **browse-only** (0 indexed records listed; images must be browsed).
- **Quaker note:** Quaker wills sometimes reference meeting membership or bequeath funds to the meeting. A will may confirm family structure that meeting records document.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; the Penn proprietorship granted land, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Penn family Land Office granted patents through the colonial period; the Commonwealth Land Office continued after independence. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original warrant, survey, and patent records.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds (county recorder of deeds), and tax records.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for original grants; county courthouses for deeds.
- **Quaker note:** Quaker communities often settled in clusters. A neighbor search in land records can identify other meeting members adjacent to the family of interest.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Quaker note:** Quaker discipline forbade military service. Those who served were typically disowned. Revolutionary War pension files (at NARA) and state militia records may name Quakers who did serve, and those names often appear in the meeting's disownment minutes as a cross-check.
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files, Continental Army service records); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records); Fold3.com (digitized pension files).

### Cemetery records
- Quaker meetings maintained burial grounds adjacent to meetinghouses. Quaker graves in the 1700s were typically plain and unmarked or minimally marked.
- **Sexton records:** Some monthly meetings kept burial registers (captured in Hinshaw's abstracts and FamilySearch microfilm).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com has entries for some Quaker burial grounds, but coverage for 18th-century graves is sparse.

### Newspaper records
- The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) published marriage and death notices; Quakers sometimes appeared, though the Society officially discouraged ostentation.
- **Where held:** Accessible via Accessible Archives and Newspapers.com; also microfilmed and at the Library of Congress.

### Immigration and emigration records
- Many Pennsylvania Quakers arrived from England and Wales in the 1680s–1720s; by the 1750s most were second or third generation. Certificates of removal within the meeting network document internal migration.
- For those still immigrating: Philadelphia was the primary port of entry. Pennsylvania ship passenger lists are available at NARA and online (Ancestry, FamilySearch).
- Quaker meetings in England (particularly London Yearly Meeting) and Wales may hold corresponding certificates of removal for ancestors who emigrated earlier.

### Tax records
- Pennsylvania county tax lists (assessments) survive from the 1750s onward for many counties and name taxable residents, including non-landowners.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, county historical societies. Published abstracts exist for some counties.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can place a family in a specific township in the years between censuses and before the 1790 federal census.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections relevant to this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322; browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 and 1800 federal censuses (indexed); Pennsylvania passenger lists; some county deed abstracts | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Revolutionary War pension files, Continental Army records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Pennsylvania Gazette and other colonial-era papers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave.com | Quaker burial ground listings (variable coverage) | Free |

**Coverage note:** FamilySearch volume search returned 1 digitized volume matching Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 (the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes). This is not the complete picture — additional monthly meeting registers have been microfilmed and are in the FamilySearch Catalog but may not surface in volume search. Always also search the FamilySearch Catalog directly for county-level Quaker records.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Original Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records, monthly meeting minutes, registers, certificates | In-person; finding aids online |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Philadelphia-area meeting records, Quaker publications | In-person; finding aids online |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Colonial and Commonwealth land records, militia records, early county records | In-person; some online |
| County courthouses / Register of Wills | County probate, deeds, tax assessment records | In-person or mail |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) | Broad manuscript holdings including Quaker-adjacent records | In-person; some digitized |

## Records NOT online
- Most individual monthly meeting registers and minutes for the 1750–1800 period are on FamilySearch microfilm but are NOT name-indexed — they must be browsed or located via Hinshaw's abstracts first.
- Original certificates of removal are largely held at Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or Haverford, not digitized.
- Pennsylvania colonial tax lists are often only partially digitized; many remain physical-only at the State Archives or county historical societies.
- Welsh and English meeting records (for immigrant ancestors) require contact with the relevant meeting archive in Britain.

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic statewide loss of Quaker records is known for Pennsylvania. Individual meetings may have gaps due to poor storage, but the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting network was unusually well organized and its records largely survive.
- Some county courthouse records from the revolutionary period are incomplete due to wartime disruption.

## Research tips
- **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia before the original minutes.** The 6-volume abstract set is the indexed entry point to Pennsylvania Quaker records. Once you find a family in Hinshaw, note the meeting name and then pull the original minutes via FamilySearch microfilm or the Swarthmore/Haverford collections for full detail. ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))
- **Identify the specific monthly meeting.** Each family belonged to a monthly meeting, not just a yearly meeting. Knowing the meeting (e.g., Gwynedd Monthly Meeting, Abington Monthly Meeting, Falls Monthly Meeting) is essential before searching; the FamilySearch Catalog is organized at this level.
- **Certificates of removal follow the family across moves.** If a family disappears from a meeting's minutes, search for a certificate of removal. The destination meeting's records should contain a corresponding certificate of arrival.
- **Quaker calendar conventions.** Before searching original minutes, understand that months were numbered. "1st Month" = January after 1752 (when England adopted the Gregorian calendar). Before 1752, "1st Month" was March under the Old Style calendar. Dates near the turn of the year may need double-dating.
- **Disownment is not the end of the record trail.** A disowned member may later be reinstated; the reinstatement record names them again and often explains the original offense. Disowned relatives sometimes appear as witnesses on later certificates for family members still in good standing.
- **Cross-reference with neighboring counties' meetings.** Monthly meeting territories did not always follow county lines. A family in one county might belong to a meeting headquartered in an adjacent county. The Swarthmore finding aids organize records by meeting, not by county.
- **1790 federal census as a locator.** The 1790 census is the first systematic name-indexed tool for placing a Pennsylvania family in a specific county and township — use it to anchor which county (and therefore which meeting records) to search for the decade before.
- **The wiki pages for Pennsylvania Church Records** ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)) provide the foundational research guidance for this jurisdiction.

This locality guide has been saved as **loc_001** for your project. Here's a summary of what was found:

---

## Pittsburgh & Allegheny County, PA — Late 1800s Steel Industry Research Guide

**Time period covered:** ~1860–1910

### Key Record Sets

1. **Federal Censuses (1860–1910)** — Fully indexed online; list each person's occupation. Essential for placing ancestors in the mills year by year.

2. **Ethnic Catholic Parish Registers** — Often the *only* family record before Pennsylvania statewide vital registration began in **1906**. Critical for immigrant steel-worker families.

3. **Naturalization Records** — Held at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives (Philadelphia); frequently name the exact Old World town of origin.

4. **Pittsburgh City Directories** — Held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**; list address and employer every year between censuses.

5. **Company Employment Records** — Fragmentary and uneven, but some survive at:
   - **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center)
   - **Rivers of Steel archives**

6. **Pennsylvania Marriage Records (from 1885)** and **Death Certificates (from 1906)** — Indexed on FamilySearch.

7. **Probate Records** — Approximately 3.2 million browse-only images on FamilySearch.

### Key Pitfalls to Avoid

- **Don't expect civil vital records before 1906** — Pennsylvania statewide registration didn't exist. Go to the parish instead.
- **Watch for "Allegheny City"** — The independent City of Allegheny was a separate municipality until **1907**. Pre-annexation records are filed under *"Allegheny City,"* not Pittsburgh.

### Next Steps

Once you identify a specific ancestor's name, approximate dates, and ethnic background, a targeted research plan can sequence which repositories to contact and in what order. Let me know if you'd like to proceed!

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh incorporated as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Pittsburgh was a rapidly growing industrial city. Exact figures from `place_population` were not returned by the tool; Wikipedia notes massive immigrant influx from Ireland, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Croatia, and Italy in this period.
- **Economy:** Steel production dominated from the late 1860s forward. Carnegie's steel empire and other major firms (iron, glass, coke) drew hundreds of thousands of workers. Pittsburgh earned the name 'Steel City' by the 1880s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German (early arrivals); Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, and other Eastern/Southern European immigrants surged in from the 1880s–1900s.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), German Lutheran and Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Great Pittsburgh Fire (1845, predates target period); Homestead Strike (1892); major immigration waves 1880s–1900s.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were stable during the 1860–1910 target period.
- The independent City of Allegheny (across the river) was annexed into Pittsburgh in 1907 — records created in the City of Allegheny before 1907 are filed separately under that municipality, not under Pittsburgh.
- Always search both Pittsburgh and Allegheny City records for events near or before 1907.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration began in 1906 at the state level. Some county-level registration predates this, but coverage is inconsistent.
- **What exists:** Death certificates from 1906 onward are well-covered. Marriage records at the county level begin around 1885 in indexed FamilySearch collections. Birth certificates at the statewide level begin in 1906.
- **FamilySearch collections covering this period:**
  - *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* (collection 2255317): 4,218,763 indexed records with images — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* (collection 1921317): 524,189 indexed records with images — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection 1571957): 312,045 indexed records — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection 1502909): 198,765 records, no images — **index only**
- **Gaps:** For births, marriages, and deaths before 1885–1906, civil records are largely absent; church records are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German, Irish), German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Ethnic Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh are among the most important genealogical sources for the steel-industry immigrant population.
- **Where held:** Local parish offices; diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh); FamilySearch has microfilmed some Pennsylvania church records. The FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records* (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) returned in the tool but is labeled as a test fixture for Schuylkill County — do not apply it to Allegheny County.
- **Language:** Records in Catholic ethnic parishes may be in Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Latin, or German depending on the parish served.
- **Access:** Contact the Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives and individual surviving parishes directly. Some records have been microfilmed by FamilySearch — search the FamilySearch Catalog for Allegheny County church records.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 censuses are available (1890 was largely destroyed). The 1880 census includes a Soundex index. Federal censuses 1860–1900 list occupation for each adult male — critical for identifying steel workers and their specific trade.
- **Access:** 1860–1910 federal censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1860, 1870, 1880 (deaths in the year preceding the census) — useful for the gap before death certificate registration.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a regular state census during this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions — held at the Allegheny County Register of Wills.

---

Philadelphia in 1793 was the nation's capital and largest city, hit by a yellow fever epidemic that killed roughly one-tenth of its 50,000 residents between August and November. Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration of births or deaths in 1793 (that did not begin until 1906), so the primary death evidence comes from **church burial registers**, a **published name list compiled by pamphleteer Mathew Carey**, and the **minutes of the citizen Committee of Health** — all held physically at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** and the **Philadelphia City Archives**. Families who fled the city during the epidemic may have generated records in the surrounding Pennsylvania counties (Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, Delaware) or across the river in Burlington or Gloucester counties, New Jersey. The biggest practical warning is that most of the epidemic-specific records — the Committee of Health relief rolls, the Bush Hill hospital registers, the Orphans' Court guardianship files created for children left parentless by the epidemic — are **not online** and require a visit or correspondence with those Philadelphia repositories.

The next step is to identify which specific family or families you are tracing and build a research plan targeting the **Mathew Carey name list**, the **1793–1795 window of the Philadelphia Register of Wills**, and the **burial registers of the denomination(s)** those families attended.

---

**Key repositories and record types to consult:**

- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** — Committee of Health minutes and relief rolls, Mathew Carey's 1793 pamphlet name list, church burial registers for multiple denominations
- **Philadelphia City Archives** — Orphans' Court guardianship files (for children orphaned by the epidemic), probate records, early city administrative records
- **Philadelphia Register of Wills** — Wills and administrations spiked sharply in the fall of 1793; searching the 1793–1795 window is highly productive
- **Church burial registers** — Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal), St. Peter's, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes'), St. Mary's (Catholic), First Presbyterian, German Reformed, and others; denominations vary by family origin
- **Pennsylvania state and county records in surrounding counties** — for families who fled to Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, or Delaware counties
- **New Jersey county records (Burlington, Gloucester)** — for families who crossed the Delaware River during the outbreak
- **Bush Hill hospital records** — partial survivor; held at HSP; records the sick treated during the epidemic
- **FamilySearch & Ancestry** — some Philadelphia church registers are microfilmed and partially indexed, but epidemic-era coverage is incomplete online

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (Focus Period: 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the City of Philadelphia incorporated 1701; city and county were consolidated in 1854 (outside this period).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 42,000–50,000 in the early 1790s. The 1793 epidemic killed roughly 5,000 people — about one-tenth of the population — between August and November. Thousands more fled the city during those months. (Source: Wikipedia, "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)
- **Economy:** Mercantile trade, shipping, crafts, professional services; Philadelphia was the national capital and the largest U.S. city at the time.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English, Scots-Irish, German, and Welsh settlers, with a significant free Black community; recent French Caribbean refugees also present by summer 1793.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Quaker (Friends Meeting), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic (St. Mary's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Methodist, Baptist, and African Episcopal (Mother Bethel, founded 1794).
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November); Philadelphia served as the U.S. capital 1790–1800; the epidemic caused the federal government to temporarily relocate.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County boundaries were stable throughout the 1780–1810 period. The city and county were not consolidated until 1854, so the city limits in 1793 were smaller than the county. Records may be filed at the city level (city court, city clerk) or county level (County Court of Common Pleas, Register of Wills), depending on the record type.
- Families who fled during the epidemic may have sought refuge in adjoining Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, or Delaware counties in Pennsylvania, or in Burlington or Gloucester counties in New Jersey. Records generated during those months could appear in any of those jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania vital records returned only a generic fallback during this survey; no jurisdiction-specific start date can be confirmed from a tool result for any earlier local registration system in Philadelphia. The FamilySearch Wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy should be checked for current guidance.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil death registration existed. Church burial registers and the Mathew Carey published death list ("A Short Account of the Malignant Fever," first edition 1793, with appended list of the dead) are the primary death evidence for the epidemic period.
- **Where held:** The published Carey list has been widely reprinted and is held by major research libraries. Church registers are held by individual congregations, diocesan archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and on FamilySearch microfilm (see Church records below).
- **Gaps:** No civil vital registration for this period — church records and published accounts are the only systematic death evidence.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; the Mathew Carey name list; Committee of Health minutes and relief records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal, Quaker, Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Roman Catholic, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei), Methodist, Baptist, and African Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Burial registers are the critical record type for epidemic deaths — they name the deceased, often give a date, sometimes a cause of death or age.
- **Where held:** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania hold transcriptions and indexes of many colonial and early national Philadelphia church registers. Individual denominational archives also hold originals. FamilySearch has microfilmed many registers; the wiki_search result for Philadelphia genealogy states that many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published, and that the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Key congregations for epidemic burials:** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal), Gloria Dei (Swedish Lutheran/Old Swedes'), St. Mary's (Catholic), and the Friends Meeting burial grounds all received epidemic dead.
- **Language:** English for most records; German for Lutheran and German Reformed registers; Latin for some Catholic sacramental records.
- **Digitization level:** Partial. FamilySearch's one confirmed digitized volume for the city-county in the 1780–1800 window is the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Individual congregation registers vary widely.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (first enumeration — names heads of household; taken 3 years before the epidemic, establishes pre-epidemic household composition), 1800 (first post-epidemic census — shows survivors and movers).
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct regular state censuses in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists for Philadelphia County survive and can serve as intercensal substitutes. The 1793 Committee of Health maintained a relief roll of survivors receiving aid, which functions as a partial enumeration of those who remained in the city.
- **Access:** The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate), inventories, guardianships. The epidemic caused a surge in probate filings in autumn 1793 and into 1794 as estates of the dead were settled.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records begin with county formation in 1682. FamilySearch has "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196), which holds 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — browse-only images.
- **Where held:** The Register of Wills for Philadelphia County; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds some copies. The FamilySearch collection linked above provides images.
- **Research tip:** A cluster of probate filings dated autumn 1793–early 1794 in the Register of Wills for Philadelphia County is a direct product of the epidemic. Searching this window is especially productive for epidemic families.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was distributed by the Penn proprietors, then by the Commonwealth).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (state level) issued patents; county Recorder of Deeds holds subsequent deed transfers.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, patents, tax records.
- **Date range:** County deed records from 1682.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City/County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original land office warrant and patent records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is the dominant military event just preceding the epidemic period. French Revolutionary Wars brought French Caribbean refugees to Philadelphia by 1793.
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records, Pennsylvania militia records, pension files (post-1792 invalid pension law), bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington D.C. and mid-Atlantic regional facilities; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has many NARA military records online.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Friends burial grounds, St. Mary's Catholic churchyard, and numerous smaller congregation grounds. Potter's Field received indigent and unidentified dead during the epidemic.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has entries for many Philadelphia historic cemeteries. Coverage for 1793 epidemic deaths varies by congregation.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual congregations and at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had multiple active papers in 1793, including Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and the Federal Gazette. Both published weekly mortality bills and lists of the dead during the epidemic.
- **Where held:** The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold original runs. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) have some digitized Philadelphia papers.
- **Content value:** Mortality bills published during the epidemic are a unique genealogical source, listing the dead by name, sometimes with occupation or street address. Estate settlement notices and orphans' court notices also appear in these papers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Passenger lists survive for arrivals in the 1780–1810 period.
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists, naturalization records (filed at Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas and District Court), declarations of intention.
- **Where held:** NARA holds the federal-era customs lists. FamilySearch and Ancestry have indexed many pre-1820 Philadelphia arrivals. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records) overlap this period for marriage evidence. Naturalizations before 1906 were filed in any court of record — check both Common Pleas and District Court records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching immigrant families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County property tax and provincial/state tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Pre-Revolutionary provincial tax records survive; county assessment books continue through the period.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessments taken in the years around 1793 can establish presence in the city both before and after the epidemic, and can document changes in household composition (a head of household absent from post-epidemic assessment books likely died or moved).

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793)
These record types exist specifically because of the epidemic and have no peacetime equivalent:

1. **Mathew Carey's published name list** — Appended to "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (multiple editions, 1793–1794). Lists names of the dead by date of death. Widely held by research libraries; partially transcribed online.
2. **Committee of Health minutes and relief records** — The citizens' Committee kept detailed records of who died, who received relief, and the disposition of orphaned children. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793; FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
3. **Bush Hill hospital registers** — Bush Hill was converted into the epidemic's main hospital. Admission and death registers, where surviving, are at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
4. **Orphans' Court records** — The epidemic created many orphans. The Philadelphia Orphans' Court handled guardianship appointments in the months following; these filings name both the deceased parent(s) and the surviving children.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2 million images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 and 1800 federal census (indexed); various Philadelphia church record transcriptions; passenger lists | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Some 1793 Philadelphia newspaper runs with mortality bills | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Some digitized early Philadelphia newspapers | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions for major Philadelphia churchyards | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, customs passenger lists | Free finding aids; some images on Fold3 |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume for the 1780–1810 window (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, browse-only). `collections_search` returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections, of which 3 have date ranges overlapping 1793: Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images), Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (indexed), and Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (indexed). The one Pennsylvania-level marriage collection dated only 1885–1950 and the Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 collection both postdate the target period. The FamilySearch jurisdiction-specific wiki pages for Philadelphia all resolved to a generic fallback — additional FamilySearch-digitized volumes specific to Philadelphia churches may exist and were not captured by these tool results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), Philadelphia | Committee of Health minutes; Bush Hill hospital records; church register transcriptions; manuscript collections; newspapers | In-person; some finding aids online at hsp.org |
| Philadelphia City Archives | City government records; tax assessments; Committee of Health records; deed books | In-person; contact phila.gov/city-archives |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Provincial and state tax records; land office warrant and patent records; militia records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP) | Indexes and transcriptions of Philadelphia church records | In-person and some digital resources via gspp.org |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | 18th-century newspapers; Mathew Carey imprints; city directories | In-person |
| Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center | Catholic sacramental registers | By appointment |
| Individual congregations | Original registers — Christ Church, Gloria Dei, Friends meetings, etc. | Contact each congregation |

## Records NOT online

- Committee of Health minutes and relief distribution records (Philadelphia City Archives and HSP — physical only)
- Bush Hill hospital admission and death registers (HSP — physical only, where surviving)
- Philadelphia Orphans' Court guardianship files from autumn 1793 (Philadelphia City Archives — physical only)
- Most individual congregation burial registers for 1793 (physical at congregation or HSP, with partial transcriptions in print)
- Philadelphia County tax assessment books for the 1790s (Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives — physical only)
- The Mathew Carey name list (widely held in print at research libraries; partially transcribed online but no fully indexed online database confirmed by tool results)

## Known record losses

- No courthouse fire destroyed Philadelphia County records wholesale; the city's major archival losses are more diffuse (dampness, dispersal). However, the epidemic itself disrupted record-keeping: some church registers show gaps or incomplete entries for August–November 1793, as clergy fell ill or fled along with the rest of the population.
- Some congregation burial registers do not survive at all. Potter's Field burials of indigent and unidentified dead are very poorly documented.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Mathew Carey name list.** It is the only systematic name-by-name record of epidemic deaths and covers thousands of individuals. Multiple editions exist; later editions have corrections. (Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Search probate records for autumn 1793 through 1794.** A clustering of estate filings at the Register of Wills in this window directly reflects epidemic mortality. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994) provides browse-only images; arrange results chronologically and concentrate on 1793–1795.
- **The 1790 census establishes pre-epidemic households; the 1800 census shows the aftermath.** Compare the two enumerations for the same street or ward to identify households that shrank, disappeared, or changed composition.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions for families who fled.** Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, and Delaware counties in Pennsylvania, and Burlington and Gloucester counties in New Jersey, received Philadelphia refugees. Birth, marriage, church, and tax records from those counties for August–November 1793 and the year or two following may document displaced families. The neighboring counties were not listed in a returned wiki page for this survey — consult the FamilySearch wiki for Philadelphia's neighboring county table directly.
- **Check the African American community's records carefully.** The Free African Society and African Episcopal Church (Richard Allen and Absalom Jones) played major roles in epidemic relief, and their records may name Black Philadelphians not recorded elsewhere.
- **Newspaper mortality bills are a primary source.** Philadelphia papers published weekly bills of mortality during the epidemic; these can pre-date a church burial entry and name individuals whose church registers do not survive.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's indexes** cover many Philadelphia church registers and are an important finding aid before pulling microfilm or visiting repositories. (Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (FamilySearch image group 001188322):** This Quaker volume covering 1750–1800 is digitized but browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Researchers with Quaker ancestors must page through the 145-image volume without a name index.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia County vital records and church records returned only a generic fallback page during this survey.** For the most current guidance on what FamilySearch has specifically for Philadelphia, visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly.

Families who fled the city during the epidemic may have generated records in the surrounding Pennsylvania counties (Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, Delaware) or across the river in Burlington or Gloucester counties, New Jersey. The biggest practical warning is that most of the epidemic-specific records — the Committee of Health relief rolls, the Bush Hill hospital registers, the Orphans' Court guardianship files created for children left parentless by the epidemic — are not online and require a visit or correspondence with those Philadelphia repositories.

The next step is to identify which specific family or families you are tracing and build a research plan targeting the Mathew Carey name list, the 1793\u20131795 window of the Philadelphia Register of Wills, and the burial registers of the denomination(s) those families attended.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (Focus Period: 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the City of Philadelphia incorporated 1701; city and county were consolidated in 1854 (outside this period).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 42,000–50,000 in the early 1790s. The 1793 epidemic killed roughly 5,000 people — about one-tenth of the population — between August and November. Thousands more fled the city during those months. (Source: Wikipedia, "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)
- **Economy:** Mercantile trade, shipping, crafts, professional services; Philadelphia was the national capital and the largest U.S. city at the time.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English, Scots-Irish, German, and Welsh settlers, with a significant free Black community; recent French Caribbean refugees also present by summer 1793.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Quaker (Friends Meeting), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic (St. Mary's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Methodist, Baptist, and African Episcopal (Mother Bethel, founded 1794).
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November); Philadelphia served as the U.S. capital 1790–1800; the epidemic caused the federal government to temporarily relocate.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County boundaries were stable throughout the 1780–1810 period. The city and county were not consolidated until 1854, so the city limits in 1793 were smaller than the county. Records may be filed at the city level (city court, city clerk) or county level (County Court of Common Pleas, Register of Wills), depending on the record type.
- Families who fled during the epidemic may have sought refuge in adjoining Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, or Delaware counties in Pennsylvania, or in Burlington or Gloucester counties in New Jersey. Records generated during those months could appear in any of those jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania vital records returned only a generic fallback during this survey; no jurisdiction-specific start date can be confirmed from a tool result for any earlier local registration system in Philadelphia. The FamilySearch Wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy should be checked for current guidance.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil death registration existed. Church burial registers and the Mathew Carey published death list ("A Short Account of the Malignant Fever," first edition 1793, with appended list of the dead) are the primary death evidence for the epidemic period.
- **Where held:** The published Carey list has been widely reprinted and is held by major research libraries. Church registers are held by individual congregations, diocesan archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and on FamilySearch microfilm (see Church records below).
- **Gaps:** No civil vital registration for this period — church records and published accounts are the only systematic death evidence.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; the Mathew Carey name list; Committee of Health minutes and relief records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal, Quaker, Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Roman Catholic, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei), Methodist, Baptist, and African Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Burial registers are the critical record type for epidemic deaths — they name the deceased, often give a date, sometimes a cause of death or age.
- **Where held:** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania hold transcriptions and indexes of many colonial and early national Philadelphia church registers. Individual denominational archives also hold originals. FamilySearch has microfilmed many registers; the wiki_search result for Philadelphia genealogy states that many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published, and that the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Key congregations for epidemic burials:** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal), Gloria Dei (Swedish Lutheran/Old Swedes'), St. Mary's (Catholic), and the Friends Meeting burial grounds all received epidemic dead.
- **Language:** English for most records; German for Lutheran and German Reformed registers; Latin for some Catholic sacramental records.
- **Digitization level:** Partial. FamilySearch's one confirmed digitized volume for the city-county in the 1780–1800 window is the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Individual congregation registers vary widely.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (first enumeration — names heads of household; taken 3 years before the epidemic, establishes pre-epidemic household composition), 1800 (first post-epidemic census — shows survivors and movers).
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct regular state censuses in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists for Philadelphia County survive and can serve as intercensal substitutes. The 1793 Committee of Health maintained a relief roll of survivors receiving aid, which functions as a partial enumeration of those who remained in the city.
- **Access:** The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate), inventories, guardianships. The epidemic caused a surge in probate filings in autumn 1793 and into 1794 as estates of the dead were settled.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records begin with county formation in 1682. FamilySearch has "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196), which holds 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — browse-only images.
- **Where held:** The Register of Wills for Philadelphia County; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds some copies. The FamilySearch collection linked above provides images.
- **Research tip:** A cluster of probate filings dated autumn 1793–early 1794 in the Register of Wills for Philadelphia County is a direct product of the epidemic. Searching this window is especially productive for epidemic families.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was distributed by the Penn proprietors, then by the Commonwealth).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (state level) issued patents; county Recorder of Deeds holds subsequent deed transfers.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, patents, tax records.
- **Date range:** County deed records from 1682.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City/County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original land office warrant and patent records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is the dominant military event just preceding the epidemic period. French Revolutionary Wars brought French Caribbean refugees to Philadelphia by 1793.
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records, Pennsylvania militia records, pension files (post-1792 invalid pension law), bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington D.C. and mid-Atlantic regional facilities; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has many NARA military records online.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Friends burial grounds, St. Mary's Catholic churchyard, and numerous smaller congregation grounds. Potter's Field received indigent and unidentified dead during the epidemic.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has entries for many Philadelphia historic cemeteries. Coverage for 1793 epidemic deaths varies by congregation.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual congregations and at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had multiple active papers in 1793, including Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and the Federal Gazette. Both published weekly mortality bills and lists of the dead during the epidemic.
- **Where held:** The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold original runs. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) have some digitized Philadelphia papers.
- **Content value:** Mortality bills published during the epidemic are a unique genealogical source, listing the dead by name, sometimes with occupation or street address. Estate settlement notices and orphans' court notices also appear in these papers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Passenger lists survive for arrivals in the 1780–1810 period.
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists, naturalization records (filed at Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas and District Court), declarations of intention.
- **Where held:** NARA holds the federal-era customs lists. FamilySearch and Ancestry have indexed many pre-1820 Philadelphia arrivals. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records) overlap this period for marriage evidence. Naturalizations before 1906 were filed in any court of record — check both Common Pleas and District Court records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching immigrant families.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County property tax and provincial/state tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Pre-Revolutionary provincial tax records survive; county assessment books continue through the period.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessments taken in the years around 1793 can establish presence in the city both before and after the epidemic, and can document changes in household composition (a head of household absent from post-epidemic assessment books likely died or moved).

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793)
These record types exist specifically because of the epidemic and have no peacetime equivalent:

1. **Mathew Carey's published name list** — Appended to "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (multiple editions, 1793–1794). Lists names of the dead by date of death. Widely held by research libraries; partially transcribed online.
2. **Committee of Health minutes and relief records** — The citizens' Committee kept detailed records of who died, who received relief, and the disposition of orphaned children. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793; FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
3. **Bush Hill hospital registers** — Bush Hill was converted into the epidemic's main hospital. Admission and death registers, where surviving, are at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
4. **Orphans' Court records** — The epidemic created many orphans. The Philadelphia Orphans' Court handled guardianship appointments in the months following; these filings name both the deceased parent(s) and the surviving children.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2 million images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 and 1800 federal census (indexed); various Philadelphia church record transcriptions; passenger lists | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Some 1793 Philadelphia newspaper runs with mortality bills | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Some digitized early Philadelphia newspapers | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions for major Philadelphia churchyards | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, customs passenger lists | Free finding aids; some images on Fold3 |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume for the 1780–1810 window (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, browse-only). `collections_search` returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections, of which 3 have date ranges overlapping 1793: Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images), Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (indexed), and Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (indexed). The one Pennsylvania-level marriage collection dated only 1885–1950 and the Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 collection both postdate the target period. The FamilySearch jurisdiction-specific wiki pages for Philadelphia all resolved to a generic fallback — additional FamilySearch-digitized volumes specific to Philadelphia churches may exist and were not captured by these tool results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), Philadelphia | Committee of Health minutes; Bush Hill hospital records; church register transcriptions; manuscript collections; newspapers | In-person; some finding aids online at hsp.org |
| Philadelphia City Archives | City government records; tax assessments; Committee of Health records; deed books | In-person; contact phila.gov/city-archives |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Provincial and state tax records; land office warrant and patent records; militia records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP) | Indexes and transcriptions of Philadelphia church records | In-person and some digital resources via gspp.org |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | 18th-century newspapers; Mathew Carey imprints; city directories | In-person |
| Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center | Catholic sacramental registers | By appointment |
| Individual congregations | Original registers — Christ Church, Gloria Dei, Friends meetings, etc. | Contact each congregation |

## Records NOT online

- Committee of Health minutes and relief distribution records (Philadelphia City Archives and HSP — physical only)
- Bush Hill hospital admission and death registers (HSP — physical only, where surviving)
- Philadelphia Orphans' Court guardianship files from autumn 1793 (Philadelphia City Archives — physical only)
- Most individual congregation burial registers for 1793 (physical at congregation or HSP, with partial transcriptions in print)
- Philadelphia County tax assessment books for the 1790s (Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives — physical only)
- The Mathew Carey name list (widely held in print at research libraries; partially transcribed online but no fully indexed online database confirmed by tool results)

## Known record losses

- No courthouse fire destroyed Philadelphia County records wholesale; the city's major archival losses are more diffuse (dampness, dispersal). However, the epidemic itself disrupted record-keeping: some church registers show gaps or incomplete entries for August–November 1793, as clergy fell ill or fled along with the rest of the population.
- Some congregation burial registers do not survive at all. Potter's Field burials of indigent and unidentified dead are very poorly documented.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Mathew Carey name list.** It is the only systematic name-by-name record of epidemic deaths and covers thousands of individuals. Multiple editions exist; later editions have corrections. (Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Search probate records for autumn 1793 through 1794.** A clustering of estate filings at the Register of Wills in this window directly reflects epidemic mortality. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994) provides browse-only images; arrange results chronologically and concentrate on 1793–1795.
- **The 1790 census establishes pre-epidemic households; the 1800 census shows the aftermath.** Compare the two enumerations for the same street or ward to identify households that shrank, disappeared, or changed composition.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions for families who fled.** Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, and Delaware counties in Pennsylvania, and Burlington and Gloucester counties in New Jersey, received Philadelphia refugees. Birth, marriage, church, and tax records from those counties for August–November 1793 and the year or two following may document displaced families. The neighboring counties were not listed in a returned wiki page for this survey — consult the FamilySearch wiki for Philadelphia's neighboring county table directly.
- **Check the African American community's records carefully.** The Free African Society and African Episcopal Church (Richard Allen and Absalom Jones) played major roles in epidemic relief, and their records may name Black Philadelphians not recorded elsewhere.
- **Newspaper mortality bills are a primary source.** Philadelphia papers published weekly bills of mortality during the epidemic; these can pre-date a church burial entry and name individuals whose church registers do not survive.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's indexes** cover many Philadelphia church registers and are an important finding aid before pulling microfilm or visiting repositories. (Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (FamilySearch image group 001188322):** This Quaker volume covering 1750–1800 is digitized but browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Researchers with Quaker ancestors must page through the 145-image volume without a name index.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia County vital records and church records returned only a generic fallback page during this survey.** For the most current guidance on what FamilySearch has specifically for Philadelphia, visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly.

**Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire Research Guide**

Researching Chicago through and after the Great Fire is one of the most challenging problems in American genealogy, because the October 8–10, 1871 fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with the city's **deeds, probate files, tax rolls, civil vital registrations, and many church registers**. However, several critical sources survived or were created as substitutes:

### Key Surviving & Substitute Sources

| Source | Status | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **1870 Federal Census** | Survived intact (held in Washington, D.C.) | FamilySearch / Ancestry — most important pre-fire population source |
| **Re-filed deeds (Burnt Record Act of 1872)** | Property owners required to re-file | Cook County Recorder / FamilySearch |
| **Insurance & title records** | Survived offsite | Chicago History Museum |
| **City directories (1840s onward)** | Survived intact | Newberry Library |

### FamilySearch Collections
FamilySearch holds four indexed collections beginning from 1871 — church records, birth certificates, death records, and marriage records — covering well over two million records total. There are also two small digitized volumes of pre-fire reconstructed court records and post-fire property re-recordings.

### Religious Records
**Catholic parish registers** for families who survived are held by the **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives**. Individual parishes may also have their own surviving registers.

### Legal & Court Records
- **IRAD-NEIU** (Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University) — post-fire court and naturalization records
- **NARA Great Lakes Region** (Chicago) — federal-level records including naturalization and military

---

**Research Strategy Tip:** Because of the courthouse destruction, plan to triangulate across multiple record types. The 1870 census places families in Chicago just before the fire; city directories from 1871–1873 can show who was still in the city afterward; and re-filed deeds from 1872 onward confirm who reestablished property in the area.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County formed 1831; Chicago incorporated 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this place and period. Chicago grew from roughly 109,000 (1860) to over 1 million (1890) based on the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire.
- **Economy:** Commerce, meatpacking, rail hub, manufacturing, real estate
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant communities including Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Czech, and others settled heavily in the decades before and after the fire
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among Irish and German immigrants), Lutheran (German, Scandinavian), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles, killed roughly 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse with most of the city's official records (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable throughout the 1860–1890 period.
- Chicago's city limits expanded significantly through annexations during this period, but Cook County jurisdiction remained constant.

## The Great Fire and Record Loss

This is the defining research challenge for Chicago genealogy. The Cook County Courthouse burned on October 8–10, 1871, destroying the following categories of records:

- **Deed books and land records** (pre-1871)
- **Probate and court files** (pre-1871)
- **Tax rolls** (pre-1871)
- **Civil vital records** held at the courthouse (pre-1871)
- **Many church registers** for parishes in the fire's path

The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) confirms this loss and identifies the key substitute sources described below.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Cook County civil vital records in practice begin from 1871 onward (the fire destroyed earlier registrations). The FamilySearch Wiki pages returned in this survey did not specify a confirmed pre-fire county registration start date. Illinois statewide registration was not consistently enforced until 1916.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds indexed collections for Cook County: Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (collection 2024189, ~1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (collection 1913456, ~980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (collection 1756321, ~620,000 records). All three collections begin in 1871 — the fire year. Records predating the fire are essentially absent from civil registration.
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized and indexed)
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil vital records are largely destroyed. No statewide Illinois registration existed in a consistently enforced form during the 1860s.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); city directories; federal census (1860, 1870); naturalization records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Jewish, and others
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch collection "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" (collection 1803978, ~285,000 records) covers pre- and post-fire church events. Catholic parish registers are held by the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories). Many church registers from parishes in the fire's path were destroyed; surviving registers are the most important pre-1871 substitute for vital records.
- **Language:** German-language registers are common for Lutheran and some Catholic parishes

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1890 (nearly complete loss of the 1890 federal census nationwide due to a 1921 fire at the Commerce Building). The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because originals were held in Washington — it is the critical pre-fire population source. The 1880 census is fully indexed and available on FamilySearch.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, 1880 mortality schedules recorded deaths in the year preceding each census — important for the 1871 fire victims (check the 1880 mortality schedule for those who died in 1879–1880, and the 1870 schedule for the year prior to the fire).
- **State/territorial census:** Illinois conducted a state census in 1855 and 1865; check for Cook County schedules.
- **Access:** 1860, 1870, 1880 are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, naturalizations, civil suits
- **Date range:** Cook County probate records begin effectively from 1871 due to fire destruction of earlier files
- **Where held:** Pre-fire probate is largely destroyed. Post-1871 records: Cook County Circuit Court (originals); Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) holds Cook County court records (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories). FamilySearch has 1 digitized browse-only volume of pre-fire reconstructed court records (imageGroupNumber 009982110, 38 images, 0% indexed, 1865–1871) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record. Search Cook County Circuit Court records post-1871; also check federal courts at NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a public-land state; land grants via BLM General Land Office)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. federal government (original grants/patents via BLM GLO website); subsequent transfers via Cook County Recorder of Deeds
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records; reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act of 1872
- **The Burnt Record Act (1872):** This Illinois law required property owners to re-file deeds destroyed in the fire. These reconstructed filings are the primary substitute for pre-fire property records. FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume of post-fire property re-recordings (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 112 images, 41% indexed, 1871–1880).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (original deed books and Burnt Record Act re-filings); BLM GLO website (federal land patents, searchable free online at glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection:** Insurance and title records held at the Chicago History Museum are a major substitute for destroyed property records (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many Chicago men served in Illinois units
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (pre-1856 service), draft registrations (Civil War Consolidated Lists)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and NARA Great Lakes Region in Chicago — www.archives.gov); Illinois State Archives (Springfield) for state adjutant general records; Fold3 (www.fold3.com) has Civil War service records and pension indexes online

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery, Rosehill Cemetery, and others established before and after the fire; Catholic, Jewish, and denominational cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (www.findagrave.com) has extensive Chicago cemetery coverage
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries; some transcribed by genealogical societies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (founded 1847), Chicago Times, Chicago Daily News, and immigrant-community papers in German, Scandinavian, and other languages
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (www.newspapers.com) and ProQuest Historical Newspapers (library subscription) have digitized Chicago Tribune and other papers. The Newberry Library holds extensive newspaper microfilm.
- **Content value:** The post-fire period (October–December 1871) produced extensive coverage of displaced families, relief efforts, lists of the homeless, and fire victim identifications. These newspaper accounts are among the most important genealogical sources for the event itself.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New York (Castle Garden, later Ellis Island), Port of Baltimore, Port of New Orleans — most immigrants reaching Chicago came through these eastern ports
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization declarations (filed in Cook County or federal courts), border crossings
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists); Ancestry and FamilySearch (indexed passenger lists); pre-1906 naturalizations scattered across Cook County Circuit Court and federal courts
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Real estate tax, personal property tax
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls largely destroyed. Post-1871 records held at Cook County
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor / Treasurer (originals); some available through IRAD-NEIU
- **Substitute value:** Can help establish property ownership in the years after the fire and substitute for missing census years

### City directories
- **Date range:** 1840s onward
- **Where held:** The Newberry Library (Chicago) holds the most comprehensive collection of Chicago city directories (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). Some digitized on Ancestry.
- **Research value:** City directories survived the fire and are the primary tool for placing families at specific addresses between census years. They list the head of household's name, occupation, and address — critical for tracking mobility in the 1870s–1880s rebuilding period.

### Insurance and relief records
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection:** Held at the Chicago History Museum. These insurance and title records document pre-fire property ownership and serve as substitutes for destroyed deeds and court records.
- **Post-fire relief records:** Organizations such as the Chicago Relief and Aid Society distributed aid to fire victims; their records may survive and name displaced families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000 records); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000 records); 2 digitized volumes (pre-fire court reconstructions and post-fire property re-recordings) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census; passenger lists; Cook County vital records (some overlap with FamilySearch) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records, pension indexes, draft registrations | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, federal military records, naturalization records | In-person / some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes for this place and period; both are detailed above. This appears to be the complete result set (no nextPageToken was returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories 1840s+, maps, manuscripts, newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some digital |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company collection (insurance/title records), photographs, personal papers | In-person |
| IRAD-NEIU (Illinois Regional Archives Depository, Northeastern Illinois University) | Cook County court records post-1871 | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | In-person / written request |
| Cook County Clerk's office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / mail / online portal |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Deed books and Burnt Record Act (1872) re-filings | In-person |
| NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) | Federal court records, naturalization records, some military | In-person |
| Illinois State Archives (Springfield) | State census (1855, 1865); state adjutant general military records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online

- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance/title records (Chicago History Museum — physical only)
- Most Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records (physical at IRAD-NEIU or Cook County)
- Post-fire relief and aid society records (physical, if surviving)
- Most pre-fire church registers that survived (check individual parish archives)
- Full run of city directories before the 1880s (Newberry Library)
- State census schedules for Cook County (Illinois State Archives)

## Known record losses

- **Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871:** Destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the records held there — deeds, probate files, tax rolls, court records, civil vital registrations, and many church registers for parishes in the fire zone. This is the single largest genealogical record loss in American urban history.
- **1890 federal census:** Nearly the entire nationwide 1890 population schedule was destroyed in a 1921 Commerce Building fire in Washington, D.C. — not Chicago's fault, but a compounding gap.
- **Substitute sources:** Burnt Record Act (1872) re-filed deeds; Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records; surviving church registers; federal census of 1870 (originals held in Washington, survived); city directories at the Newberry Library; newspaper accounts of the fire and relief efforts.

## Research tips
- The 1870 federal census is the most important pre-fire population source for Chicago families: originals were in Washington and survived the fire. Search it before any other source for families present in 1871. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- Search the Burnt Record Act (1872) re-filings at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds for any family that owned property before the fire. These filings can confirm Chicago residence and property ownership in the pre-fire period.
- Church records are the primary substitute for missing pre-1871 civil vital records. Even if a parish burned, it may have kept registers elsewhere or re-created them from memory and surviving copies. Contact both the individual parish and the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives for Catholic records.
- Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire (held at the Newberry Library). Use them to track a family annually between the 1860 and 1870 censuses and through the rebuilding period of the 1870s–1880s.
- Insurance and title records at the Chicago History Museum (the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection) are an underused substitute for destroyed property and court records — especially valuable for establishing pre-fire address, occupation, and family relationships.
- Post-fire newspaper coverage (Chicago Tribune and other papers, October–December 1871) names displaced families, fire victims, and aid recipients. Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library are the best access points.
- Naturalization records filed before the fire in Cook County courts are largely destroyed. Search post-1871 Cook County Circuit Court records (IRAD-NEIU) and federal courts (NARA Great Lakes Region) for declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization filed after the fire.
- The 1880 mortality schedule (deaths in the year June 1879–May 1880) and the 1870 mortality schedule are worth checking for family members who died in or around the fire period.
- Adjoining counties (DuPage to the west, Will to the south, Kane to the northwest, Lake to the north) may hold records for families who fled Chicago after the fire and resettled nearby. If a family disappears from Chicago records after 1871, check those adjacent counties before assuming emigration.
