- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (original deed books and Burnt Record Act re-filings); BLM GLO website (federal land patents, searchable free online at glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection:** Insurance and title records held at the Chicago History Museum are a major substitute for destroyed property records (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many Chicago men served in Illinois units
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (pre-1856 service), draft registrations (Civil War Consolidated Lists)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and NARA Great Lakes Region in Chicago — www.archives.gov); Illinois State Archives (Springfield) for state adjutant general records; Fold3 (www.fold3.com) has Civil War service records and pension indexes online

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery, Rosehill Cemetery, and others established before and after the fire; Catholic, Jewish, and denominational cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (www.findagrave.com) has extensive Chicago cemetery coverage
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries; some transcribed by genealogical societies

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (founded 1847), Chicago Times, Chicago Daily News, and immigrant-community papers in German, Scandinavian, and other languages
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (www.newspapers.com) and ProQuest Historical Newspapers (library subscription) have digitized Chicago Tribune and other papers. The Newberry Library holds extensive newspaper microfilm.
- **Content value:** The post-fire period (October–December 1871) produced extensive coverage of displaced families, relief efforts, lists of the homeless, and fire victim identifications. These newspaper accounts are among the most important genealogical sources for the event itself.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New York (Castle Garden, later Ellis Island), Port of Baltimore, Port of New Orleans — most immigrants reaching Chicago came through these eastern ports
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization declarations (filed in Cook County or federal courts), border crossings
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists); Ancestry and FamilySearch (indexed passenger lists); pre-1906 naturalizations scattered across Cook County Circuit Court and federal courts
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Real estate tax, personal property tax
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls largely destroyed. Post-1871 records held at Cook County
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor / Treasurer (originals); some available through IRAD-NEIU
- **Substitute value:** Can help establish property ownership in the years after the fire and substitute for missing census years

### City directories
- **Date range:** 1840s onward
- **Where held:** The Newberry Library (Chicago) holds the most comprehensive collection of Chicago city directories (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). Some digitized on Ancestry.
- **Research value:** City directories survived the fire and are the primary tool for placing families at specific addresses between census years. They list the head of household's name, occupation, and address — critical for tracking mobility in the 1870s–1880s rebuilding period.

### Insurance and relief records
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection:** Held at the Chicago History Museum. These insurance and title records document pre-fire property ownership and serve as substitutes for destroyed deeds and court records.
- **Post-fire relief records:** Organizations such as the Chicago Relief and Aid Society distributed aid to fire victims; their records may survive and name displaced families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000 records); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000 records); 2 digitized volumes (pre-fire court reconstructions and post-fire property re-recordings) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census; passenger lists; Cook County vital records (some overlap with FamilySearch) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records, pension indexes, draft registrations | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, federal military records, naturalization records | In-person / some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes for this place and period; both are detailed above. This appears to be the complete result set (no nextPageToken was returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories 1840s+, maps, manuscripts, newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some digital |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company collection (insurance/title records), photographs, personal papers | In-person |
| IRAD-NEIU (Illinois Regional Archives Depository, Northeastern Illinois University) | Cook County court records post-1871 | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | In-person / written request |
| Cook County Clerk's office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / mail / online portal |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Deed books and Burnt Record Act (1872) re-filings | In-person |
| NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) | Federal court records, naturalization records, some military | In-person |
| Illinois State Archives (Springfield) | State census (1855, 1865); state adjutant general military records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online

- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance/title records (Chicago History Museum — physical only)
- Most Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records (physical at IRAD-NEIU or Cook County)
- Post-fire relief and aid society records (physical, if surviving)
- Most pre-fire church registers that survived (check individual parish archives)
- Full run of city directories before the 1880s (Newberry Library)
- State census schedules for Cook County (Illinois State Archives)

## Known record losses

- **Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871:** Destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the records held there — deeds, probate files, tax rolls, court records, civil vital registrations, and many church registers for parishes in the fire zone. This is the single largest genealogical record loss in American urban history.
- **1890 federal census:** Nearly the entire nationwide 1890 population schedule was destroyed in a 1921 Commerce Building fire in Washington, D.C. — not Chicago's fault, but a compounding gap.
- **Substitute sources:** Burnt Record Act (1872) re-filed deeds; Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records; surviving church registers; federal census of 1870 (originals held in Washington, survived); city directories at the Newberry Library; newspaper accounts of the fire and relief efforts.

## Research tips
- The 1870 federal census is the most important pre-fire population source for Chicago families: originals were in Washington and survived the fire. Search it before any other source for families present in 1871. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- Search the Burnt Record Act (1872) re-filings at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds for any family that owned property before the fire. These filings can confirm Chicago residence and property ownership in the pre-fire period.
- Church records are the primary substitute for missing pre-1871 civil vital records. Even if a parish burned, it may have kept registers elsewhere or re-created them from memory and surviving copies. Contact both the individual parish and the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives for Catholic records.
- Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire (held at the Newberry Library). Use them to track a family annually between the 1860 and 1870 censuses and through the rebuilding period of the 1870s–1880s.
- Insurance and title records at the Chicago History Museum (the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection) are an underused substitute for destroyed property and court records — especially valuable for establishing pre-fire address, occupation, and family relationships.
- Post-fire newspaper coverage (Chicago Tribune and other papers, October–December 1871) names displaced families, fire victims, and aid recipients. Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library are the best access points.
- Naturalization records filed before the fire in Cook County courts are largely destroyed. Search post-1871 Cook County Circuit Court records (IRAD-NEIU) and federal courts (NARA Great Lakes Region) for declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization filed after the fire.
- The 1880 mortality schedule (deaths in the year June 1879–May 1880) and the 1870 mortality schedule are worth checking for family members who died in or around the fire period.
- Adjoining counties (DuPage to the west, Will to the south, Kane to the northwest, Lake to the north) may hold records for families who fled Chicago after the fire and resettled nearby. If a family disappears from Chicago records after 1871, check those adjacent counties before assuming emigration.

output.text_response:
Researching ancestors in **French colonial Louisiana (1700s)** means navigating two successive colonial regimes — **France (founding–1762)** and **Spain (1762–1800)** — with no civil vital registration at any level. Catholic sacramental registers are the backbone of every family search in this era. Here is a structured guide to records and repositories:

---

## Key Record Types

- **Catholic Sacramental Registers (baptisms, marriages, burials)** — the only record of family events; written in French before 1769, Spanish after. These are the starting point for any colonial Louisiana family.
- **Notarial Acts** — marriage contracts, estate inventories, property transactions; go back to the 1730s.
- **Superior Council Records (1699–1769)** — civil and judicial proceedings under French rule.
- **Cabildo Records (1769–1803)** — civil and judicial proceedings under Spanish rule.
- **Colonial Census Rolls & Military Rosters** — compiled periodically by both powers.
- **Administrative Correspondence** — official dispatches between Louisiana and the colonial capitals.

---

## Repositories

### U.S. — Online & Local

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** — Collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") | Name-indexed with images; best starting point |
| **FamilySearch** — Image groups 004330991 & 004330992 | Sacramental registers + Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1803; unindexed, browse only; require French/Spanish reading |
| **Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans)** | Superior Council records, Cabildo records, colonial-era notarial acts |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Marriage contracts, estate inventories, property transactions from the 1730s forward |
| **Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans** | Original parish sacramental registers |

### European Archives (for material not held in the U.S.)

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France** | French-era colonial census rolls, military rosters, official administrative correspondence |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain** | Spanish-era military rosters, administrative records, correspondence |

---

## Next Steps

1. **Identify the specific parish or district** your ancestors lived in — New Orleans, Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Attakapas, Opelousas, etc.
2. **Pull that parish's sacramental register series** via FamilySearch collection 1612905 or the Archdiocesan Archives.
3. **Pair sacramental records with notarial records** (marriage contracts, estate inventories) at the New Orleans Notarial Archives.
4. For ancestors not surfacing in U.S.-held records, write to **ANOM** (French era) or **AGI** (Spanish era) for census and military material.

quirks: Louisiana was French 1682-1762, then Spanish 1762-1800, then briefly French again 1800-1803 before the Louisiana Purchase. Colonial records are split between French and Spanish administrative systems — search both.

There were no civil vital records in colonial Louisiana. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church under both French and Spanish rule; Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the sole vital record source for the 1700s.
The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons — sacramental registers are among the few record sources that name enslaved individuals in this period.

French colonial notarial records (Superior Council acts, 1699-1769) are written in French and partially digitized; Spanish colonial notarial records (1769-1803) are in Spanish. Researchers must be able to read French or Spanish, or obtain translations.
The two digitized colonial volumes on FamilySearch (image group 004330991 and 004330992) have 0% name indexing and are not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image.

Louisiana used French and Spanish land-grant systems (concessions, not English-style deeds); these records are at the Louisiana State Land Office and in the American State Papers: Public Lands series, not county deed books.

The oldest continuous notarial archives in North America are the New Orleans Notarial Archives (from the 1730s), holding contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions — accessible at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.
Administrative records for French Louisiana (correspondence, census rolls) are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France — not in any U.S. repository.

Louisiana parishes (civil and ecclesiastical) do not follow county boundaries as in other U.S. states. The ecclesiastical parish that served a given place may differ from the civil parish — search both the civil district records and the Catholic parish registers separately.

Civil vital registration did not begin at the state level until well after 1800; no statewide civil registration system existed in the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Louisiana-specific Vital Records page in this session — consult the Louisiana State Archives directly for precise start dates at each level.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States (1700-1800 — French and Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French Louisiana founded 1682 by La Salle; New Orleans established 1718 by Bienville
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (colonial capital throughout the period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (French, 1682-1762); Captaincy General of Louisiana (Spanish, 1762-1800)
- **Population during period:** Population data for the colonial period was not returned by the population tool. French colonial census rolls survive partially — see ANOM (France) below.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo cultivation, tobacco, sugar cane (late 18th century), timber, and Mississippi River trade
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (from France and Canada/Acadia), Spanish administrators (post-1762), enslaved Africans and people of African descent, free people of color, Indigenous peoples, and German and Swiss settlers in the German Coast settlements
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively (only legally recognized church under both French and Spanish rule); Protestant worship was prohibited
- **Key historical events:** French founding 1699-1718; Code Noir enforcement throughout; Acadian expulsion refugees arriving 1760s (Cajun ancestors); Spanish takeover 1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau), effective 1769; brief French retrocession 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- **1682-1762:** French Louisiana encompassed the entire Mississippi River basin, administered as part of New France
- **1762:** France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi and New Orleans to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau); eastern portion to Britain
- **1769:** Spain effectively took administrative control; Spanish colonial record-keeping begins in earnest
- **1800:** Spain secretly retroceded Louisiana to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso)
- **1803:** United States acquired Louisiana through the Louisiana Purchase — American territorial records begin
- **Implication for research:** A family present throughout the 1700s will appear in French-language records before 1769 and Spanish-language records after. Records must be sought in both administrative systems.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was NO civil vital registration in colonial Louisiana during the 1700s. The Catholic Church held the only legally recognized vital records. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Louisiana-specific Vital Records page in this survey — consult the Louisiana State Archives for precise dates when civil registration later began at each level.
- **What exists for 1700s:** None (civil). Catholic sacramental registers are the substitute — see Church Records below.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers; notarial records (marriage contracts, estate inventories); Superior Council court records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (legally) throughout the French and Spanish colonial periods
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons, per the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Earliest records:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans — registers from 1720 ([Louisiana Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

- **Notarial archives are essential for property, marriage, and estate information.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds records from the 1730s and is the oldest continuous notarial office in North America ([Louisiana Land and Property, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Browse-only volumes require patience.** Image groups 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720-1803) and 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699-1769) are 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed page by page. French and Spanish reading ability is essential.
- **Go to France and Spain for administrative records.** Colonial censuses, military rosters, and official correspondence are at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). Both repositories have online portals (archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr; PARES portal) with partial digitization.
- **Land records reveal family relationships.** French concessions and Spanish grants name grantees, neighbors, and sometimes heirs. The American State Papers: Public Lands confirms colonial land claims after 1803 and is widely digitized.
- **Acadian families:** If researching Cajun (Acadian-descended) families, specialized Acadian genealogical societies and published deportation/resettlement lists significantly supplement the colonial record base.
- **Naming customs:** French Catholic naming customs of the period frequently used compound given names (Jean-Baptiste, Marie-Anne) and godparent names that recur across generations — tracking godparent relationships can extend a family line when direct vital records are absent. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Louisiana-specific Naming Customs page in this survey.
- **The Code Noir and enslaved persons:** The mandate for Catholic baptism means sacramental registers record enslaved individuals — often by given name only, with enslaver named. Superior Council manumission records also name free persons of color and formerly enslaved individuals.

**Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Late 1800s Research Guide**
*(Schuylkill County / Anthracite Region, ca. 1840–1910)*

---

### Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

1. **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County)**
   - ~95% name-indexed; searchable free on FamilySearch

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (1840–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools for this county and period.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; the county was the heart of the Pennsylvania anthracite region. Related industries included iron works, railroads (the Reading Railroad was central), and company-owned collieries.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic, Welsh, English, and (from the 1880s onward) Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian, and Italian immigrant communities, all recruited for mine labor.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes — Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, and German Reformed congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires trials (1876–1879) are documented in court records; the Long Strike of 1875; the rise of the United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890).

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its formation in 1811. No further subdivisions occurred.
- Records before 1811 for this territory fall under Berks County or Northampton County — search those parent counties for ancestors present before the county's formation.
- Neighboring Lackawanna County was formed from Luzerne County in 1878; before that date, records for the Scranton area appear under Luzerne County. Families who moved between the anthracite fields may have records in both counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only a generic page rather than jurisdiction-specific content, so specific start dates by level cannot be stated from tool results. Based on what the collections_search and wiki_search results indicate: Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906 (the Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 collection begins that year). Statewide birth and marriage registration also began at the state level around 1906. No county-level or town-level registration start date was confirmed by the tools for Schuylkill County.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images — indexed + images). For marriages: "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, 312,045 images — indexed + images) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records — indexed + images). A compiled marriage index, "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, index only, no images) covers the target period. No birth certificate collection for the pre-1906 period appeared in tool results.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, free); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for originals.
- **Gaps:** Births before 1906 are not recorded in any statewide civil registration series returned by the tools. Deaths before 1906 require substitute sources.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers of baptism, marriage, and burial — see Church records below. Also newspaper notices, cemetery transcriptions, and federal mortality schedules (1850–1880).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct ethnic parishes for Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian communities), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, confirmations. Confirmations are a separately dated event and appear in distinct registers — do not assume christening and confirmation are the same entry.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985, 1,245,830 records with 607,220 images — indexed + images). Diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown and Diocese of Scranton cover this region) hold original registers for Catholic parishes. Welsh denominational archives hold records for Congregational and Baptist congregations.
- **Language:** Most English-language; Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Ukrainian immigrant parish registers may be in the heritage language or in Latin for Catholic sacramental records.
- **Critical note:** The FamilySearch Wiki search results state that ethnic parish registers often contain the most detailed family data for mining communities. Identify which parish served the specific mining patch or town where your ancestor lived — coal patch towns often had a single dominant ethnic parish.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal censuses for Schuylkill County are available at decennial intervals: 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 (1890 was largely destroyed). The 1880 census and later list relationship to head of household. Occupation fields identify miners throughout this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1880) record persons who died in the year preceding the census and can substitute for missing death records.
- **State census:** The Pennsylvania State Archives and the FamilySearch Wiki generic page did not confirm a Pennsylvania state census series for this period. No state census collection appeared in tool results — the tools returned no Pennsylvania state census collection.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images — browse-only images; 0 indexed records, so must be browsed image by image with no name search). Originals held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse (Orphans' Court), Pottsville.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalization records were filed in any court of record in Pennsylvania (Common Pleas Court, Orphans' Court). Schuylkill County naturalization records from the 1840s through 1906 are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, per the FamilySearch Wiki search results ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).
- **Court minute books:** County court minutes record road maintenance assignments, poor relief payments, and other local business that names ordinary residents who appear in no other court series.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (not a federal-land state), meaning the Commonwealth — not the federal government — issued original land grants. The Pennsylvania land survey system uses metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds original land warrant and patent records. The FamilySearch Wiki land-and-property page returned only a generic page and did not provide jurisdiction-specific detail.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, warrants, patents, and tax records. Tax records survive and substitute for missing census years.
- **Date range:** County deed records begin from county formation in 1811; state land records predate that.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville) for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for warrants and patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many Schuylkill County miners served. Spanish-American War (1898). World War I draft registration (1917–1918, slightly outside the target window).
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files at NARA (Washington, D.C. and National Personnel Records Center); Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; bounty-land warrant records at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (free finding aids; records available via Fold3 subscription and Ancestry subscription). Pennsylvania State Archives for state muster rolls.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous denominational and municipal cemeteries in Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, Tamaqua, Minersville, and the coal patch towns.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — curated link returned by external_links_search for this place.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual cemeteries and in some cases at local churches. The Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds some transcriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pottsville was home to the Miners' Journal, one of the most significant coal-region newspapers, publishing from 1825. It contains obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports, and community news of direct genealogical value.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) — curated link returned by external_links_search. Library of Congress Chronicling America project. Pennsylvania State Library (microfilm).
- **Content value:** Obituaries in the Miners' Journal frequently name parents, siblings, place of origin, and surviving family members. Mine accident reports name victims with nationality and age.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island) were the principal ports of entry for immigrants coming to the Pennsylvania anthracite region.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry); naturalization records filed at county courts (see Court records above); declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — curated link returned by external_links_search. FamilySearch (free). Ancestry (subscription).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members. Post-1906 manifests (and some earlier ones) include the name and address of a contact in the destination, which can confirm the specific mining town.
- **UMWA records:** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) maintained membership rolls and grievance files. Per the FamilySearch Wiki search results, these are held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and the Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax records.
- **Date range:** Tax lists for Schuylkill County survive from the county's formation (1811) onward. They are particularly valuable for the 1840s–1880s when civil vital registration did not exist.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives. Some series have been microfilmed by FamilySearch (check the FamilySearch Catalog).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can place a person in a specific township in years between censuses and in years when the census is missing (especially the destroyed 1890 census).

### Occupational records (coal mining)
This is a distinctive record class for the anthracite region:
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002240015):** Schuylkill County, 1870–1900. 410 images, 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — search directly on FamilySearch. This is the most accessible digitized mining-specific record returned by the tools.
- **Mine Inspector Reports:** Published annually by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from 1870. List fatal accidents with name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Per the FamilySearch Wiki search results, these are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).
- **Mine Accident Reports (imageGroupNumber 002240016):** Luzerne County, 1870–1895. 287 images. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse only, image by image.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (imageGroupNumber 002240017):** Lackawanna County, 1878–1900. 199 images. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse only, image by image.
- **Company employment records (payrolls, accident reports):** Survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).

**Coverage note:** The volume_search returned 23 total digitized volumes for the Pennsylvania coal region 1840–1910; only the 3 volumes above represent the first page of results. A nextPageToken was returned — additional volumes exist and have not been examined in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (1840–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools for this county and period.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; the county was the heart of the Pennsylvania anthracite region. Related industries included iron works, railroads (the Reading Railroad was central), and company-owned collieries.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic, Welsh, English, and (from the 1880s onward) Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian, and Italian immigrant communities, all recruited for mine labor.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes — Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, and German Reformed congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires trials (1876–1879) are documented in court records; the Long Strike of 1875; the rise of the United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890).

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its formation in 1811. No further subdivisions occurred.
- Records before 1811 for this territory fall under Berks County or Northampton County — search those parent counties for ancestors present before the county's formation.
- Neighboring Lackawanna County was formed from Luzerne County in 1878; before that date, records for the Scranton area appear under Luzerne County. Families who moved between the anthracite fields may have records in both counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only a generic page rather than jurisdiction-specific content, so specific start dates by level cannot be stated from tool results. Based on what the collections_search and wiki_search results indicate: Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906 (the Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 collection begins that year). Statewide birth and marriage registration also began at the state level around 1906. No county-level or town-level registration start date was confirmed by the tools for Schuylkill County.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images — indexed + images). For marriages: "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, 312,045 images — indexed + images) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records — indexed + images). A compiled marriage index, "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, index only, no images) covers the target period. No birth certificate collection for the pre-1906 period appeared in tool results.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, free); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for originals.
- **Gaps:** Births before 1906 are not recorded in any statewide civil registration series returned by the tools. Deaths before 1906 require substitute sources.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers of baptism, marriage, and burial — see Church records below. Also newspaper notices, cemetery transcriptions, and federal mortality schedules (1850–1880).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct ethnic parishes for Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian communities), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, confirmations. Confirmations are a separately dated event and appear in distinct registers — do not assume christening and confirmation are the same entry.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985, 1,245,830 records with 607,220 images — indexed + images). Diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown and Diocese of Scranton cover this region) hold original registers for Catholic parishes. Welsh denominational archives hold records for Congregational and Baptist congregations.
- **Language:** Most English-language; Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Ukrainian immigrant parish registers may be in the heritage language or in Latin for Catholic sacramental records.
- **Critical note:** The FamilySearch Wiki search results state that ethnic parish registers often contain the most detailed family data for mining communities. Identify which parish served the specific mining patch or town where your ancestor lived — coal patch towns often had a single dominant ethnic parish.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal censuses for Schuylkill County are available at decennial intervals: 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 (1890 was largely destroyed). The 1880 census and later list relationship to head of household. Occupation fields identify miners throughout this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1880) record persons who died in the year preceding the census and can substitute for missing death records.
- **State census:** The Pennsylvania State Archives and the FamilySearch Wiki generic page did not confirm a Pennsylvania state census series for this period. No state census collection appeared in tool results — the tools returned no Pennsylvania state census collection.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images — browse-only images; 0 indexed records, so must be browsed image by image with no name search). Originals held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse (Orphans' Court), Pottsville.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalization records were filed in any court of record in Pennsylvania (Common Pleas Court, Orphans' Court). Schuylkill County naturalization records from the 1840s through 1906 are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, per the FamilySearch Wiki search results ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).
- **Court minute books:** County court minutes record road maintenance assignments, poor relief payments, and other local business that names ordinary residents who appear in no other court series.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (not a federal-land state), meaning the Commonwealth — not the federal government — issued original land grants. The Pennsylvania land survey system uses metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds original land warrant and patent records. The FamilySearch Wiki land-and-property page returned only a generic page and did not provide jurisdiction-specific detail.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, warrants, patents, and tax records. Tax records survive and substitute for missing census years.
- **Date range:** County deed records begin from county formation in 1811; state land records predate that.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville) for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for warrants and patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many Schuylkill County miners served. Spanish-American War (1898). World War I draft registration (1917–1918, slightly outside the target window).
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files at NARA (Washington, D.C. and National Personnel Records Center); Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; bounty-land warrant records at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (free finding aids; records available via Fold3 subscription and Ancestry subscription). Pennsylvania State Archives for state muster rolls.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous denominational and municipal cemeteries in Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, Tamaqua, Minersville, and the coal patch towns.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — curated link returned by external_links_search for this place.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual cemeteries and in some cases at local churches. The Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds some transcriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pottsville was home to the Miners' Journal, one of the most significant coal-region newspapers, publishing from 1825. It contains obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports, and community news of direct genealogical value.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) — curated link returned by external_links_search. Library of Congress Chronicling America project. Pennsylvania State Library (microfilm).
- **Content value:** Obituaries in the Miners' Journal frequently name parents, siblings, place of origin, and surviving family members. Mine accident reports name victims with nationality and age.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island) were the principal ports of entry for immigrants coming to the Pennsylvania anthracite region.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry); naturalization records filed at county courts (see Court records above); declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — curated link returned by external_links_search. FamilySearch (free). Ancestry (subscription).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members. Post-1906 manifests (and some earlier ones) include the name and address of a contact in the destination, which can confirm the specific mining town.
- **UMWA records:** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) maintained membership rolls and grievance files. Per the FamilySearch Wiki search results, these are held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and the Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax records.
- **Date range:** Tax lists for Schuylkill County survive from the county's formation (1811) onward. They are particularly valuable for the 1840s–1880s when civil vital registration did not exist.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives. Some series have been microfilmed by FamilySearch (check the FamilySearch Catalog).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can place a person in a specific township in years between censuses and in years when the census is missing (especially the destroyed 1890 census).

### Occupational records (coal mining)
This is a distinctive record class for the anthracite region:
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002240015):** Schuylkill County, 1870–1900. 410 images, 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — search directly on FamilySearch. This is the most accessible digitized mining-specific record returned by the tools.
- **Mine Inspector Reports:** Published annually by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from 1870. List fatal accidents with name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Per the FamilySearch Wiki search results, these are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).
- **Mine Accident Reports (imageGroupNumber 002240016):** Luzerne County, 1870–1895. 287 images. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse only, image by image.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (imageGroupNumber 002240017):** Lackawanna County, 1878–1900. 199 images. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse only, image by image.
- **Company employment records (payrolls, accident reports):** Survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).

**Coverage note:** The volume_search returned 23 total digitized volumes for the Pennsylvania coal region 1840–1910; only the 3 volumes above represent the first page of results. A nextPageToken was returned — additional volumes exist and have not been examined in this survey.

---

**Early Colonial Massachusetts (c. 1620–1700): Records & Repositories for Tracing Puritan Families**

This period is actually **unusually well-documented** for American genealogy. Records survive at the town level from as early as **1639**, when the Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated that towns record births, marriages, and deaths — making it one of the earliest civil registration systems in North America.

---

### Two Crucial Cautions Up Front

1. **Plymouth Colony vs. Massachusetts Bay Colony are separate jurisdictions** with distinct published record series. Ancestors in Plymouth (founded 1620) are found in different sources than those in the Bay Colony (founded 1630). Both must be searched.
2. **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** destroyed the early records of several inland and western towns. If your ancestor lived in that region, originals may be gone — you'll need to rely on published abstracts, church registers, and neighboring-town sources.

---

### Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

**Town Vital Records**
- Each town was required to record births, marriages, and deaths. These have been widely published in the *Vital Records of Massachusetts* series (known as "the Tan Books"), now available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- The **Massachusetts State Archives** (Boston) holds many originals.

**Church Records (Congregational)**
- Puritans were Congregationalists. Church registers (baptisms, admissions, dismissals, deaths) are often the only record of non-civil events. Many have been transcribed and published by the *New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)*.

**Probate Records**
- Organized by county. Early county courts handled probate. Published abstracts exist for Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Plymouth, and Barnstable counties.
- **FamilySearch** has digitized many original probate files.

**Deeds & Land Records**
- Held at the county level. The earliest deeds (1630s–1640s) are often in the *Suffolk Deeds* series (published in volumes).
- Also search original colony land grants recorded in the *Massachusetts Bay Colony Records*.

**Colony Court Records**
- *Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay in New England* (5 vols., published 1853–1854) — covers legislation, freemen lists, land grants, and court actions.
- *Plymouth Colony Records* (12 vols., Shurtleff & Pulsifer, 1855–1861) — covers Plymouth Colony courts, land, vital events, and wills.

**Passenger & Immigration Lists**
- Many early arrivals documented in the *Great Migration* project by Robert Charles Anderson (NEHGS) — arguably the most important published resource for 1620–1640 Bay Colony settlers.
- *Banks's Topographical Dictionary of 2885 English Emigrants to New England, 1620–1650* for English-origin research.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org)** | Published vital records, church registers, probate abstracts, *Great Migration* database, NEHGS Register (journal) |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** | Original colonial and state records, land grants, court files |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized probate, deeds, vital records (many indexed) |
| **Mayflower Society / Plimoth Patuxent** | Plymouth Colony–specific lineage records |
| **Harvard's Houghton Library** | Manuscript church records, Puritan diaries and correspondence |
| **Town Clerk Offices** | Some original 17th-century registers still held locally |

---

### Published Finding Aids to Prioritize

- **Robert Charles Anderson, *The Great Migration Begins* and *The Great Migration* series** — prosopographies of every documented settler, 1620–1640
- **Vital Records of Massachusetts** ("Tan Books") — town-by-town published transcriptions
- **New England Ancestors** (NEHGS online database)
- **FamilySearch Catalog** — search by Massachusetts county for digitized collections

---

### Next Step

Identify the **specific town(s)** where your ancestors lived. That will determine which town vital records, county deed and probate series, and Congregational church registers to consult first — and whether to lead with Plymouth Colony or Bay Colony sources.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (Early Colonial, 1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628; Plymouth Colony founded 1620; the two merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Suffolk County); additional county seats at Salem (Essex), Cambridge (Middlesex), Plymouth (Plymouth County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Crown of England; administered by the Massachusetts Bay Company (1628-1684), then as a royal province (1691 onward)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this period; Wikipedia notes approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630-1640
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, fur trade, early maritime commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Almost entirely English Puritan settlers; small numbers of indentured servants and enslaved Africans by mid-century
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) — the established church; small number of Anglican, Baptist, and Quaker settlers (often persecuted or expelled)
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640 (Winthrop fleet and subsequent waves); Pequot War 1636-1638; establishment of Harvard College 1636; King Philip's War 1675-1676 (devastating to many inland towns, destroying some early records); Salem Witch Trials 1692

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) were separate jurisdictions with separate record series. They merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- County formation began in 1643: Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Norfolk Counties were established that year. Additional counties were created thereafter. Always determine which county existed at the event date, as county boundaries shifted throughout the 17th century.
- Records created under Plymouth Colony are published and indexed separately — researchers must search both Plymouth and Bay Colony series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level registration was mandated by the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1639 — this is a town-level requirement, not a county or statewide system. Each town's clerk recorded births, marriages, and deaths independently. There was no statewide civil registration in the 1600s.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by individual town clerks from approximately 1639 onward (coverage varies significantly by town; some towns have complete runs, others have gaps)
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives (Boston); published abstracts in the Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series, covering over 200 towns
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection 2061550) — indexed and searchable online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550; approximately 3.4 million records
- **Gaps:** Coverage is uneven before 1650. King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed some early town records. Plymouth Colony vital records are a separate series.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism and burial registers; town meeting minutes listing births of selectmen's families

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) — the dominant and legally established church of the colony throughout this period. Small Baptist and Quaker congregations existed by the 1650s-1660s but were often suppressed.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments, censures). Confirmation was not a Congregational practice, so there is no separate confirmation series.
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and by local historical societies. FamilySearch holds microfilm of many originals. The Massachusetts Church Records collection (1921657) covers 1630-1920 and is indexed online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 (approximately 987,000 records).
- **Digitized volume:** One browse-only, full-text searchable volume (DGS 007612045, 121 images) covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700. It is not name-indexed but can be searched by full text. Must be browsed image by image for other counties.
- **Language:** English throughout
- **Key resource:** The FamilySearch wiki notes that Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy and that many have been published in accessible printed form (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — no federal census records exist for the 1620-1700 period.
- **Colonial-era substitutes:** Tax lists ("rates"), militia muster rolls, and church membership lists function as population enumerations. Town proprietors' lists document landholding householders. These are the closest equivalents to a census for this era.
- **Digitized volume:** One browse-only, non-name-indexed volume (DGS 007612044, 188 images) covers Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698. It must be browsed image by image and is not full-text searchable.
- **Access:** Browse-only for the digitized volumes; additional materials physical or on microfilm

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, estate distributions; county court of general sessions records; Court of Assistants (colony-level)
- **Date range:** County probate courts began with county formation in 1643. Earlier probate matters were handled by the Court of Assistants.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals at county courthouses); Massachusetts Archives holds colonial court records. FamilySearch's Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection 1678901) is indexed online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 (approximately 567,000 records).
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** Wills (testate estates) are in the will books; estates without wills (intestate) generated administration files. Both series exist from the 1630s onward and name family members, making them among the most valuable sources for this period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey in colonial Massachusetts)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Massachusetts Bay Company initially granted land; after 1691, the Crown. Town proprietors controlled local land allocation. County registries of deeds recorded subsequent transfers.
- **Types:** Town grants, proprietary shares, deeds, mortgages. County deed books survive in remarkably complete runs from the 1630s at county registries of deeds, per the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Date range:** Earliest colonial grants from the 1620s-1630s
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (original records); Massachusetts Archives (colony-era land grants)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638), King Philip's War (1675-1676)
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colonial service records, pension records (rare for this era); King Philip's War service lists
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives holds colonial militia records. Published lists exist for King Philip's War participants. NARA does not hold colonial-era Massachusetts military records (NARA's holdings begin with the Revolution).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Granary Burying Ground (Boston, 1660), King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston, 1630), Copp's Hill Burying Ground (Boston, 1659), and town churchyards throughout the colony
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many colonial-era stones; transcription quality varies. Many early stones have been transcribed by local historical societies.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are rare for the 1600s; gravestone inscriptions are often the only cemetery source. Many early stones are eroded or lost.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers existed in Massachusetts before 1690. The first colonial newspaper, Publick Occurrences, appeared in Boston in 1690 and was immediately suppressed after one issue. The Boston News-Letter began in 1704, outside the target period.
- **No newspaper source applies to 1620-1700.**

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston was the primary port of entry for the Great Migration settlers (1630-1643). Salem and Plymouth also received early arrivals.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists; the Great Migration study series (NEHGS) is the authoritative compiled source for arrivals 1620-1643. Naturalization was not required of English colonists.
- **Where held:** The Great Migration series is available at NEHGS and in many genealogical libraries. Individual ship records have been published and compiled. FamilySearch's Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (collection 1784312) covers only 1820-1891 and does not apply to this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** "Rates" (property and poll taxes levied by towns and the colony)
- **Date range:** Colonial tax lists survive from the 1640s onward for many towns
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town records; some published by historical societies
- **Substitute value:** Colonial tax lists ("rates") are the primary substitute for census records in this period. They list adult male householders and provide a snapshot of who was present in a town in a given year.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Record local governance decisions, appointments, road assignments, and poor relief — naming ordinary people not found elsewhere. These run continuously from a town's founding and are among the richest sources for this era.
- **Court of Assistants records:** The colony's highest court; records are published and cover 1630-1692.
- **Published town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories often reprint or abstract early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. They frequently preserve transcriptions of records since lost (especially from towns damaged in King Philip's War).
- **The Great Migration series (NEHGS):** The most authoritative single reference for the 1620-1643 period — documents every known settler, with source citations and biographical sketches.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3.4M records, indexed); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987K records, indexed); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567K records, indexed); 2 browse-only/full-text volumes (town meetings 1620-1698; Suffolk Congregational baptisms 1630-1700) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (not applicable pre-1790); various colonial record compilations | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions including colonial-era burying grounds | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Not applicable for colonial Massachusetts military or immigration records (holdings begin with the Revolution) | Free/Fee |
| NEHGS (americanancestors.org) | Great Migration series; manuscript collections; published genealogies; largest genealogical research library in New England | Membership/Fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 2 total digitized volumes for Massachusetts, 1620-1700 — both are detailed above; this is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward, colonial tax lists | In-person; some records available on microfilm |
| County registries of deeds | Deed books from 1630s onward (complete runs) | In-person at each county courthouse |
| County probate courts | Probate files from county formation (1643) onward | In-person at each county courthouse |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (Boston) | Great Migration series, manuscript collections, published genealogies, microfilm | In-person research room; membership database online |
| Local historical societies | Town-specific manuscripts, transcriptions, published histories | Contact individually; many have digitized finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Original town meeting minutes (beyond the 2 digitized browse-only volumes)
- Most county deed books (deeds must generally be consulted at county registries of deeds or on FamilySearch microfilm)
- Colonial "rates" (tax lists) beyond scattered published abstracts
- Original Congregational church registers outside Suffolk County (outside the digitized full-text volume)
- King Philip's War service lists (published in printed form but not fully indexed online)
- Court of Assistants records (published in print but not fully digitized)

## Known record losses
- **King Philip's War (1675-1676):** Multiple inland towns were burned during the conflict, and town records were destroyed with them. Lancaster, Deerfield, Northampton, and several other communities lost early vital and town records. Researchers should check contemporary copies, published abstracts, and church records as substitutes.
- **Normal attrition:** Some early town clerk books were never transferred to archives and are held (or have been lost) at local town halls. Researchers should always contact the town clerk directly as well as consulting archives.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Great Migration series** (NEHGS): if your ancestor arrived before 1643, there is almost certainly a published entry for them with source citations. This is the single most efficient starting point for the 1620-1643 period.
- **Search both Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony records** separately. The two colonies had different record-keeping systems, and their records are published and indexed in different series. Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published and indexed separately (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Town vital records are at the town level, not county or state.** Identify the specific town where an ancestor lived before searching. The Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series is the published standard for over 200 towns.
- **Congregational church records complement and sometimes predate town records.** Even where town records survive, the church register may record a baptism or burial date that the town omitted (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Use colonial tax lists as a census substitute** — no census exists before 1790. A "rate" list placing an ancestor in a given town in a given year can anchor the research.
- **The Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** is the essential physical repository for colony-era materials that have not been digitized or published.
- **County boundaries changed during this period.** Confirm which county your ancestor's town fell within at the date of the event — this determines where deeds and probate records are filed.
- **King Philip's War research:** If ancestors lived in western or central Massachusetts towns, assume records may be missing and look for published abstracts, church records, and neighboring-town sources.
