- **Gaps:** Coverage is uneven before 1650. King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed some early town records. Plymouth Colony vital records are a separate series.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism and burial registers; town meeting minutes listing births of selectmen's families

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) — the dominant and legally established church of the colony throughout this period. Small Baptist and Quaker congregations existed by the 1650s-1660s but were often suppressed.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments, censures). Confirmation was not a Congregational practice, so there is no separate confirmation series.
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and by local historical societies. FamilySearch holds microfilm of many originals. The Massachusetts Church Records collection (1921657) covers 1630-1920 and is indexed online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 (approximately 987,000 records).
- **Digitized volume:** One browse-only, full-text searchable volume (DGS 007612045, 121 images) covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700. It is not name-indexed but can be searched by full text. Must be browsed image by image for other counties.
- **Language:** English throughout
- **Key resource:** The FamilySearch wiki notes that Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy and that many have been published in accessible printed form (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — no federal census records exist for the 1620-1700 period.
- **Colonial-era substitutes:** Tax lists ("rates"), militia muster rolls, and church membership lists function as population enumerations. Town proprietors' lists document landholding householders. These are the closest equivalents to a census for this era.
- **Digitized volume:** One browse-only, non-name-indexed volume (DGS 007612044, 188 images) covers Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698. It must be browsed image by image and is not full-text searchable.
- **Access:** Browse-only for the digitized volumes; additional materials physical or on microfilm

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, estate distributions; county court of general sessions records; Court of Assistants (colony-level)
- **Date range:** County probate courts began with county formation in 1643. Earlier probate matters were handled by the Court of Assistants.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals at county courthouses); Massachusetts Archives holds colonial court records. FamilySearch's Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection 1678901) is indexed online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 (approximately 567,000 records).
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** Wills (testate estates) are in the will books; estates without wills (intestate) generated administration files. Both series exist from the 1630s onward and name family members, making them among the most valuable sources for this period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey in colonial Massachusetts)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Massachusetts Bay Company initially granted land; after 1691, the Crown. Town proprietors controlled local land allocation. County registries of deeds recorded subsequent transfers.
- **Types:** Town grants, proprietary shares, deeds, mortgages. County deed books survive in remarkably complete runs from the 1630s at county registries of deeds, per the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Date range:** Earliest colonial grants from the 1620s-1630s
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (original records); Massachusetts Archives (colony-era land grants)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638), King Philip's War (1675-1676)
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colonial service records, pension records (rare for this era); King Philip's War service lists
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives holds colonial militia records. Published lists exist for King Philip's War participants. NARA does not hold colonial-era Massachusetts military records (NARA's holdings begin with the Revolution).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Granary Burying Ground (Boston, 1660), King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston, 1630), Copp's Hill Burying Ground (Boston, 1659), and town churchyards throughout the colony
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many colonial-era stones; transcription quality varies. Many early stones have been transcribed by local historical societies.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are rare for the 1600s; gravestone inscriptions are often the only cemetery source. Many early stones are eroded or lost.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers existed in Massachusetts before 1690. The first colonial newspaper, Publick Occurrences, appeared in Boston in 1690 and was immediately suppressed after one issue. The Boston News-Letter began in 1704, outside the target period.
- **No newspaper source applies to 1620-1700.**

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston was the primary port of entry for the Great Migration settlers (1630-1643). Salem and Plymouth also received early arrivals.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists; the Great Migration study series (NEHGS) is the authoritative compiled source for arrivals 1620-1643. Naturalization was not required of English colonists.
- **Where held:** The Great Migration series is available at NEHGS and in many genealogical libraries. Individual ship records have been published and compiled. FamilySearch's Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (collection 1784312) covers only 1820-1891 and does not apply to this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** "Rates" (property and poll taxes levied by towns and the colony)
- **Date range:** Colonial tax lists survive from the 1640s onward for many towns
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town records; some published by historical societies
- **Substitute value:** Colonial tax lists ("rates") are the primary substitute for census records in this period. They list adult male householders and provide a snapshot of who was present in a town in a given year.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Record local governance decisions, appointments, road assignments, and poor relief — naming ordinary people not found elsewhere. These run continuously from a town's founding and are among the richest sources for this era.
- **Court of Assistants records:** The colony's highest court; records are published and cover 1630-1692.
- **Published town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories often reprint or abstract early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. They frequently preserve transcriptions of records since lost (especially from towns damaged in King Philip's War).
- **The Great Migration series (NEHGS):** The most authoritative single reference for the 1620-1643 period — documents every known settler, with source citations and biographical sketches.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3.4M records, indexed); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987K records, indexed); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567K records, indexed); 2 browse-only/full-text volumes (town meetings 1620-1698; Suffolk Congregational baptisms 1630-1700) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (not applicable pre-1790); various colonial record compilations | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions including colonial-era burying grounds | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Not applicable for colonial Massachusetts military or immigration records (holdings begin with the Revolution) | Free/Fee |
| NEHGS (americanancestors.org) | Great Migration series; manuscript collections; published genealogies; largest genealogical research library in New England | Membership/Fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 2 total digitized volumes for Massachusetts, 1620-1700 — both are detailed above; this is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward, colonial tax lists | In-person; some records available on microfilm |
| County registries of deeds | Deed books from 1630s onward (complete runs) | In-person at each county courthouse |
| County probate courts | Probate files from county formation (1643) onward | In-person at each county courthouse |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (Boston) | Great Migration series, manuscript collections, published genealogies, microfilm | In-person research room; membership database online |
| Local historical societies | Town-specific manuscripts, transcriptions, published histories | Contact individually; many have digitized finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Original town meeting minutes (beyond the 2 digitized browse-only volumes)
- Most county deed books (deeds must generally be consulted at county registries of deeds or on FamilySearch microfilm)
- Colonial "rates" (tax lists) beyond scattered published abstracts
- Original Congregational church registers outside Suffolk County (outside the digitized full-text volume)
- King Philip's War service lists (published in printed form but not fully indexed online)
- Court of Assistants records (published in print but not fully digitized)

## Known record losses
- **King Philip's War (1675-1676):** Multiple inland towns were burned during the conflict, and town records were destroyed with them. Lancaster, Deerfield, Northampton, and several other communities lost early vital and town records. Researchers should check contemporary copies, published abstracts, and church records as substitutes.
- **Normal attrition:** Some early town clerk books were never transferred to archives and are held (or have been lost) at local town halls. Researchers should always contact the town clerk directly as well as consulting archives.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Great Migration series** (NEHGS): if your ancestor arrived before 1643, there is almost certainly a published entry for them with source citations. This is the single most efficient starting point for the 1620-1643 period.
- **Search both Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony records** separately. The two colonies had different record-keeping systems, and their records are published and indexed in different series. Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published and indexed separately (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Town vital records are at the town level, not county or state.** Identify the specific town where an ancestor lived before searching. The Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series is the published standard for over 200 towns.
- **Congregational church records complement and sometimes predate town records.** Even where town records survive, the church register may record a baptism or burial date that the town omitted (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Use colonial tax lists as a census substitute** — no census exists before 1790. A "rate" list placing an ancestor in a given town in a given year can anchor the research.
- **The Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** is the essential physical repository for colony-era materials that have not been digitized or published.
- **County boundaries changed during this period.** Confirm which county your ancestor's town fell within at the date of the event — this determines where deeds and probate records are filed.
- **King Philip's War research:** If ancestors lived in western or central Massachusetts towns, assume records may be missing and look for published abstracts, church records, and neighboring-town sources.

**Oklahoma Territory & Early State of Oklahoma (1889–1910) — Locality Research Guide**

The guide (saved as **loc_001**) covers the Land Run of 1889 through Oklahoma statehood (1907) and into the early state period (to ~1910). Key highlights:

### 🏆 Highest-Priority Records

1. **General Land Office (GLO) Homestead Case Files** — The core record for Land Run settlers. Survive intact at the National Archives and are partially searchable on:
   - [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org)
   - **BLM GLO Records** (free): [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)

2. **1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census** — A rare survival. The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire, but Oklahoma Territory has a **surviving territorial census** held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)**. This is nearly unique in the country and an exceptional find for this period.

### ⚠️ Critical Jurisdictional Note
Before statehood, the area was divided between **Oklahoma Territory** and **Indian Territory** — two legally separate jurisdictions with **different record systems**. A family living near the boundary may need to be traced through both sets of records. If your ancestor has Native American heritage or lived in Indian Territory, the **Dawes Rolls** (Five Civilized Tribes enrollment) are essential.

### Other Key Record Sets & Repositories

| Record Type | Where Held |
|---|---|
| Federal land/homestead records | National Archives (Ft. Worth, SW region) |
| Territorial & state court records | Oklahoma State Archives, OHS |
| Vital records (post-1908) | Oklahoma State Dept. of Health |
| Church records | Varies by denomination; OHS holds many |
| Newspapers (territorial era) | OHS; Chronicling America (LOC) |
| Indian Territory records | National Archives; OHS; Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, Seminole Nation archives |
| 1900 & 1910 federal censuses | FamilySearch, Ancestry, Fold3 |

### Recommended Next Steps
- Identify which **specific county or township** your ancestor settled in — records are organized by county, and the 1889 Run created many counties simultaneously.
- Start with the **homestead case file** and **1890 territorial census** as anchors, then trace backward to the **state of origin** (many families came from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, or the South).

quirks: Oklahoma did not exist as a territory until May 2, 1890 (Organic Act). The Land Run of April 22, 1889 predates any territorial government — records of claims filed that day are federal General Land Office records, not territorial records.

The area was split between Oklahoma Territory (the Unassigned Lands opened in 1889) and Indian Territory (the Five Civilized Tribes' jurisdictions) — a family's records could fall under either, depending on exactly where they settled. Search both jurisdictions.

The 1890 federal census for most of the country was destroyed by fire. Oklahoma Territory has a surviving special 1890 territorial census — one of the few 1890 enumerations in the nation — held at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

Land Run claimants filed homestead applications at GLO land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher in 1889; later openings used other land offices. The GLO case file for a claim includes the application, proof of settlement (with witnesses who may be neighbors or relatives), and the final patent.
Rejected homestead applications also survive and can contain detailed family information — do not skip them.
Before 1906, naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — district courts, county courts, and probate courts — so there is no single repository for territorial-era naturalizations.
Settlers came primarily from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas, and other border states. Tracing origins requires searching departure-state records, not just Oklahoma records.
The Dawes Commission (1898-1914) enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes. Enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389) are browse-only images (0% name-indexed) and must be examined image-by-image.
Oklahoma statehood occurred November 16, 1907, when Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged. County boundaries and record-keeping authority shifted at that date.
Territorial court records 1890-1907 are split between the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives — check both.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Oklahoma, United States (1889-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory formally established May 2, 1890 (Organic Act), from the Unassigned Lands. The Land Run of April 22, 1889 preceded territorial organization. Oklahoma achieved statehood November 16, 1907, when Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged.
- **Capital / administrative center:** Guthrie (territorial capital, 1890-1910); Oklahoma City became state capital 1910.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal territory under U.S. congressional authority; General Land Office (GLO) administered land claims directly.
- **Population during period:** No tool-returned population figures available for this period. Wikipedia notes an estimated 50,000 participants in the 1889 Land Run alone. The federal census was taken in Oklahoma Territory in 1900.
- **Economy:** Homestead agriculture (wheat, cotton), cattle ranching, and nascent oil industry (first commercial wells ca. 1897). Many settlers were subsistence farmers staking 160-acre homestead claims.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Euro-American settlers from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas, and other border states; significant African American communities (including Boley and other all-Black towns); Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) throughout Indian Territory.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian predominated among settlers; Catholic missions predating 1889; various tribal denominations and mission churches.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889 (Unassigned Lands); Organic Act May 2, 1890 (creates Oklahoma Territory); subsequent land runs 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895, 1901; Cherokee Strip opening 1893; Dawes Commission enrollment 1898-1914; statehood November 16, 1907.

## Boundary changes
- The area in 1889 was divided between the Unassigned Lands (opened by the Land Run) and Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes). These were legally separate jurisdictions with different record systems.
- Oklahoma Territory was created in 1890 from the Unassigned Lands and grew through subsequent land openings. Indian Territory remained a separate jurisdiction until statehood in 1907.
- At statehood (1907), Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged into the State of Oklahoma. County boundaries were reorganized. Records created before 1907 under territorial or tribal authority transferred to county courthouses or state/federal archives.
- A family's records could fall under Oklahoma Territory, Indian Territory, or both, depending on where within the combined area they settled. This is a geographic split, not a simple temporal one — search both jurisdictions unless the specific location is pinned down.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific vital records page. Oklahoma did not have statewide civil registration of births and deaths in the territorial period (1890-1907). Civil registration at the state level began after statehood (1907), but the FamilySearch Wiki does not confirm the exact statewide start date from pages returned in this survey.
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890 are available in the FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (collection 2134789, 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images). No indexed birth or death registration collections for the 1889-1907 period were returned by collections_search.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriage registers); Oklahoma State Archives for statewide registration once it began.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration in the territorial period. Church records are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; homestead proof affidavits sometimes note family members; newspaper vital notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic (mission churches predating 1889), and various tribal-denomination churches.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls, and poor/benevolent aid lists.

(Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Search departure-state records.** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas, and other border states. Tracing origins requires searching records from those states, not just Oklahoma. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **The 1890 territorial census is rare and valuable.** Unlike the destroyed 1890 federal census, Oklahoma Territory has a surviving territorial census held at the Oklahoma Historical Society. This places families in the new territory within months of the Land Run. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Do not confuse Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.** These were legally distinct jurisdictions with different record systems until 1907. A family near the boundary between them may have generated records under both authorities. Know which side your ancestor was on, or search both.
- **For Indian Territory families, the Dawes Rolls are essential.** The Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (DGS 005221389) are browse-only and must be examined image-by-image; the separately indexed Dawes Rolls on Ancestry and tribal websites are the searchable entry point.
- **County-level tax rolls from the 1890s** can bridge the gap between the 1890 territorial census and the 1900 federal census, placing a family in a specific county in intervening years. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Territorial court records are split between two repositories.** District court records 1890-1907 are at both NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives; check both before concluding a record is unavailable.
- **Naturalization before 1906** could be filed in any court of record (district, county, probate). There is no single index — search all court levels for the relevant county.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki did not return dedicated Oklahoma-specific pages** for vital records, land records, probate, church records, or census at the constructed URLs. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki for the most current Oklahoma research guidance, as page titles may have changed.

## Locality Guide: Alabama Region, circa 1800 (Pre-Statehood)

The locality guide has been written to your project as `loc_001`. Here is a summary of the key findings:

---

### Jurisdictional History — The Most Important Starting Point

The Alabama region around 1800 had not yet achieved statehood. It passed through two territorial phases:
- **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817) — Alabama-region records from this era are *Mississippi Territory* records. Searching Alabama-only indexes will miss them entirely.
- **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819)
- **Alabama Statehood** — December 1819

The **Mobile area** is a special case: it has Spanish Catholic church registers and census returns predating U.S. control, with those records held in archives in Spain and France.

---

### Digitized Browsable Volumes

> **A genuine digitization gap.** The volume search returned zero image volumes for Alabama in the entire 1780–1830 window. There are no browsable, unindexed image collections confirmed online for this period.

---

### What *Is* Available Online (FamilySearch Indexed Collections)

These are indexed (name-searchable) collections that touch the territorial period:
| Record Type | Earliest Date |
|---|---|
| County Marriage Records | 1809 |
| Probate Records | 1809 |
| Census Substitutes Index | 1810 |
| Church Records | 1803 |

The **1810 federal census** is the earliest federal enumeration for this region and is fully searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

### Physical Holdings (Not Online)

The **territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808** are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery, Alabama — not available online.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Identify the specific county or district within Alabama you are researching. County formation dates vary significantly, and the ADAH can provide county-specific record availability and start dates. That will determine exactly which record series applies to your ancestors.

Spanish-era church and census records are in Seville (Archivo General de Indias) and at the Library of Congress; French records are in Aix-en-Provence (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer) with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.

No civil vital registration (statewide births, marriages, deaths) existed before statehood; the county marriage bond series begins at the county level only from 1809 in the earliest Alabama counties. The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page did not resolve to Alabama-specific content — check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records directly.

volume_search returned zero digitized browsable volumes for Alabama in the 1780-1830 window — this is a digitization gap, not evidence that records do not exist. The territorial census series (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) and territorial land/court records are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery.
Alabama is a federal-land state. Original land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO) website (glorecords.blm.gov), not at the county courthouse.
Territorial-era settlers migrated heavily from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — especially after the Creek War (1813-1814). Searching the origin states' records is often necessary to fill gaps.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood) (ca. 1780-1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. Before that, the territory passed through three successive jurisdictions: Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), Alabama Territory (1817-1819), and before U.S. control, the Mobile area was under French (1702-1763), British (1763-1780), and Spanish (1780-1813) administration.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); Huntsville (early Alabama Territory center for the northern districts); Mobile (southern/coastal center throughout).
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), Alabama Territory (1817-1819).
- **Population during period:** Population data for Alabama as such does not apply before 1819. The federal census of 1810 enumerated settlers in the present-day Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory. Significant population growth came after the Creek War of 1813-1814, when land cessions opened the interior. (No population figures returned by place_population for this pre-state period.)
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, trade via the Mobile port, fur trade, and river navigation. Mobile was the principal commercial hub.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers (from Virginia, Carolinas, Georgia); French Creole and Spanish Creole families around Mobile; Cherokee and Creek nations across much of the interior; enslaved African Americans; small numbers of free people of color in Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant in Mobile; served by Spanish-era parish registers); Methodist and Baptist circuit preachers active in the interior from the early 1800s; Presbyterian missionaries present.
- **Key historical events:** U.S. acquisition of the Mississippi Territory (1798); Creek War / Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1813-1814), which opened interior lands to U.S. settlement; formation of the Alabama Territory (1817); Alabama statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1763:** Region part of French Louisiana and later the Province of Louisiana.
- **1763-1780:** British West Florida / Province of West Florida.
- **1780-1798:** Spanish West Florida (Mobile District under Spain).
- **1798-1817:** Mississippi Territory — present-day Alabama was the eastern portion of this territory. ALL records created for the Alabama region in this window are Mississippi Territory records.
- **1817-1819:** Alabama Territory — separated from the Mississippi Territory when Mississippi achieved statehood. Records from this two-year window are filed under the early Alabama Territory county structure.
- **1819-present:** State of Alabama. The earliest counties (Madison, Limestone, Lawrence, and others in the north; Mobile in the south) were established before statehood; their record series begins at their respective formation dates.
- The colonial boundary between the Mobile area (formerly Spanish/French) and the interior (U.S. territorial) creates a geographic split in record type and language. Records from Mobile and the coastal area follow the Catholic/Spanish-language chain; records from the interior follow the Anglo-American territorial/county chain. Which system applies to a given ancestor depends on where within the region they lived — both must be searched when location is uncertain.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil vital registration existed before Alabama statehood (1819), and even after statehood, mandatory statewide registration did not begin until 1908 at the state level. At the **county level**, the earliest Alabama county marriage bond/license series begin ca. 1809 in the first organized counties (e.g., Madison County formed 1808). The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Vital Records page did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records directly for precise county-by-county start dates.
- **What exists for this period:** County marriage records from ca. 1809 (for the earliest-organized counties only). FamilySearch holds the indexed collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images), which covers the tail end of the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery; county probate court offices; FamilySearch (collection 1598408).
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registers for this period. No statewide marriage registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers (see Church records below); Spanish colonial census returns (Mobile area); territorial census enumerations.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, with continuous records from the French and Spanish periods); Methodist and Baptist (interior, from early 1800s, though early registers are sparse and scattered).
- **Record types:** Catholic registers include baptisms, marriages, and burials in Spanish and Latin. Protestant circuit records are irregular for this period.
- **Where held:** Mobile-area Spanish-period Catholic registers: originals at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives. French-period records: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives. FamilySearch holds the indexed collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — this begins in 1803 and reaches into the territorial era. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.)
- **Language:** Catholic registers are in Spanish and Latin for the Mobile/colonial period.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in the present-day Alabama portion of the territory. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.)
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory, including the Alabama portion. It is the first federal census that reaches this region.
- **Compiled substitutes:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images) begins in 1810 and is name-indexed but image-free.
- **Access:** The 1810 federal census for the Mississippi Territory/Alabama portion is available on Ancestry and FamilySearch. The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 are physical holdings at ADAH; check whether any have been microfilmed or published by genealogical societies.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. Also territorial court minutes, which record a broad range of county business.
- **Date range:** County probate records begin at each county's formation date. The earliest Alabama counties were organized from 1800 onward under territorial authority.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals); ADAH (many microfilmed copies); FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (collection 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins in 1809 and covers the late territorial period.
- **Note on intestate vs. testate:** When an ancestor died without a will (intestate), look for administration records; when a will was left (testate), look for the will book proper. Both series are typically included in county probate holdings.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township-range-section) for all U.S. territorial-era grants. The Spanish and British colonial era used metes-and-bounds grants, particularly in the Mobile area.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Alabama is a federal-land state. Original land patents from the U.S. period are held by the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) — not the county courthouse. Colonial (Spanish/British) grants are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (GLO), Spanish land grants, British grants, county deed books (post-county-formation), tax lists.
- **Date range:** Colonial grants from 1702 onward; U.S. territorial land patents from 1798 onward.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents, searchable online); ADAH (territorial-era land records and tax lists); county probate courts (deed books); Library of Congress and Seville (colonial grants). (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast / Mobile); various territorial militia engagements.
- **Record types:** Militia rolls (territorial period, at ADAH); War of 1812 service records and pension files (NARA); bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pensions, bounty land warrants); ADAH (territorial militia rolls); Fold3 (online access to many NARA military records, subscription required).

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Formal cemetery records for this early period are sparse. Many burials in the interior were in family plots or informal community cemeteries without sexton records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has transcribed some early Alabama cemetery inscriptions; coverage of pre-1820 burials is limited but worth checking. BillionGraves is an additional resource.
- **Physical records:** For Mobile-area Catholic cemeteries, burial records are in the Catholic church registers described above.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had early Spanish and American newspapers. The first significant English-language paper in the interior was the _Madison County Republican_ (Huntsville), founded ca. 1816.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress) have some digitized coverage, though pre-1820 Alabama newspapers are very sparse online.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (estate settlements, land sales, sheriff's sales) are genealogically valuable even when obituaries and marriage notices are absent.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast entry point, active from the French period); New Orleans (nearest major port for the Gulf South).
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial passenger lists and census returns for Mobile; post-1798 U.S. passenger lists at New Orleans (NARA); naturalization records filed in territorial courts.
- **Where held:** Spanish-era Mobile records at Archivo General de Indias, Seville, and Library of Congress; U.S. passenger manifests at NARA and Ancestry/FamilySearch; NARA (www.archives.gov).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.
- **Inland naturalization:** Even for inland settlers, declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization were filed in territorial and county courts — search court minute books, not just port-of-entry records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county ad valorem (property) tax lists; poll tax.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists begin as early as 1805 for some districts of the Mississippi Territory.
- **Where held:** ADAH (territorial and early county tax lists); county probate courts. The compiled census substitutes collection (FamilySearch 2016756) incorporates some tax list data.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a primary substitute for census gaps — the 1800 and 1805 federal censuses do not cover this region, making territorial tax lists the only name-level enumerations for many families in those years.

### Other record types
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th- and early-20th-century county histories sometimes reprint territorial-era records and name founding families. Check WorldCat and ADAH's published holdings.
- **Indian removal records:** Creek and Cherokee census rolls and removal records (post-1830, held at NARA) are genealogically relevant for families with Native American ancestry, though they fall just after this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (1986396) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from territorial era onward | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (1810 onward for this region); military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 and other military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some early Alabama newspaper digitization | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military pension files | Free/in-person |
| Library of Congress (Chronicling America) | Early American newspapers; colonial grant copies | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 0 digitized browsable image volumes for Alabama in the 1780-1830 window across two separate calls. This is a digitization gap — it does not mean the underlying records do not exist. # Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood) (ca. 1780-1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. Before that, the territory passed through three successive jurisdictions: Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), Alabama Territory (1817-1819), and before U.S. control, the Mobile area was under French (1702-1763), British (1763-1780), and Spanish (1780-1813) administration.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); Huntsville (early Alabama Territory center for the northern districts); Mobile (southern/coastal center throughout).
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), Alabama Territory (1817-1819).
- **Population during period:** Population data for Alabama as such does not apply before 1819. The federal census of 1810 enumerated settlers in the present-day Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory. Significant population growth came after the Creek War of 1813-1814, when land cessions opened the interior. (No population figures returned by place_population for this pre-state period.)
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, trade via the Mobile port, fur trade, and river navigation. Mobile was the principal commercial hub.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers (from Virginia, Carolinas, Georgia); French Creole and Spanish Creole families around Mobile; Cherokee and Creek nations across much of the interior; enslaved African Americans; small numbers of free people of color in Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant in Mobile; served by Spanish-era parish registers); Methodist and Baptist circuit preachers active in the interior from the early 1800s; Presbyterian missionaries present.
- **Key historical events:** U.S. acquisition of the Mississippi Territory (1798); Creek War / Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1813-1814), which opened interior lands to U.S. settlement; formation of the Alabama Territory (1817); Alabama statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1763:** Region part of French Louisiana and later the Province of Louisiana.
- **1763-1780:** British West Florida / Province of West Florida.
- **1780-1798:** Spanish West Florida (Mobile District under Spain).
- **1798-1817:** Mississippi Territory — present-day Alabama was the eastern portion of this territory. ALL records created for the Alabama region in this window are Mississippi Territory records.
- **1817-1819:** Alabama Territory — separated from the Mississippi Territory when Mississippi achieved statehood. Records from this two-year window are filed under the early Alabama Territory county structure.
- **1819-present:** State of Alabama. The earliest counties (Madison, Limestone, Lawrence, and others in the north; Mobile in the south) were established before statehood; their record series begins at their respective formation dates.
- The colonial boundary between the Mobile area (formerly Spanish/French) and the interior (U.S. territorial) creates a geographic split in record type and language. Records from Mobile and the coastal area follow the Catholic/Spanish-language chain; records from the interior follow the Anglo-American territorial/county chain. Which system applies to a given ancestor depends on where within the region they lived — both must be searched when location is uncertain.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil vital registration existed before Alabama statehood (1819), and even after statehood, mandatory statewide registration did not begin until 1908 at the state level. At the **county level**, the earliest Alabama county marriage bond/license series begin ca. 1809 in the first organized counties (e.g., Madison County formed 1808). The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Vital Records page did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records directly for precise county-by-county start dates.
- **What exists for this period:** County marriage records from ca. 1809 (for the earliest-organized counties only). FamilySearch holds the indexed collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images), which covers the tail end of the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery; county probate court offices; FamilySearch (collection 1598408).
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registers for this period. No statewide marriage registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers (see Church records below); Spanish colonial census returns (Mobile area); territorial census enumerations.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, with continuous records from the French and Spanish periods); Methodist and Baptist (interior, from early 1800s, though early registers are sparse and scattered).
- **Record types:** Catholic registers include baptisms, marriages, and burials in Spanish and Latin. Protestant circuit records are irregular for this period.
- **Where held:** Mobile-area Spanish-period Catholic registers: originals at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives. French-period records: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives. FamilySearch holds the indexed collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — this begins in 1803 and reaches into the territorial era. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.)
- **Language:** Catholic registers are in Spanish and Latin for the Mobile/colonial period.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in the present-day Alabama portion of the territory. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.)
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory, including the Alabama portion. It is the first federal census that reaches this region.
- **Compiled substitutes:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images) begins in 1810 and is name-indexed but image-free.
- **Access:** The 1810 federal census for the Mississippi Territory/Alabama portion is available on Ancestry and FamilySearch. The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 are physical holdings at ADAH; check whether any have been microfilmed or published by genealogical societies.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. Also territorial court minutes, which record a broad range of county business.
- **Date range:** County probate records begin at each county's formation date. The earliest Alabama counties were organized from 1800 onward under territorial authority.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals); ADAH (many microfilmed copies); FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (collection 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins in 1809 and covers the late territorial period.
- **Note on intestate vs. testate:** When an ancestor died without a will (intestate), look for administration records; when a will was left (testate), look for the will book proper. Both series are typically included in county probate holdings.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township-range-section) for all U.S. territorial-era grants. The Spanish and British colonial era used metes-and-bounds grants, particularly in the Mobile area.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Alabama is a federal-land state. Original land patents from the U.S. period are held by the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) — not the county courthouse. Colonial (Spanish/British) grants are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (GLO), Spanish land grants, British grants, county deed books (post-county-formation), tax lists.
- **Date range:** Colonial grants from 1702 onward; U.S. territorial land patents from 1798 onward.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents, searchable online); ADAH (territorial-era land records and tax lists); county probate courts (deed books); Library of Congress and Seville (colonial grants). (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast / Mobile); various territorial militia engagements.
- **Record types:** Militia rolls (territorial period, at ADAH); War of 1812 service records and pension files (NARA); bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pensions, bounty land warrants); ADAH (territorial militia rolls); Fold3 (online access to many NARA military records, subscription required).

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Formal cemetery records for this early period are sparse. Many burials in the interior were in family plots or informal community cemeteries without sexton records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has transcribed some early Alabama cemetery inscriptions; coverage of pre-1820 burials is limited but worth checking. BillionGraves is an additional resource.
- **Physical records:** For Mobile-area Catholic cemeteries, burial records are in the Catholic church registers described above.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had early Spanish and American newspapers. The first significant English-language paper in the interior was the _Madison County Republican_ (Huntsville), founded ca. 1816.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress) have some digitized coverage, though pre-1820 Alabama newspapers are very sparse online.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (estate settlements, land sales, sheriff's sales) are genealogically valuable even when obituaries and marriage notices are absent.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast entry point, active from the French period); New Orleans (nearest major port for the Gulf South).
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial passenger lists and census returns for Mobile; post-1798 U.S. passenger lists at New Orleans (NARA); naturalization records filed in territorial courts.
- **Where held:** Spanish-era Mobile records at Archivo General de Indias, Seville, and Library of Congress; U.S. passenger manifests at NARA and Ancestry/FamilySearch; NARA (www.archives.gov).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.
- **Inland naturalization:** Even for inland settlers, declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization were filed in territorial and county courts — search court minute books, not just port-of-entry records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county ad valorem (property) tax lists; poll tax.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists begin as early as 1805 for some districts of the Mississippi Territory.
- **Where held:** ADAH (territorial and early county tax lists); county probate courts. The compiled census substitutes collection (FamilySearch 2016756) incorporates some tax list data.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a primary substitute for census gaps — the 1800 and 1805 federal censuses do not cover this region, making territorial tax lists the only name-level enumerations for many families in those years.

### Other record types
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th- and early-20th-century county histories sometimes reprint territorial-era records and name founding families. Check WorldCat and ADAH's published holdings.
- **Indian removal records:** Creek and Cherokee census rolls and removal records (post-1830, held at NARA) are genealogically relevant for families with Native American ancestry, though they fall just after this period.

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (1986396) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from territorial era onward | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (1810 onward for this region); military records | Subscription |

| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military pension files | Free/in-person |
| Library of Congress (Chronicling America) | Early American newspapers; colonial grant copies | Free |

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) → 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry throughout this period. Collieries, breaker operations, and related rail transport employed the overwhelming majority of adult males. Company towns (patches) were a defining settlement form.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic immigration beginning in the 1840s–1850s, concentrated in the mining patches. Later waves of Eastern European (Welsh, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian) workers arrived from the 1870s onward. German and Welsh settlers predated the Irish in some areas.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Congregationalist and Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed, Episcopal. Catholic parishes were the primary institutional anchor for Irish immigrant families.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875–1878) involving Schuylkill County miners; labor strikes and the formation of the Workingmen's Benevolent Association (1868); the Long Strike of 1875; Reading Railroad consolidation of collieries.

**Note on the broader anthracite region:** This guide surveys Schuylkill County as the primary jurisdiction. The five anthracite coal counties are Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon each require their own locality survey — Irish coal-region families were highly mobile across these county lines and records should be checked in all counties where they are known to have lived.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has had stable boundaries since its formation in 1811. No further subdivisions occurred during the 1860–1900 research period.
- Records before 1811 are held by Berks County (Berks County Courthouse, Reading, PA) and Northampton County (Northampton County Government Center, Easton, PA).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906, and of marriages until 1885 at the state level (county-level marriage license recording preceded this). For the 1860–1900 period, no reliable civil birth or death registration system existed at the state level.
- **What exists:** Marriage licenses were recorded at the county level at the Schuylkill County courthouse beginning in the 1880s. A FamilySearch digitized volume of Schuylkill County marriage records (DGS 007936753, 94 images, 1870–1910) exists but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg (post-1906 statewide registrations)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths for 1860–1900 are not captured in civil registration for this period. Church records are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal registers, burial registers, and marriage registers are the most important alternative source for Irish families in this period. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple parishes established 1840–1870 in the mining patches), Welsh Congregationalist, Methodist Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Baptist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages (with banns), burials, confirmations. Confirmations are a separate dated event occurring years after baptism and provide an additional dated record.
- **Diocesan jurisdiction:** During 1860–1900, Schuylkill County and Carbon County fell entirely under the Diocese of Philadelphia. The Diocese of Scranton (erected 1868) covers Luzerne and Lackawanna. The Diocese of Harrisburg (erected 1868) covers Northumberland. Route Catholic record requests to the appropriate diocesan archives: for Schuylkill County records, contact the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center.
- **Where held:** Individual parish offices; diocesan archives; FamilySearch microfilm. A digitized volume of Schuylkill County church records exists on FamilySearch (DGS 007936751, 187 images, 1842–1895, in English and German) but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only images.
- **Language:** Records are primarily in English for Irish Catholic parishes in this period. German-language records exist for German ethnic parishes. Latin may appear in formal register headings.
- **Coal Region Parish Survival note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) notes that many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. Survival of early registers varies by parish.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 (1890 destroyed). The 1880 and 1900 censuses include relationship to head of household and birthplace of parents — critical for tracing Irish origins.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration, giving cause of death and birthplace.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a statewide census between federal enumerations during this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and image-available on both FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1880 and 1900 censuses are the most fully indexed.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, estate inventories
- **Date range:** From county formation 1811 onward
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville. A digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 007936749, 412 images, 1851–1930) covers Schuylkill County probate records but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. The broader FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID 1999196, 3,200,560 images) covers this period.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Working-class Irish miners frequently died intestate (no will). Search administration records as well as wills.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was not distributed through the federal rectangular survey system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania issued land warrants and patents through the Commonwealth's land office. The General Land Office (BLM) website does not cover Pennsylvania.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax assessment records. Miners in company towns frequently did not own land — land records may be sparse for this population, but tax assessments will still name them as residents.
- **Date range:** From 1811 for Schuylkill County deed records
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives (warrants and surveys). A digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 007936752, 543 images, 1815–1900) of deed records exists and is partially indexed at 22% — the only partly name-searchable volume in this survey.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** U.S. Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files (NARA); Civil War draft registrations (1863, available at Ancestry and FamilySearch); Pennsylvania State Archives adjutant general records; GAR (Grand Army of the Republic) post records for veterans in Schuylkill County
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington, DC and Philadelphia regional facility; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg
- **Note for Irish men:** Civil War pension files often contain birthplace, date and place of marriage, and names and ages of children — highly useful for tracing Irish origins.

### Cemetery records
- **Types of cemeteries:** Catholic parish cemeteries (the most important for Irish families), nondenominational borough cemeteries, Protestant church cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has coverage for major Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage varies by individual cemetery
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at the individual parish or cemetery office. Catholic diocesan archives may hold some burial registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, published from 1825) is the primary coal-region newspaper and carries obituaries, marriage notices, accident reports, and legal notices throughout the 1860–1900 period.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal archives are available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville, and partially through the Pennsylvania State Library. Check Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank for digitized runs.
- **Content value:** Mine accident reports name individual victims (occupational hazard for Irish miners); obituaries from the 1880s and 1890s increasingly include birthplace and survivors.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary port for Irish arrivals to Pennsylvania), New York (Castle Garden through 1891, Ellis Island from 1892), Baltimore, Boston
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (indexed on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Findmypast); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions filed at Schuylkill County courts
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906, a man could file his declaration of intention ("first papers") in any court of record — Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or U.S. District Court. A digitized FamilySearch volume of Schuylkill County naturalization records exists (DGS 007936750, 298 images, 1849–1915) but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. Search all courts.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists, post-1906 naturalization records); Schuylkill County courthouse (pre-1906 naturalization papers)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members. Naturalization declarations often state county of origin in Ireland — one of the few documents that can point back to the home parish.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania state triennial tax assessments (from 1853); county property and personal property tax
- **Date range:** Triennial assessments from 1853 onward; surviving county tax lists from the 1820s
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Schuylkill County Historical Society
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessment ledgers (from the FamilySearch Wiki page "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — particularly valuable in intercensal years when census records are unavailable.

### Specialized coal-region records
The FamilySearch Wiki page "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) identifies the following specialized indexes:

**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers, drawn from company payroll books, across the anthracite field. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. Note: this index is described in the context of the lower anthracite field (Luzerne and Lackawanna counties); Schuylkill County workers in the upper anthracite field may not appear.

**Company payroll books vs. accident reports:** The wiki distinguishes payroll indexes (naming individual workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person). Payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.

**Colliery employment indexes:** Drawn from company payroll books; include occupation and wage rate. Survival depends on whether the original coal company records have been preserved and indexed.

### Other record types
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association / labor union records:** The WBA and successor unions maintained membership rolls that may name individual miners. Check the Historical Collections and Labor Archives at Penn State University Libraries.
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians records:** The AOH was a major Irish fraternal organization in the coal region. Lodge membership records may survive in local or national AOH archives.
- **Company store records / scrip:** Coal companies operated company stores and issued scrip; store ledgers naming individual miners sometimes survive in corporate or historical society collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3.2M images, collection 1999196); 5 digitized volumes for Schuylkill County (probate, naturalization, church, deeds, marriages — 4 of 5 browse-only); Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850–1900 federal census (indexed); Civil War records; Pennsylvania marriage indexes; Miners' Journal partial runs; Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists (pre-period) | Subscription |
| Findmypast | Irish and British passenger lists and emigration records; some Pennsylvania Catholic records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions for Schuylkill County | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County for the 1860–1900 period (volume_search returned all 5; no nextPageToken present). This is the complete set returned by the tool. Of these, 4 are browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable); 1 (deed records, DGS 007936752) is 22% name-indexed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, marriage licenses, naturalization papers (pre-1906), probate files, court minutes | In-person; some records available by mail request |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Miners' Journal microfilm, local histories, obituary files, cemetery indexes | In-person; contact for hours |
| Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center | Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers for Schuylkill and Carbon county parishes (1860–1900 period) | In-person and written request; appointment recommended |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State tax assessments, military records, land warrant surveys, post-1906 vital records | In-person and online finding aids |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional Facility | Federal census originals, military pension files, naturalization records | In-person |
| Historical Collections and Labor Archives, Penn State University | Coal company records, union records, WBA materials | In-person; contact for holdings |

## Records NOT online
- Catholic parish registers for most Schuylkill County parishes before the 1890s (held at individual parishes or the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center)
- Pre-1906 court-level naturalization declarations and petitions (the FamilySearch volume is browse-only; originals at the courthouse)
- Triennial state tax assessment ledgers (held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not indexed online)
- Coal company employment and payroll records (survival varies; held in corporate archives or donated to Penn State Historical Collections)
- Ancient Order of Hibernians lodge membership records
- Miners' Journal for most of the 1860–1880 period (available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society, not fully digitized online)

## Known record losses
No major courthouse fire or flood affecting Schuylkill County records during the 1860–1900 period is documented in the tools consulted for this survey. The FamilySearch Coal Region Records page notes that a 1903 records consolidation by the coal companies affected surviving payroll books — some colliery payroll records were destroyed at that point, which is why the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index drew from books that survived that consolidation. Researchers should verify the survival status of specific colliery records before assuming a given miner will appear.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1880 and 1900 censuses**, which give parents' birthplaces. A birthplace of "Ireland" is a starting point; the goal is to narrow it to a county or parish using naturalization papers, death certificates (post-1906), and Catholic registers.
- **Catholic parish registers before civil registration:** For 1860–1900 Irish families, the Catholic baptismal register is effectively the birth record. Identify the specific parish that served the mining patch where the family lived. Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia throughout this period; contact the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center for register access.
- **Naturalization papers as origin documents:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention sometimes state county of origin in Ireland. Browse the FamilySearch volume DGS 007936750 (Schuylkill County naturalization records, 1849–1915, 298 images) image by image, and check the Court of Common Pleas minute books at the courthouse.
- **Use the Miners' Journal for obituaries and accident reports:** The paper named victims of mine accidents with occupational detail. Irish miners who died in accidents in the 1860s–1880s will appear in the Miners' Journal before death certificates existed. Available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- **Triennial tax assessments as census substitutes:** The Pennsylvania state triennial assessments (from 1853, per the FamilySearch Wiki page https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) list householder, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Use them in years between censuses (e.g., 1863, 1866, 1869) to trace residence and mobility.
- **Check adjoining counties:** Irish mining families moved frequently between collieries across county lines. The adjoining anthracite counties — Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland — all had significant Irish mining communities. Records for family members may be found in those counties even when the primary research target is in Schuylkill County. Each of those counties requires its own locality survey.
- **Payroll indexes vs. accident reports:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records), use payroll-derived indexes to find individual workers by name; accident and inspection reports are organized by colliery and are less useful as name-finding aids.
- **Irish naming conventions:** Irish families frequently reused a small set of given names across generations (naming children after grandparents). Do not assume all same-named individuals in the same locality are the same person, and do not assume variant spellings in census and church records refer to different people. The FamilySearch Wiki does not have a Pennsylvania-specific naming customs page — consult an Irish-specific naming customs guide for the patterns.
- **Schuylkill County formed 1811:** Records before 1811 are held by Berks County (Berks County Courthouse, Reading) and Northampton County (Northampton County Government Center, Easton). This is background context only for the 1860–1900 period.

The county had a massive Irish Catholic population drawn to the collieries, and the most important records for that community are Catholic parish registers (held by the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center, since Schuylkill County remained in the Diocese of Philadelphia for the entire period), the FamilySearch digitized volumes of naturalization, probate, church, deed, and marriage records (all browse-only except deeds, which are 22% name-indexed), the federal censuses of 1860 through 1900, the Miners' Journal newspaper on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society, and a specialized coal-region finding aid on FamilySearch's wiki (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) that describes the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index of roughly 41,000 colliery workers and the Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers. Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906, so church records are the primary vital-record substitute throughout the entire target period. Pre-1906 naturalization papers filed in any county court are a key source for Irish county of origin.

The four other anthracite coal counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon) each need their own locality survey, since Irish mining families moved frequently across county lines and each county falls under a different diocese for Catholic records after 1868.
