# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) → 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry throughout this period. Collieries, breaker operations, and related rail transport employed the overwhelming majority of adult males. Company towns (patches) were a defining settlement form.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic immigration beginning in the 1840s–1850s, concentrated in the mining patches. Later waves of Eastern European (Welsh, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian) workers arrived from the 1870s onward. German and Welsh settlers predated the Irish in some areas.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Congregationalist and Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed, Episcopal. Catholic parishes were the primary institutional anchor for Irish immigrant families.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875–1878) involving Schuylkill County miners; labor strikes and the formation of the Workingmen's Benevolent Association (1868); the Long Strike of 1875; Reading Railroad consolidation of collieries.

**Note on the broader anthracite region:** This guide surveys Schuylkill County as the primary jurisdiction. The five anthracite coal counties are Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon each require their own locality survey — Irish coal-region families were highly mobile across these county lines and records should be checked in all counties where they are known to have lived.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has had stable boundaries since its formation in 1811. No further subdivisions occurred during the 1860–1900 research period.
- Records before 1811 are held by Berks County (Berks County Courthouse, Reading, PA) and Northampton County (Northampton County Government Center, Easton, PA).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906, and of marriages until 1885 at the state level (county-level marriage license recording preceded this). For the 1860–1900 period, no reliable civil birth or death registration system existed at the state level.
- **What exists:** Marriage licenses were recorded at the county level at the Schuylkill County courthouse beginning in the 1880s. A FamilySearch digitized volume of Schuylkill County marriage records (DGS 007936753, 94 images, 1870–1910) exists but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg (post-1906 statewide registrations)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths for 1860–1900 are not captured in civil registration for this period. Church records are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal registers, burial registers, and marriage registers are the most important alternative source for Irish families in this period. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple parishes established 1840–1870 in the mining patches), Welsh Congregationalist, Methodist Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Baptist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages (with banns), burials, confirmations. Confirmations are a separate dated event occurring years after baptism and provide an additional dated record.
- **Diocesan jurisdiction:** During 1860–1900, Schuylkill County and Carbon County fell entirely under the Diocese of Philadelphia. The Diocese of Scranton (erected 1868) covers Luzerne and Lackawanna. The Diocese of Harrisburg (erected 1868) covers Northumberland. Route Catholic record requests to the appropriate diocesan archives: for Schuylkill County records, contact the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center.
- **Where held:** Individual parish offices; diocesan archives; FamilySearch microfilm. A digitized volume of Schuylkill County church records exists on FamilySearch (DGS 007936751, 187 images, 1842–1895, in English and German) but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only images.
- **Language:** Records are primarily in English for Irish Catholic parishes in this period. German-language records exist for German ethnic parishes. Latin may appear in formal register headings.
- **Coal Region Parish Survival note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) notes that many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. Survival of early registers varies by parish.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 (1890 destroyed). The 1880 and 1900 censuses include relationship to head of household and birthplace of parents — critical for tracing Irish origins.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration, giving cause of death and birthplace.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a statewide census between federal enumerations during this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and image-available on both FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1880 and 1900 censuses are the most fully indexed.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, estate inventories
- **Date range:** From county formation 1811 onward
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville. A digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 007936749, 412 images, 1851–1930) covers Schuylkill County probate records but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. The broader FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID 1999196, 3,200,560 images) covers this period.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Working-class Irish miners frequently died intestate (no will). Search administration records as well as wills.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was not distributed through the federal rectangular survey system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania issued land warrants and patents through the Commonwealth's land office. The General Land Office (BLM) website does not cover Pennsylvania.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax assessment records. Miners in company towns frequently did not own land — land records may be sparse for this population, but tax assessments will still name them as residents.
- **Date range:** From 1811 for Schuylkill County deed records
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives (warrants and surveys). A digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 007936752, 543 images, 1815–1900) of deed records exists and is partially indexed at 22% — the only partly name-searchable volume in this survey.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** U.S. Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files (NARA); Civil War draft registrations (1863, available at Ancestry and FamilySearch); Pennsylvania State Archives adjutant general records; GAR (Grand Army of the Republic) post records for veterans in Schuylkill County
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington, DC and Philadelphia regional facility; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg
- **Note for Irish men:** Civil War pension files often contain birthplace, date and place of marriage, and names and ages of children — highly useful for tracing Irish origins.

### Cemetery records
- **Types of cemeteries:** Catholic parish cemeteries (the most important for Irish families), nondenominational borough cemeteries, Protestant church cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has coverage for major Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage varies by individual cemetery
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at the individual parish or cemetery office. Catholic diocesan archives may hold some burial registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, published from 1825) is the primary coal-region newspaper and carries obituaries, marriage notices, accident reports, and legal notices throughout the 1860–1900 period.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal archives are available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville, and partially through the Pennsylvania State Library. Check Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank for digitized runs.
- **Content value:** Mine accident reports name individual victims (occupational hazard for Irish miners); obituaries from the 1880s and 1890s increasingly include birthplace and survivors.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary port for Irish arrivals to Pennsylvania), New York (Castle Garden through 1891, Ellis Island from 1892), Baltimore, Boston
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (indexed on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Findmypast); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions filed at Schuylkill County courts
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906, a man could file his declaration of intention ("first papers") in any court of record — Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or U.S. District Court. A digitized FamilySearch volume of Schuylkill County naturalization records exists (DGS 007936750, 298 images, 1849–1915) but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. Search all courts.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists, post-1906 naturalization records); Schuylkill County courthouse (pre-1906 naturalization papers)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members. Naturalization declarations often state county of origin in Ireland — one of the few documents that can point back to the home parish.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania state triennial tax assessments (from 1853); county property and personal property tax
- **Date range:** Triennial assessments from 1853 onward; surviving county tax lists from the 1820s
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Schuylkill County Historical Society
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessment ledgers (from the FamilySearch Wiki page "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — particularly valuable in intercensal years when census records are unavailable.

### Specialized coal-region records
The FamilySearch Wiki page "Pennsylvania Coal Region Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) identifies the following specialized indexes:

**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers, drawn from company payroll books, across the anthracite field. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. Note: this index is described in the context of the lower anthracite field (Luzerne and Lackawanna counties); Schuylkill County workers in the upper anthracite field may not appear.

**Company payroll books vs. accident reports:** The wiki distinguishes payroll indexes (naming individual workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person). Payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.

**Colliery employment indexes:** Drawn from company payroll books; include occupation and wage rate. Survival depends on whether the original coal company records have been preserved and indexed.

### Other record types
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association / labor union records:** The WBA and successor unions maintained membership rolls that may name individual miners. Check the Historical Collections and Labor Archives at Penn State University Libraries.
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians records:** The AOH was a major Irish fraternal organization in the coal region. Lodge membership records may survive in local or national AOH archives.
- **Company store records / scrip:** Coal companies operated company stores and issued scrip; store ledgers naming individual miners sometimes survive in corporate or historical society collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3.2M images, collection 1999196); 5 digitized volumes for Schuylkill County (probate, naturalization, church, deeds, marriages — 4 of 5 browse-only); Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850–1900 federal census (indexed); Civil War records; Pennsylvania marriage indexes; Miners' Journal partial runs; Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists (pre-period) | Subscription |
| Findmypast | Irish and British passenger lists and emigration records; some Pennsylvania Catholic records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions for Schuylkill County | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County for the 1860–1900 period (volume_search returned all 5; no nextPageToken present). This is the complete set returned by the tool. Of these, 4 are browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable); 1 (deed records, DGS 007936752) is 22% name-indexed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, marriage licenses, naturalization papers (pre-1906), probate files, court minutes | In-person; some records available by mail request |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Miners' Journal microfilm, local histories, obituary files, cemetery indexes | In-person; contact for hours |
| Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center | Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers for Schuylkill and Carbon county parishes (1860–1900 period) | In-person and written request; appointment recommended |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State tax assessments, military records, land warrant surveys, post-1906 vital records | In-person and online finding aids |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional Facility | Federal census originals, military pension files, naturalization records | In-person |
| Historical Collections and Labor Archives, Penn State University | Coal company records, union records, WBA materials | In-person; contact for holdings |

## Records NOT online
- Catholic parish registers for most Schuylkill County parishes before the 1890s (held at individual parishes or the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center)
- Pre-1906 court-level naturalization declarations and petitions (the FamilySearch volume is browse-only; originals at the courthouse)
- Triennial state tax assessment ledgers (held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not indexed online)
- Coal company employment and payroll records (survival varies; held in corporate archives or donated to Penn State Historical Collections)
- Ancient Order of Hibernians lodge membership records
- Miners' Journal for most of the 1860–1880 period (available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society, not fully digitized online)

## Known record losses
No major courthouse fire or flood affecting Schuylkill County records during the 1860–1900 period is documented in the tools consulted for this survey. The FamilySearch Coal Region Records page notes that a 1903 records consolidation by the coal companies affected surviving payroll books — some colliery payroll records were destroyed at that point, which is why the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index drew from books that survived that consolidation. Researchers should verify the survival status of specific colliery records before assuming a given miner will appear.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1880 and 1900 censuses**, which give parents' birthplaces. A birthplace of "Ireland" is a starting point; the goal is to narrow it to a county or parish using naturalization papers, death certificates (post-1906), and Catholic registers.
- **Catholic parish registers before civil registration:** For 1860–1900 Irish families, the Catholic baptismal register is effectively the birth record. Identify the specific parish that served the mining patch where the family lived. Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia throughout this period; contact the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center for register access.
- **Naturalization papers as origin documents:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention sometimes state county of origin in Ireland. Browse the FamilySearch volume DGS 007936750 (Schuylkill County naturalization records, 1849–1915, 298 images) image by image, and check the Court of Common Pleas minute books at the courthouse.
- **Use the Miners' Journal for obituaries and accident reports:** The paper named victims of mine accidents with occupational detail. Irish miners who died in accidents in the 1860s–1880s will appear in the Miners' Journal before death certificates existed. Available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- **Triennial tax assessments as census substitutes:** The Pennsylvania state triennial assessments (from 1853, per the FamilySearch Wiki page https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) list householder, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Use them in years between censuses (e.g., 1863, 1866, 1869) to trace residence and mobility.
- **Check adjoining counties:** Irish mining families moved frequently between collieries across county lines. The adjoining anthracite counties — Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland — all had significant Irish mining communities. Records for family members may be found in those counties even when the primary research target is in Schuylkill County. Each of those counties requires its own locality survey.
- **Payroll indexes vs. accident reports:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records), use payroll-derived indexes to find individual workers by name; accident and inspection reports are organized by colliery and are less useful as name-finding aids.
- **Irish naming conventions:** Irish families frequently reused a small set of given names across generations (naming children after grandparents). Do not assume all same-named individuals in the same locality are the same person, and do not assume variant spellings in census and church records refer to different people. The FamilySearch Wiki does not have a Pennsylvania-specific naming customs page — consult an Irish-specific naming customs guide for the patterns.
- **Schuylkill County formed 1811:** Records before 1811 are held by Berks County (Berks County Courthouse, Reading) and Northampton County (Northampton County Government Center, Easton). This is background context only for the 1860–1900 period.

---

**Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide**

You are researching ancestors who lived in what is now Vermont during the late 1700s, before it became a state in 1791. That territory had a complicated legal identity:

- **New Hampshire** issued land grants there beginning in 1749
- **New York** disputed those grants from 1764 and claimed the same land under its own authority
- From **1777**, settlers declared themselves the independent **Vermont Republic** and ran their own government until joining the Union in 1791

Records from those same years can therefore appear under **three different jurisdictions**, depending on which authority the record-maker recognized.

---

### Key Record Gaps & Substitutes

**No civil vital registration** (births, marriages, deaths) existed in Vermont at any level until **1857**. The best substitutes for the pre-statehood period are:

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Church records** | Baptist, Congregational, and Methodist congregations where they existed |
| **Town clerk records** | Some towns kept informal records from the 1770s |
| **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** | Earliest name list for the territory; ~1,800 grantees |
| **Tax lists (1778 onward)** | From the Vermont Republic period |
| **Revolutionary War pension files** | At the National Archives; often contain detailed biographical narrative |
| **Proprietary records** | Land grants under NH and NY authority |
| **19th-century town histories** | Frequently reprint colonial-era records found nowhere else |

---

### Where Records Are Held

- Individual **town clerk offices**
- **Vermont State Archives**
- **Vermont Historical Society**
- **New Hampshire State Archives** (for NH-grant period)
- **New York State Archives** (for NY-claim period)

Most of these are **not comprehensively online**.

---

When you are ready, a research plan can be built that sequences these sources for your specific ancestor and town.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1750-1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted to the Union as the 14th state on March 4, 1791. Before that it existed as the Vermont Republic (self-declared January 15, 1777), and before that the territory was known as the "New Hampshire Grants" — land granted by New Hampshire Governor Benning Wentworth beginning in 1749, later disputed by New York Colony from 1764 onward.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single capital during the Republic period; Montpelier became the permanent capital in 1805. During the Republic, functions rotated among several towns.
- **Parent jurisdiction (disputed):** New Hampshire Colony (grants 1749-1764), then Province of New York (claimed authority 1764-1777), then the Vermont Republic (independent, 1777-1791).
- **Population during period:** The `place_population` tool did not return population figures for Vermont in this date range. Vermont's 1790 federal census (the first after statehood) counted 85,341 inhabitants — the earliest federal figure available.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and small-scale agriculture; timber; some potash production. Communities were newly settled frontier towns throughout most of this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers from southern New England (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island), with smaller numbers of Scots-Irish and German settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (predominant), Baptist, Methodist, and some Presbyterian congregations. The Church of England had minimal presence. Many early communities had no organized congregation at all during the first years of settlement.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754-1763) — the territory was a contested frontier zone; New Hampshire Grants controversy and the Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York authority (1764-1777); Vermont Declaration of Independence (January 15, 1777); Vermont Constitution adopted (July 1777) — the first in North America to prohibit adult slavery; American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), including the Battle of Bennington (1777); border negotiations with New York and Canada throughout the Republic period; admission to the Union March 4, 1791.

## Boundary changes

The jurisdictional history of pre-statehood Vermont is unusually complex and directly determines where records are held:

- **Before 1749:** The territory was sparsely inhabited. French colonial claims overlapped English ones. No English civil jurisdiction created records here.
- **1749-1764:** New Hampshire Colony, under Governor Benning Wentworth, issued grants for more than 100 townships across the territory. Land records from this period are in New Hampshire colonial records.
- **1764:** The British Crown ruled in favor of New York, placing the territory under New York colonial authority. New York refused to recognize the New Hampshire grants and issued competing grants. Two sets of land records — New Hampshire and New York — now cover the same territory for the same years.
- **1777-1791:** The Vermont Republic operated its own government, courts, and land system. Records created under the Republic are held in Vermont archives, not in New York or New Hampshire.
- **1791:** Vermont admitted to the Union. All subsequent records are state records.
- **County formation:** Vermont counties were created by the Vermont Republic beginning in 1778 (Bennington, Chittenden, and others). County formation continued through the early statehood period. Earlier records may exist only at the town level, with no county structure yet in place.

**A geographic note on the New York / New Hampshire dispute:** The competing jurisdictions covered the entire territory of present-day Vermont, not divided sub-regions. Which jurisdiction's records apply to a given ancestor depends on which authority that ancestor recognized and interacted with — not on where within Vermont they lived. Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records for the 1764-1777 period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration did **not** begin until 1857 (state level). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont Genealogy ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) states statewide registration began in 1857. For the entire pre-statehood period (ca. 1750-1791) there is **no civil vital registration at any level**.
- **What exists:** Some town clerk offices began recording vital events informally as early as the 1770s, but survival is uneven. Consult individual town clerk offices directly.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices for surviving town records; Vermont State Archives for compiled/deposited records.
- **Gaps:** Substantial. For most of the pre-statehood period, no systematic vital registration existed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); proprietors' records; town meeting minutes; probate records; gravestone inscriptions; 19th-century town histories that reprint earlier data.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common in early New England settlements), Baptist, Methodist, some Presbyterian. Many early towns had no organized congregation; circuit-riding ministers served some areas.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (where congregations were established) membership rolls and disciplinary proceedings.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; denominational archives (e.g., Congregational records are often at local historical societies or state depositories); Vermont Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm (check the FamilySearch Catalog for specific towns).
- **Language:** English.
- **Digitization level:** Varies widely by congregation. Many remain physical only or on microfilm. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) should be checked for each specific town — the topic-specific wiki pages (Vermont_Church_Records) returned only generic content in this survey and could not confirm specific digitized collections.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census that includes Vermont is **1790** — taken shortly before and after formal statehood (March 4, 1791). This is the only federal enumeration for the pre-statehood period and is the closest systematic population record available. It is available online and indexed.
- **State/colonial enumeration:** No Vermont colonial census is known. The Vermont Republic did not conduct a formal census.
- **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** This is the most significant pre-statehood population-type document. Prepared under New York colonial authority, it lists approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants. It is not a census — it does not list families or household members — but it places named individuals in specific townships at a specific date and is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory. Confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)).
- **Tax lists:** The Vermont Republic levied taxes; town-level tax lists from the Republic period survive in some towns and function as the best substitute for a census in the 1777-1791 window.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship records, court minutes.
- **Date range:** Vermont probate districts were established by the Vermont Republic beginning in 1778. Earlier probate (pre-1778) would have been handled under New York or New Hampshire colonial courts if at all.
- **Where held:** Vermont probate district courts (which align roughly with counties); Vermont State Archives holds older records. The FamilySearch Catalog should be checked for specific probate districts.
- **Digitization level:** Varies. The Vermont_Probate_Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; specific collection details could not be confirmed from tool results.
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** For the pre-statehood period, many settlers died without formal wills (intestate), and estate administration was informal or nonexistent. When a probate record exists, it is a significant find for establishing family relationships.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Vermont is a state-land state. Land was granted by the government of New Hampshire (1749-1764), then disputed by New York (1764-1777), then regranted or confirmed by the Vermont Republic (1777-1791). Do **not** use the federal BLM-GLO patent database for Vermont — federal public-domain land laws did not apply here.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Three overlapping authorities:
  - New Hampshire colonial government (Wentworth grants, 1749-1764): records at New Hampshire State Archives, Concord, NH.
  - New York colonial government (competing grants, 1764-1777): records at New York State Archives, Albany, NY.
  - Vermont Republic / State of Vermont (confirmations and new grants, 1777 onward): records at Vermont State Archives and individual town land offices.
- **Types:** Township grants (proprietors' records), deeds, surveys, tax records, and bounty land grants to Revolutionary War veterans.
- **Date range:** New Hampshire grants begin 1749. Town-level deed recording began as towns organized (typically within a few years of settlement, so 1760s-1770s for the earliest towns).
- **Where held:** Town land records are held at town clerk offices (Vermont towns record deeds locally, not at the county level). State-level grant records are at the Vermont State Archives. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) emphasizes that the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is a key pre-statehood land document.
- **Digitization level:** The Vermont_Land_and_Property wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; specific collection details could not be confirmed from tool results.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754-1763) — Vermont territory was a military frontier, and men from neighboring colonies served here; American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), including the Green Mountain Boys (Vermont's own militia) and Continental Army service.
- **Record types:**
  - Revolutionary War service records: at NARA (National Archives), online via Fold3.
  - Revolutionary War pension files: at NARA, online via Fold3 and Ancestry. These often contain the most detailed biographical information of any pre-statehood source — depositions name spouses, children, neighbors, and describe life events in detail.
  - Bounty land warrants: issued to veterans after the war; relevant land records follow.
  - Vermont militia records: separate from Continental Army records; held at the Vermont State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal records); Vermont State Archives (state militia); Fold3 and Ancestry (digitized online).
- **Digitization level:** Federal service records and pension files are largely indexed and available as images via Fold3 (subscription) and partially via FamilySearch. Vermont militia records have variable digitization.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Town burying grounds (most Vermont towns established a public cemetery as part of original settlement). Many small family plots on farmsteads.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) has coverage for Vermont cemeteries, including transcriptions of pre-statehood gravestones. Coverage is volunteer-driven and not comprehensive.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare; most burial information comes from gravestone transcriptions.
- **Note:** Gravestones from the 1770s-1790s survive in many Vermont towns and may be the only direct evidence of birth and death dates for this period.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspaper, the Vermont Gazette (later Spooner's Vermont Journal), began publication in 1781 in Westminster. A small number of other papers appeared in the 1780s.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; Newspapers.com ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) has some holdings; state library microfilm collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, land sale announcements, and public notices appear from the early 1780s onward. Coverage before 1781 is a gap — no Vermont newspapers existed.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Boston, MA and Providence, RI were the nearest ports for settlers arriving from Europe, though most pre-statehood Vermont settlers migrated overland from southern New England rather than directly from overseas.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for overseas arrivals (at NARA and online via Ancestry/FamilySearch); naturalization records (not applicable for most settlers, who were already British subjects before the Revolution; post-Revolution naturalization records begin in Vermont courts after 1791).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants. For the pre-statehood period, most Vermont ancestors arrived overland from Massachusetts or Connecticut rather than by sea — do not limit the search to port records. Check Massachusetts and Connecticut records for the origin community.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal); state archives of origin states.

### Tax records

- **Types:** The Vermont Republic levied property and poll taxes from 1778 onward. Town-level tax lists are the primary surviving record.
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic tax records begin 1778. Pre-1778 tax records for the territory would be under New York or New Hampshire colonial authority.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for census records during the 1778-1790 gap before the first federal census. A man listed on the tax roll is placed in a specific town in a specific year.

### Proprietors' records

- **What they are:** When a township was granted (by New Hampshire or Vermont), the original grantees ("proprietors") organized themselves and kept records of their meetings, lot divisions, and membership. These are distinct from town records and may predate formal town organization.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; individual town archives; some have been transcribed in 19th-century town histories.
- **Value:** Proprietors' records name the original settlers of a town and document lot assignments. They are often the first record placing a family in a specific Vermont location.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Vermont towns governed themselves through town meetings from their earliest days. Town meeting minutes record who was present, who held office, and what business was transacted — naming ordinary residents who appear in no other record.
- **Town histories:** 19th-century town histories (most published 1860-1900) routinely reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) specifically notes this. These are frequently the only surviving transcription of pre-statehood records.
- **Family bibles:** Bible records noting births, marriages, and deaths were kept by many New England families. These circulate in published genealogical society volumes and are held by historical societies and private families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census (indexed); some church record microfilm via Catalog; generic vital records category page | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (1790); Revolutionary War pension and service records; some Vermont town histories | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions for Vermont towns | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some Vermont newspapers from 1781 onward | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military and pension records; 1790 census | Free online via affiliated databases |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `external_links_search` tool returned 6 results for Vermont in the 1750-1791 date range, but these were all generic national-level resources (census, vital records category, cemetery, newspapers, military, NARA) with no Vermont-specific curated collections. The `totalForPlace` was 6, matching `results.length`, so this represents the complete FamilySearch-curated external link set for Vermont in this period — it is sparse. The `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not called in this survey due to the place resolution issues; researchers should search the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Vermont-specific holdings.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Land records, Vermont Republic records, probate district records, legislative records, militia records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier, VT) | Town histories, genealogical collections, newspapers, church records, manuscripts | In-person; some digitized holdings |
| Town clerk offices (each Vermont town) | Deeds, proprietors' records, vital records (from when recording began), tax lists, town meeting minutes | In-person or mail request to each town |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire Grants records, Wentworth grant documents (1749-1764) | In-person; some online |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial land records covering the New Hampshire Grants territory (1764-1777) | In-person; some online |
| NARA (Washington, DC / regional) | 1790 federal census; Revolutionary War service and pension records | In-person; online via affiliated databases |
| Denominational archives | Church records by denomination | Varies by denomination |

## Records NOT online

- **Most pre-statehood town clerk records** (vital events informally recorded before 1791): held at individual town clerk offices; not systematically digitized.
- **Vermont Republic tax lists and town meeting minutes:** held at town offices and Vermont State Archives; digitization is limited.
- **Proprietors' records** for most townships: held in town archives or Vermont State Archives; not digitized except where incorporated into published town histories.
- **New Hampshire colonial grant records** (Wentworth grants, 1749-1764): at New Hampshire State Archives; some available on microfilm but not comprehensively online.
- **New York colonial land records** covering the disputed territory (1764-1777): at New York State Archives; not comprehensively online.
- **Local church records** for most early congregations: at church offices, denominational archives, or Vermont Historical Society; digitization varies.
- **Vermont militia records**: at Vermont State Archives; not comprehensively online.

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fires or mass record destructions for Vermont's pre-statehood period were confirmed in the tool results for this survey. However:

- The general fragility of record-keeping on a settlement frontier means many records were simply never created or were lost to normal attrition (fires in private homes, water damage, etc.).
- The contested jurisdictional situation (New Hampshire vs. New York vs. Vermont Republic) means some records were created under an authority that was later repudiated, and those records may have been neglected or lost as a result.
- Researchers should not interpret the absence of a record online as evidence the record does not exist — for this period, absence online is the norm, not the exception.

## Research tips

- **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the starting point for any pre-statehood ancestor.** It lists approximately 1,800 grantees by name, township, grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. It is the earliest systematic name list for the territory. Confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Town-level research is essential.** Vermont's primary record-keeping unit is the town, not the county. Identify the specific town of residence before searching; a county-level search alone will miss most records.
- **Work backward from the 1790 census.** The 1790 federal census is the first enumeration of the territory and the most accessible indexed source. Use it to confirm location, then work backward using land, church, tax, and proprietors' records.
- **Check 19th-century town histories.** The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) specifically notes that town histories published 1860-1900 frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. These are a primary research tool, not just background reading.
- **Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records for the 1764-1777 period.** Both jurisdictions claimed authority and both created records. An ancestor who held land under a New Hampshire grant may appear in New Hampshire records even though they lived in what is now Vermont, and a competing claimant may appear in New York records.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are often the most detailed pre-statehood biographical source.** Veteran depositions name family members, describe life events, and were given decades after the war — they routinely describe the 1770s-1790s in detail. Search via Fold3 ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)) and the pension index at NARA.
- **Gravestones survive.** Vermont's pre-statehood burying grounds are well preserved in many towns. Gravestone transcriptions on Find A Grave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) may provide birth, death, and sometimes spousal information that appears nowhere else.
- **Vermont naming customs:** The Vermont_Naming_Customs wiki page returned only generic content in this survey. New England naming patterns (naming children after parents and grandparents, alternating maternal and paternal family names) were prevalent; be alert to collateral relatives who share given names with your subject.
- **Consider the origin community.** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers came from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island. When records are sparse in Vermont, look for the family in the town of origin in the sending state — church records, land records, and vital records there may document the family before migration.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** Vermont borders New Hampshire to the east (Connecticut River), New York to the west (Lake Champlain and the Taconic highlands), Massachusetts to the south, and Canada (Quebec) to the north. Families near any of these borders may have generated records on both sides. The county-level neighboring jurisdictions were not listed in tool results for this survey, so researchers should check records in Cheshire and Sullivan Counties (NH) along the Connecticut River border, Rensselaer, Washington, and Clinton Counties (NY) along the western border, and Franklin County (MA) along the southern border.

You are researching ancestors who lived in what is now Vermont during the late 1700s, before it became a state in 1791. That territory had a complicated legal identity: New Hampshire issued land grants there beginning in 1749, New York disputed those grants from 1764 and claimed the same land under its own authority, and then from 1777 the settlers declared themselves the independent Vermont Republic and ran their own government until joining the Union. Records from those same years can therefore appear under three different jurisdictions, depending on which authority the record-maker recognized. Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did not begin in Vermont at any level until 1857, so for the pre-statehood period there is simply no vital registration to find. The best substitutes are church records (Baptist, Congregational, and Methodist congregations where they existed), town clerk records that some towns kept informally from the 1770s, the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (the earliest name list for the territory, listing roughly 1,800 grantees), tax lists from the Vermont Republic period (1778 onward), Revolutionary War pension files at the National Archives (which often contain detailed biographical narrative), proprietary records, and 19th-century town histories that frequently reprint colonial-era records found nowhere else. Most of these are held at individual town clerk offices, the Vermont State Archives, the Vermont Historical Society, and the New Hampshire and New York state archives for the disputed-grant period — not comprehensively online.

When you are ready, a research plan can be built that sequences these sources for your specific ancestor and town.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1750-1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted to the Union as the 14th state on March 4, 1791. Before that it existed as the Vermont Republic (self-declared January 15, 1777), and before that the territory was known as the "New Hampshire Grants" — land granted by New Hampshire Governor Benning Wentworth beginning in 1749, later disputed by New York Colony from 1764 onward.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single capital during the Republic period; Montpelier became the permanent capital in 1805. During the Republic, functions rotated among several towns.
- **Parent jurisdiction (disputed):** New Hampshire Colony (grants 1749-1764), then Province of New York (claimed authority 1764-1777), then the Vermont Republic (independent, 1777-1791).
- **Population during period:** The `place_population` tool did not return population figures for Vermont in this date range. Vermont's 1790 federal census (the first after statehood) counted 85,341 inhabitants — the earliest federal figure available.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and small-scale agriculture; timber; some potash production. Communities were newly settled frontier towns throughout most of this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers from southern New England (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island), with smaller numbers of Scots-Irish and German settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (predominant), Baptist, Methodist, and some Presbyterian congregations. The Church of England had minimal presence. Many early communities had no organized congregation at all during the first years of settlement.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754-1763) — the territory was a contested frontier zone; New Hampshire Grants controversy and the Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York authority (1764-1777); Vermont Declaration of Independence (January 15, 1777); Vermont Constitution adopted (July 1777) — the first in North America to prohibit adult slavery; American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), including the Battle of Bennington (1777); border negotiations with New York and Canada throughout the Republic period; admission to the Union March 4, 1791.

## Boundary changes

The jurisdictional history of pre-statehood Vermont is unusually complex and directly determines where records are held:

- **Before 1749:** The territory was sparsely inhabited. French colonial claims overlapped English ones. No English civil jurisdiction created records here.
- **1749-1764:** New Hampshire Colony, under Governor Benning Wentworth, issued grants for more than 100 townships across the territory. Land records from this period are in New Hampshire colonial records.
- **1764:** The British Crown ruled in favor of New York, placing the territory under New York colonial authority. New York refused to recognize the New Hampshire grants and issued competing grants. Two sets of land records — New Hampshire and New York — now cover the same territory for the same years.
- **1777-1791:** The Vermont Republic operated its own government, courts, and land system. Records created under the Republic are held in Vermont archives, not in New York or New Hampshire.
- **1791:** Vermont admitted to the Union. All subsequent records are state records.
- **County formation:** Vermont counties were created by the Vermont Republic beginning in 1778 (Bennington, Chittenden, and others). County formation continued through the early statehood period. Earlier records may exist only at the town level, with no county structure yet in place.

**A geographic note on the New York / New Hampshire dispute:** The competing jurisdictions covered the entire territory of present-day Vermont, not divided sub-regions. Which jurisdiction's records apply to a given ancestor depends on which authority that ancestor recognized and interacted with — not on where within Vermont they lived. Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records for the 1764-1777 period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration did **not** begin until 1857 (state level). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont Genealogy ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) states statewide registration began in 1857. For the entire pre-statehood period (ca. 1750-1791) there is **no civil vital registration at any level**.
- **What exists:** Some town clerk offices began recording vital events informally as early as the 1770s, but survival is uneven. Consult individual town clerk offices directly.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices for surviving town records; Vermont State Archives for compiled/deposited records.
- **Gaps:** Substantial. For most of the pre-statehood period, no systematic vital registration existed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); proprietors' records; town meeting minutes; probate records; gravestone inscriptions; 19th-century town histories that reprint earlier data.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common in early New England settlements), Baptist, Methodist, some Presbyterian. Many early towns had no organized congregation; circuit-riding ministers served some areas.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (where congregations were established) membership rolls and disciplinary proceedings.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; denominational archives (e.g., Congregational records are often at local historical societies or state depositories); Vermont Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm (check the FamilySearch Catalog for specific towns).
- **Language:** English.
- **Digitization level:** Varies widely by congregation. Many remain physical only or on microfilm. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) should be checked for each specific town — the topic-specific wiki pages (Vermont_Church_Records) returned only generic content in this survey and could not confirm specific digitized collections.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census that includes Vermont is **1790** — taken shortly before and after formal statehood (March 4, 1791). This is the only federal enumeration for the pre-statehood period and is the closest systematic population record available. It is available online and indexed.
- **State/colonial enumeration:** No Vermont colonial census is known. The Vermont Republic did not conduct a formal census.
- **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** This is the most significant pre-statehood population-type document. Prepared under New York colonial authority, it lists approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants. It is not a census — it does not list families or household members — but it places named individuals in specific townships at a specific date and is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory. Confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)).
- **Tax lists:** The Vermont Republic levied taxes; town-level tax lists from the Republic period survive in some towns and function as the best substitute for a census in the 1777-1791 window.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship records, court minutes.
- **Date range:** Vermont probate districts were established by the Vermont Republic beginning in 1778. Earlier probate (pre-1778) would have been handled under New York or New Hampshire colonial courts if at all.
- **Where held:** Vermont probate district courts (which align roughly with counties); Vermont State Archives holds older records. The FamilySearch Catalog should be checked for specific probate districts.
- **Digitization level:** Varies. The Vermont_Probate_Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; specific collection details could not be confirmed from tool results.
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** For the pre-statehood period, many settlers died without formal wills (intestate), and estate administration was informal or nonexistent. When a probate record exists, it is a significant find for establishing family relationships.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Vermont is a state-land state. Land was granted by the government of New Hampshire (1749-1764), then disputed by New York (1764-1777), then regranted or confirmed by the Vermont Republic (1777-1791). Do **not** use the federal BLM-GLO patent database for Vermont — federal public-domain land laws did not apply here.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Three overlapping authorities:
  - New Hampshire colonial government (Wentworth grants, 1749-1764): records at New Hampshire State Archives, Concord, NH.
  - New York colonial government (competing grants, 1764-1777): records at New York State Archives, Albany, NY.
  - Vermont Republic / State of Vermont (confirmations and new grants, 1777 onward): records at Vermont State Archives and individual town land offices.
- **Types:** Township grants (proprietors' records), deeds, surveys, tax records, and bounty land grants to Revolutionary War veterans.
- **Date range:** New Hampshire grants begin 1749. Town-level deed recording began as towns organized (typically within a few years of settlement, so 1760s-1770s for the earliest towns).
- **Where held:** Town land records are held at town clerk offices (Vermont towns record deeds locally, not at the county level). State-level grant records are at the Vermont State Archives. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) emphasizes that the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is a key pre-statehood land document.
- **Digitization level:** The Vermont_Land_and_Property wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; specific collection details could not be confirmed from tool results.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754-1763) — Vermont territory was a military frontier, and men from neighboring colonies served here; American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), including the Green Mountain Boys (Vermont's own militia) and Continental Army service.
- **Record types:**
  - Revolutionary War service records: at NARA (National Archives), online via Fold3.
  - Revolutionary War pension files: at NARA, online via Fold3 and Ancestry. These often contain the most detailed biographical information of any pre-statehood source — depositions name spouses, children, neighbors, and describe life events in detail.
  - Bounty land warrants: issued to veterans after the war; relevant land records follow.
  - Vermont militia records: separate from Continental Army records; held at the Vermont State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal records); Vermont State Archives (state militia); Fold3 and Ancestry (digitized online).
- **Digitization level:** Federal service records and pension files are largely indexed and available as images via Fold3 (subscription) and partially via FamilySearch. Vermont militia records have variable digitization.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Town burying grounds (most Vermont towns established a public cemetery as part of original settlement). Many small family plots on farmsteads.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) has coverage for Vermont cemeteries, including transcriptions of pre-statehood gravestones. Coverage is volunteer-driven and not comprehensive.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare; most burial information comes from gravestone transcriptions.
- **Note:** Gravestones from the 1770s-1790s survive in many Vermont towns and may be the only direct evidence of birth and death dates for this period.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspaper, the Vermont Gazette (later Spooner's Vermont Journal), began publication in 1781 in Westminster. A small number of other papers appeared in the 1780s.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; Newspapers.com ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) has some holdings; state library microfilm collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, land sale announcements, and public notices appear from the early 1780s onward. Coverage before 1781 is a gap — no Vermont newspapers existed.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Boston, MA and Providence, RI were the nearest ports for settlers arriving from Europe, though most pre-statehood Vermont settlers migrated overland from southern New England rather than directly from overseas.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for overseas arrivals (at NARA and online via Ancestry/FamilySearch); naturalization records (not applicable for most settlers, who were already British subjects before the Revolution; post-Revolution naturalization records begin in Vermont courts after 1791).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants. For the pre-statehood period, most Vermont ancestors arrived overland from Massachusetts or Connecticut rather than by sea — do not limit the search to port records. Check Massachusetts and Connecticut records for the origin community.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal); state archives of origin states.

### Tax records

- **Types:** The Vermont Republic levied property and poll taxes from 1778 onward. Town-level tax lists are the primary surviving record.
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic tax records begin 1778. Pre-1778 tax records for the territory would be under New York or New Hampshire colonial authority.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for census records during the 1778-1790 gap before the first federal census. A man listed on the tax roll is placed in a specific town in a specific year.

### Proprietors' records

- **What they are:** When a township was granted (by New Hampshire or Vermont), the original grantees ("proprietors") organized themselves and kept records of their meetings, lot divisions, and membership. These are distinct from town records and may predate formal town organization.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; individual town archives; some have been transcribed in 19th-century town histories.
- **Value:** Proprietors' records name the original settlers of a town and document lot assignments. They are often the first record placing a family in a specific Vermont location.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Vermont towns governed themselves through town meetings from their earliest days. Town meeting minutes record who was present, who held office, and what business was transacted — naming ordinary residents who appear in no other record.
- **Town histories:** 19th-century town histories (most published 1860-1900) routinely reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) specifically notes this. These are frequently the only surviving transcription of pre-statehood records.
- **Family bibles:** Bible records noting births, marriages, and deaths were kept by many New England families. These circulate in published genealogical society volumes and are held by historical societies and private families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census (indexed); some church record microfilm via Catalog; generic vital records category page | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (1790); Revolutionary War pension and service records; some Vermont town histories | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions for Vermont towns | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some Vermont newspapers from 1781 onward | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military and pension records; 1790 census | Free online via affiliated databases |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `external_links_search` tool returned 6 results for Vermont in the 1750-1791 date range, but these were all generic national-level resources (census, vital records category, cemetery, newspapers, military, NARA) with no Vermont-specific curated collections. The `totalForPlace` was 6, matching `results.length`, so this represents the complete FamilySearch-curated external link set for Vermont in this period — it is sparse. The `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not called in this survey due to the place resolution issues; researchers should search the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Vermont-specific holdings.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Land records, Vermont Republic records, probate district records, legislative records, militia records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier, VT) | Town histories, genealogical collections, newspapers, church records, manuscripts | In-person; some digitized holdings |
| Town clerk offices (each Vermont town) | Deeds, proprietors' records, vital records (from when recording began), tax lists, town meeting minutes | In-person or mail request to each town |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire Grants records, Wentworth grant documents (1749-1764) | In-person; some online |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial land records covering the New Hampshire Grants territory (1764-1777) | In-person; some online |
| NARA (Washington, DC / regional) | 1790 federal census; Revolutionary War service and pension records | In-person; online via affiliated databases |
| Denominational archives | Church records by denomination | Varies by denomination |

## Records NOT online

- **Most pre-statehood town clerk records** (vital events informally recorded before 1791): held at individual town clerk offices; not systematically digitized.
- **Vermont Republic tax lists and town meeting minutes:** held at town offices and Vermont State Archives; digitization is limited.
- **Proprietors' records** for most townships: held in town archives or Vermont State Archives; not digitized except where incorporated into published town histories.
- **New Hampshire colonial grant records** (Wentworth grants, 1749-1764): at New Hampshire State Archives; some available on microfilm but not comprehensively online.
- **New York colonial land records** covering the disputed territory (1764-1777): at New York State Archives; not comprehensively online.
- **Local church records** for most early congregations: at church offices, denominational archives, or Vermont Historical Society; digitization varies.
- **Vermont militia records**: at Vermont State Archives; not comprehensively online.

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fires or mass record destructions for Vermont's pre-statehood period were confirmed in the tool results for this survey. However:

- The general fragility of record-keeping on a settlement frontier means many records were simply never created or were lost to normal attrition (fires in private homes, water damage, etc.).
- The contested jurisdictional situation (New Hampshire vs. New York vs. Vermont Republic) means some records were created under an authority that was later repudiated, and those records may have been neglected or lost as a result.
- Researchers should not interpret the absence of a record online as evidence the record does not exist — for this period, absence online is the norm, not the exception.

## Research tips

- **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the starting point for any pre-statehood ancestor.** It lists approximately 1,800 grantees by name, township, grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. It is the earliest systematic name list for the territory. Confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Town-level research is essential.** Vermont's primary record-keeping unit is the town, not the county. Identify the specific town of residence before searching; a county-level search alone will miss most records.
- **Work backward from the 1790 census.** The 1790 federal census is the first enumeration of the territory and the most accessible indexed source. Use it to confirm location, then work backward using land, church, tax, and proprietors' records.
- **Check 19th-century town histories.** The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) specifically notes that town histories published 1860-1900 frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. These are a primary research tool, not just background reading.
- **Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records for the 1764-1777 period.** Both jurisdictions claimed authority and both created records. An ancestor who held land under a New Hampshire grant may appear in New Hampshire records even though they lived in what is now Vermont, and a competing claimant may appear in New York records.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are often the most detailed pre-statehood biographical source.** Veteran depositions name family members, describe life events, and were given decades after the war — they routinely describe the 1770s-1790s in detail. Search via Fold3 ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)) and the pension index at NARA.
- **Gravestones survive.** Vermont's pre-statehood burying grounds are well preserved in many towns. Gravestone transcriptions on Find A Grave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) may provide birth, death, and sometimes spousal information that appears nowhere else.
- **Vermont naming customs:** The Vermont_Naming_Customs wiki page returned only generic content in this survey. New England naming patterns (naming children after parents and grandparents, alternating maternal and paternal family names) were prevalent; be alert to collateral relatives who share given names with your subject.
- **Consider the origin community.** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers came from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island. When records are sparse in Vermont, look for the family in the town of origin in the sending state — church records, land records, and vital records there may document the family before migration.
- **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** Vermont borders New Hampshire to the east (Connecticut River), New York to the west (Lake Champlain and the Taconic highlands), Massachusetts to the south, and Canada (Quebec) to the north. Families near any of these borders may have generated records on both sides. The county-level neighboring jurisdictions were not listed in tool results for this survey, so researchers should check records in Cheshire and Sullivan Counties (NH) along the Connecticut River border, Rensselaer, Washington, and Clinton Counties (NY) along the western border, and Franklin County (MA) along the southern border.
